Clarification of the peruta's value as one-eighth of an Italian issar.
She releases herself by a bill of divorce or by the husband's death.

Betrothal makes the woman forbidden to all like consecrated property, hence the term.

If so, the verses and the mishnayot contradict each other on the gender of derekh.

The masculine derekh in Deuteronomy concerns war, which is a man's way, so it is masculine there.

The feminine form fits a woman's case, and the masculine fits a man's examination; a woman is impure even by force.
Why does the mishna teach 'three ways' in the masculine-feminine form instead of 'matters' or 'three'?
The mishna wants to include intercourse, which the Torah calls a way.
Proverbs 30:19-20 calls the way of a man with a woman a way, supporting intercourse as a derekh.

Because intercourse had to be included, the mishna used 'way' for the other modes too.

In accordance with whose opinion is this mishna, which uses the term derekh?

A baraita quotes Rabbi Shimon on why the verse says 'a man takes a woman' using the term derekh.
The Torah wrote 'a man takes a woman' because pursuing is a man's way, not a woman's.
It is not a woman's way to pursue a man.
A parable of a man who lost an object: the owner seeks it, illustrating that the man pursues.
A mishna says examining a zav uses seven ways; why not teach matters instead?
The mishna teaches that excessive eating and excessive drinking each can lead to zava.
Why does the etrog mishna say three ways rather than matters?

Why not also say 'matter' in the latter clause?

Perhaps a married woman can be released by halitza after all.
Deuteronomy 24:3 'a scroll of severance' shows only a written document severs the marriage.
The mishna says a woman is acquired with money; from where is that derived?

Rav, as transmitted by Rav Yehuda, gives the reason.

The other master who receives money is the father.

Suggested derivations of betrothal money from vows or fines, rejected because monetary law is not derived from ritual or penal cases.
Suggested derivation from the compensation for a violated young woman's humiliation.

A Nedarim mishna: a betrothed young woman's vows are annulled by her father and husband together.
Does the verse 'then she shall go out for nothing' serve only to show money goes to another master?
A baraita reads 'for nothing' as adulthood and 'without money' as youth, so the verse is needed for both.
If so, Ravina asks, the verse could have been spelled without the yod.
The full spelling 'ein kasef' teaches that money goes to another master, namely the father.
From where do we know the verse is interpreted this way?

But grandchildren were already derived from the word zar'ah, so that derivation is redundant.
A verse was needed not for grandchildren, which follow by principle, but for children of flawed lineage.
How does the tanna know to expound the yod in this way?
The yod is absent in 'me'en' for Balaam and for yavam in other verses, showing it is written as an exposition.
The yod in 'ein' is superfluous and is there only for an exposition.
Two verses are needed: one for the betrothal money, one for earnings, since each cannot be derived from the other.
A baraita: 'for nothing' means adulthood, and 'without money' means youth.
Why would the verse write 'youth' if she left at puberty anyway?
Rabba says one phrase teaches about the other, since the adulthood case is a lesser novelty.
A baraita on teruma: a tenant is a permanently acquired slave, a hired worker a six-year slave.
Why is 'hired worker' needed; the verse could have said only 'tenant' with a kal vachomer.
Reply: the tenant alone would be read as six-year servants, so the hired worker word clarifies the tenant case.
Abaye objects that the tenant and hired worker are two separate bodies, so the cases are not comparable.
Principle: even an a fortiori derivable matter may be written explicitly by the verse.
Here the woman is one body, so once she leaves at youth, why would she still be in servitude as an adult?
Abaye: the verse concerns only an adult ailonit who never becomes a young woman.
Without the verse one might think a woman who skips youth never leaves servitude.
The verse teaches that she does leave even when reaching adulthood directly.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects: a kal vachomer shows an ailonit leaves at adulthood, making the verse unnecessary.

One might think a sale is valid only if the woman shows signs of youth, which the verse must rule out.

Refutation: a maidservant can be redeemed by money, but this woman cannot be divorced by money.
With the inference rejected, the verse 'when a man takes' is the source for betrothal by money.

ranges.en: A fortiori argument: money betroths though it cannot divorce, so a document, which divorces, should also be able to betroth.
Objection: money redeems consecrated property and second tithe, while a document does not, so the analogy fails.
A verse about redeeming with money is cited, then the juxtaposition of leaving and becoming in Deuteronomy links betrothal to divorce modes.
Reverse the juxtaposition: if becoming is done with money, then leaving should also be done with money.
Abaye objects that symmetry would let the roles of advocate and prosecutor swap, which is improper for a single mode.
Reply: each document's wording is distinct for its purpose, while coins are interchangeable, so documents cannot serve both roles.
Rava states that a woman is divorced only through writing, not through money.
The verse says he writes her a scroll, indicating divorce requires writing and not money.
Counter-suggestion: perhaps writing divorces but does not betroth, reversing the derivation.
Reply: the juxtaposition of leaving and becoming in the verse shows that betrothal can also be done through writing.
Why read the verses this way? The reverse reading is equally plausible, so what justifies this interpretation?
How does Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derive that money cannot divorce, given that he reads the verse differently?
The phrase scroll of severance teaches that only a written document severs the marriage, and nothing else does.
What do the Rabbis do with the phrase scroll of severance, since they reject that exposition?
A baraita: a conditional divorce with an indefinite condition does not sever, while a thirty-day condition does, derived from the word severance.
Where does Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derive that a divorce must completely sever the marriage?
The Rabbis do not derive any distinction from the form keritut versus karet.
Why not derive one betrothal mode from the other two, as the baraita does not?
Deriving writing-based betrothal from money and intercourse fails, since those modes apply more broadly and bring greater benefit.
Deriving intercourse-based betrothal from the others fails, since money and writing have broader application.
Deriving money-based betrothal from the others fails, since those modes apply against the woman's will and money also does.
Objection: money does act against a woman's will in the case of a Hebrew maidservant, but this is refuted, as no marriage case parallels it.
Rav Huna holds that a wedding canopy effects acquisition, by a fortiori reasoning from money and teruma.
Does betrothal money not enable a woman to eat teruma? This challenges Rav Huna's premise.
Ulla cites a verse showing that by Torah law a priest's betrothed daughter may eat teruma, since she is his acquired money.
What is the reason the Sages said she may not eat teruma after betrothal?
A rabbinic decree: lest her father's household pour her teruma wine for her siblings, who may not drink it.
Rather, Rav Huna's argument is restated: money, which does not complete acquisition, still betroths, so the canopy should betroth as well.

ranges.en: A fortiori: money redeems consecrated property and tithes, so a wedding canopy, which completes marriage, should acquire the woman for betrothal.

Reply: money shows that a mode can betroth without acquiring a yevama, so the canopy argument still stands.
Restating the derivation: money, intercourse and the canopy share the feature of generally effecting acquisition and betrothal.
Objection: money and intercourse share great benefit, which a document lacks, so this common denominator is not a valid basis.
Reply: a document betroths though it gives no pleasure, while money and intercourse do not release a woman, so the features are not decisive.
Restating the a fortiori from common features: the canopy generally effects acquisition and should therefore effect betrothal here too.
Objection: all three modes act against a woman's will in certain cases, while a canopy works only with her consent.
Rav Huna answers that no marriage case exists where money acquires a woman against her will, so the derivation stands.
Rava offers two refutations: the mishna lists only three modes, and a canopy completes marriage only after betrothal.
Abaye responds that a tanna teaches only what is explicit in the Torah, so the mishna's list does not bar the canopy.
Abaye argues that Rav Huna incorporates the completion point: the canopy is more powerful than money, so it should betroth.
A baraita on betrothal by money: the man giving money with the formula betroths, while the woman giving and speaking does not.
Rav Pappa objects that the baraita contradicts itself, since its two clauses imply opposite inferences about the woman's giving.
Reply: the first clause is exact and can be relied upon, while the latter clause was stated without precision.
Rather, the baraita means: his giving and speaking betroths, hers does not, and mixed cases are uncertain under rabbinic law.
Shmuel rules that formulas defining the woman in relation to the man betroth or divorce, while reversed formulas create no concern.
Rav Pappa asks whether Shmuel holds that ambiguous intimations count as unambiguous ones, given that his cases omit 'to me'.
Rav Pappa cites a mishna about the vow 'I will be' to show that ambiguous speech is not treated as explicit.
Reply: Shmuel refers to a case where the man said the full formula, so the mishna's ambiguity does not apply.

ranges.en: Shmuel's teaching explained: the verses say the man takes or sends the woman, not himself, so these phrases do not betroth.

The tanna received the formulas as two sets of three and preserved them in that form.

Resolving one dilemma: a baraita says 'my taken one' betroths, since the verse reads when a man takes a woman.

In what case does the man speak? If out of context, how does she know his meaning; if in context, why is money needed?
A mishna: if a man discusses divorce or betrothal and hands over the document or money without clarifying, Rabbi Yosei deems it sufficient.
The Sages explain: the cases concern discussion of divorce or betrothal, and the words were said when he gave her something.
Did he speak these words for betrothal, or for hiring her as a worker? The dilemma is left unresolved.
Shmuel rules that unexplained delivery suffices if the discussion concerned the same matter, and tannaitic disputes on this are reported.
If they changed topic, how does she know his meaning, since the words alone are ambiguous?
Abaye: they moved within the same general topic, not to an entirely different one, so his intent was clear.
Rav Huna cites Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yeimar asks Rav Ashi: does Shmuel's rule that the unlearned may not judge such cases apply even to one who never heard Rav Huna's teaching?
Rav Ashi affirms: such a person is deemed to lack the knowledge needed for these cases.
Shmuel's rule extends to divorce: phrases such as you are sent away or divorced, given with a bill, effect divorce.

ranges.en: A woman who commits herself through a third party's loan is betrothed, derived from a guarantor who commits himself even without benefit.
Derivation from the emancipation of a Canaanite slave: a third party acquires the woman by paying, losing nothing of his own.
Combining the guarantor and slave cases: if a woman says give money to a man and I will be betrothed to him, she is betrothed.
Objection: the guarantor loses money while the third party does not, so the cases differ.
Reply: the emancipation of a slave shows one can acquire without losing one's own money, so the derivation holds.
Objection: in the slave case the transferor acquires, while the woman transfers herself and acquires nothing.
Reply: the guarantor case proves it, since the guarantor commits himself without benefit, as the woman does.
Rava asks: if a woman says here are one hundred dinars and I will be betrothed to you, is she betrothed?
Mar Zutra, in the name of Rav Pappa, rules that she is betrothed.
Rav Ashi objects that a mishna teaches the opposite: guaranteed property cannot be acquired by means of non-guaranteed property.
Mar Zutra replies that the case concerns an important man whose acceptance of her gift gives her benefit, so she transfers herself.
This is also stated in Rava's name: monetary acquisitions follow the same modes, and both betrothal and money must be taught.
If only betrothal were taught, one might limit it since women desire any husband; if only money, one might limit it since claims can be waived.
Rava rules: if a man says be betrothed to half of me, she is betrothed; if half of you is betrothed to me, she is not.
Abaye asks why the two cases differ, and whether the verse's wording about a woman and a man explains it.

A Tosefta on an animal: if one says its leg is a burnt offering, the whole animal becomes one.
Mar Zutra adds: even by the view that the whole is not offered, the rule applies where the life depends on the consecrated part.
The Gemara rejects the comparison: an animal lacks intellect, while the woman's own consent is needed.

ranges.en: Conclusion drawn from the preceding ruling: living animals can be permanently deferred, deferral applies from the outset, and it extends to monetary value.

If speech is counted as one act, does saying one peruta and another peruta divide the statement, or is everything done that day one act?
If that day counts as one act, does saying one half-peruta today and another tomorrow divide the statement, or does the betrothal begin now?
If he says your two halves are betrothed with one peruta, was it said at one time so it is valid, or are women not betrothed in halves at all?

Rabba holds that silk garments need no appraisal, while Rav Yosef requires it; all agree no appraisal is needed if any amount is named.
If the garments are worth fifty as he said, Rabba requires no appraisal, while Rav Yosef requires it since the woman cannot judge value.

ranges.en: Conclusion: an item worth money must have a clearly defined value, just as money does.

Rabba's reply, for whom appraisal is not needed: the baraita refers to symbolic exchange, which cannot acquire a slave.

Rejected: the cloak is not worth five sela, but the priest agreed to value it at five sela, as Rav Kahana did.
Rav Ashi: this works only for a great man such as Rav Kahana who needs a head covering; for others it does not.

Objection from a baraita: if one of them retracts while counting, even at the last dinar, the betrothal is not complete until all is paid.
Reply: the case is with this one hundred dinars, where the full sum is the betrothal money, so the baraita is consistent.
The baraita's latter clause: if the sum is short or includes copper she is not betrothed; a flawed dinar must be exchanged.
Reply: the latter clause explains the first, so both refer to this one hundred dinars, and either may retract before the last dinar.

Rejected: the latter clause was stated to prevent misreading the first clause, not to teach a new ruling, so the inference is inconclusive.
Rav Ashi: counting is different, since she has the whole sum in mind, so both may retract until he finishes counting.
If she knows the dinar is copper, she accepted it knowingly and cannot retract; what situation is the baraita describing?
He gave her the copper dinar at night when she could not see it, or it was mixed among other coins unnoticed.
What about a flawed dinar in the baraita? If it cannot be spent, it is like copper, since it lacks full value.
Rav Pappa: the flawed dinar can be spent only with difficulty, meaning one can find someone to accept it under strain.
Rava, citing Rav Naḥman: if a man betroths a woman with one hundred dinars but gives collateral instead, she is not betrothed.

ranges.en: No hundred dinars were given and the collateral is merely security, so nothing was transferred and she is not betrothed.

Reply: that case involves collateral belonging to others, following the view of Rabbi Yitzḥak.
