ranges.en: A slave is freed when his master cuts off an extra finger on his hand.
Rav Huna limits this ruling to an extra finger that lines up with the others on the back of the hand.
Narrative: Rav Hisda tells Rav Hamnuna to ostracize the Elders of Nezonya for skipping his lecture.
Rav Hamnuna asks what the reason was for the rabbis not attending.
The Elders explain they stayed away because Rav Hisda left their question unresolved.
Rav Hamnuna retorts that they never asked him anything he failed to resolve, and invites their question.
The Elders pose the dilemma whether castrated testicles count as an exposed blemish that frees a slave.
Narrative: Hamnuna cannot answer, and the Elders jokingly mock his name, renaming him Karnuna.
Narrative: Hamnuna reports the episode to Rav Hisda, who responds.
Rav Hisda cites a mishna listing the twenty-four extremities that are exempt from leprous impurity.
The mishna's list of the twenty-four extremities, including fingers, toes, ears, nose, penis and female nipples.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that male nipples are also included among the extremities.
A baraita states that a slave is freed for injuries to all these extremities.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds that castration by the master also frees the slave.
Ben Azzai adds that severing the tongue also frees the slave.
The Gemara asks what kind of castration Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi means.
If it means the penis, it repeats the mishna, so it must mean the testicles, which resolves the dilemma.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi includes castration but not the tongue, unlike ben Azzai.
The Gemara asks whether, on this view, the tongue is not considered an exposed organ.
A baraita on sprinkling the red heifer water on a mouth contradicts the claim that the tongue is not exposed.
The Gemara proposes that the baraita refers to water sprinkled on the tongue.
No, it refers to water sprinkled on the lips, which are exposed.
If so, purity is obvious; the Gemara asks why the case needs to be taught.
It is taught in case one thinks the lips may be sealed shut and thus concealed.
Another baraita says sprinkling on the tongue is valid according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, contradicting the view.
A baraita on blemishes says removing most of the tongue is a disqualifying blemish for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
The baraita is reread so that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi includes castration and ben Azzai alone includes the tongue.
The Gemara asks why ben Azzai's ruling appears second if he is adding to the first tanna.
The tanna first learned Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view and then ben Azzai's, and a mishna cannot be reordered.
Ulla says all agree the tongue is exposed for ritual impurity conveyed by touching a creeping animal.
The Gemara asks for the reason.
The verse Leviticus 15:5 says whoever touches, which covers touching with the tongue.
The tongue can touch, so the Torah's wording applies to it.
All agree the tongue is concealed for immersion, so it need not be exposed to the water.
The Gemara asks the reason.
The verse Leviticus 15:13 says he shall bathe his flesh in water.
Just as his flesh is external, all immersion applies only to what is external.
The disagreement concerns only sprinkling: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi likens it to impurity, the Rabbis to immersion.
Both sides derive their positions from the same verse about sprinkling.
The verse Numbers 19:19 says the pure person shall sprinkle upon the impure person.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reads the phrase as sprinkling on the third and seventh days, linking it to impurity.
The Rabbis read the phrase as cleansing on the seventh day, linking it to immersion.
The Gemara asks whether the Rabbis too should compare sprinkling to impurity.
Purification should be derived from purification, so sprinkling is compared to immersion.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cannot compare sprinkling to immersion.
The phrase and he shall wash his clothes starts a new clause, so sprinkling is compared to impurity.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi really holds that the tongue is concealed for immersion.
An anecdote about a maidservant who had a bone between her teeth shows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required re-immersion.
The water need not enter the mouth, but the mouth must be a place fit for water to enter.
Rabbi Zeira's principle about meal-offerings shows that unfit spaces require the rule, supporting this distinction.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara introduces the parallel with a tanna dispute about testicles.
Leviticus 22:24 lists bruised, crushed, torn and cut animals as unfit, which the Gemara reads as referring to testicles.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that all these blemishes refer to the testicles.
Could Rabbi Yehuda mean the blemishes apply only to the testicles and not to the penis?
Rather, Rabbi Yehuda means the blemishes apply to the testicles as well as the penis.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that all the blemishes apply only to the penis.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: bruising and crushing apply to testicles, but breaking and cutting apply only to the penis.
Mishna: a large domesticated animal is acquired by passing, and a small one by lifting, per Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer.
The Rabbis hold that a small animal may also be acquired by pulling, with no need to lift it.
Rav taught in Kimhonya that a large domesticated animal is acquired by pulling.
Narrative: Shmuel encounters Rav's students.
Shmuel asks whether Rav really said pulling, since the mishna teaches passing and he heard Rav say passing.
Shmuel notes that Rav also said acquisition is by passing.
Rav's students reply that Rav retracted and adopted the earlier view.
A baraita states that the Rabbis hold both kinds are acquired by pulling, which supports Rav's retracted view.
Rabbi Shimon holds that both kinds are acquired by lifting.
Rav Yosef objects: by Rabbi Shimon's view, how could an elephant be acquired, since it cannot be lifted?
Abaye replies that an elephant can be acquired by symbolic exchange or by renting the ground it stands on.
Rabbi Zeira offers another method: placing four vessels under the elephant's feet to acquire it.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Zeira's case proves that buyer's vessels in the seller's domain effect acquisition.
No, the case is one where the vessels lie in an alley, neither public nor private domain.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An alternative method: a movable elephant is lifted when it stands on bundles of vines the buyer leads it to.
Mishna: property with a guarantee is acquired by money, document or possession.
Mishna: property without a guarantee is acquired only by pulling.
Mishna: property without a guarantee is acquired together with guaranteed property by money, document or possession.
Mishna: the defendant must swear on guaranteed property in a dispute involving both kinds.
The Gemara asks how we know that land is acquired by money.
Hezekiah cites Jeremiah 32:44 saying fields shall be acquired for money.
Could the verse mean acquisition requires a document, since it says written in the book and sealed?
The verse in fact says they shall acquire first, so money acquires from the outset.
Money acquires; a document is merely evidence.
Rav rules this applies only where documents are not customarily written; where they are, acquisition is not effected.
Narrative: the case of Rav Idi bar Avin selling land, which the Gemara cites as precedent.
Rav Idi declares he acquires by money or by document, and that he may retract only if the sale permits it.
The Gemara asks how we know that acquisition by document applies.
If the verse refers to the document, then it is merely evidence and does not effect acquisition.
Instead, the source is Jeremiah 32:11, which speaks of taking the deed of purchase.
Shmuel rules this applies only to a document of gift; in a sale, nothing is acquired until money is paid.
Rav Hamnuna objects with a case where a document written on paper or pottery transfers a field despite no value.
The objection is resolved: the sale case concerns a seller acting out of distress, and in a gift the wording of sale is used to strengthen it.
The Gemara asks how we know that acquisition by possession applies.
Hezekiah cites Jeremiah 40:10 telling them to return to their cities which they have taken.
The Gemara asks by what means they took possession.
A baraita of the house of Rabbi Yishmael cites Deuteronomy 11:31 showing possession is by sitting on the land.
Property without a guarantee is acquired only by pulling.
The Gemara asks how we know this.
Leviticus 25:14 says when you sell to your neighbor, meaning an item acquired from hand to hand.
Rabbi Yochanan holds money acquires by Torah law, so the rule must be a rabbinic enactment; the Gemara asks what can be said.
The Gemara asks what source supports property without a guarantee.
Hezekiah cites 2 Chronicles 21:3, where their father gave them gifts with fortified cities in Judah.
The Gemara asks whether the property must be communal or not.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva says land is subject to peah and first-fruits.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A creditor may write a prosbol on land and acquire guarantee-less movables along with it.
If movables must be piled on the land, what size of land could be suitable for that?
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna explains that the mishna means a needle stuck into a small plot is acquired with it.
Rav Yosef rejects this, asking why the tanna would teach that a needle is acquired by land.
Rav Ashi defends the view: the needle may have held a pearl of great value acquired through a tiny plot.
Introducing a proof: Rabbi Elazar reports a case.
Narrative: a man in Jerusalem with much movable property gives it away by acquiring a beit sela of land.
If movables must be piled on the land, what use is a beit sela, which is too small?
The beit sela is a large area; its name means it is hard as rock.
Introducing a second proof: Rav Yehuda reports a similar case of a man in Jerusalem who fell ill.
Narrative: the sick man acquires a beit rova of land near Jerusalem to transfer his movables as a gift.
If movables must be piled on land, what use is a single square handbreadth?
The case involved money, which fits a small plot, and so symbolic exchange would not have worked.
But he could have pulled the property, so the case must concern a recipient who was not present.
Could he not have transferred the property through another person by means of an agent?
The giver did not rely on an agent, fearing the third party would take the goods and eat them.
The case shows that without this option the giver had no remedy but to acquire land.
A further proof: an incident with Rabban Gamliel and elders on a ship, where he said tithing must be learned.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: the first tithe is given to Yehoshua, its place rented to him, and another tithe is taught later.
The tithe given to Akiva ben Yosef, with its place rented, suggests that movables must be piled on the land.
The case differs because Rabban Gamliel acted to spare the Sages the trouble of moving the tithes.
Rava bar Yitzchak cites Rav on two kinds of documents, depending on whether the field or the document was conditioned.
Rav Huna adds a third type: a seller who wrote the document first, which the buyer acquires wherever it is.
From this one can learn that movables need not be piled on the land.
A document is different because it is the bridle of the land, so it is acquired by the land.
The Gemara asks why the mishna teaches that guarantee-less property is acquired along with the land, as if the document were no different.
The mishna's wording supports that guarantee-less property is acquired by land without piling.
The Gemara asks whether one must specify that the acquisition is done along with the land.
The baraitot do not teach the expression along with, so it appears it is not required.
On this reasoning, the baraitot should also teach that the seller must say acquire, which they do not.
The resolution: the baraitot omit the requirement, and the conclusion is that land need not be piled but the acquire wording is required.
What is the rule if a field is sold and movables are given as a gift?
The baraita on the tithe to Yehoshua and its place rented to him is brought as support.
What is the rule if a field is given to one person and the movables to another?
The baraita on the poor man's tithe with its place rented is cited as a proof.
What does rented to him mean with regard to the tithe?
Alternatively, Akiva's case differs because the tithe belonged to the poor.
Rava rules that the acquisition is effective only for the money actually paid, proportionally.
A baraita agrees with Rava: the power of money derives from the document, and money redeems consecrated items and second tithe.
The baraita continues: a document carries power that money lacks, and possession is needed for both to acquire a Hebrew slave.
The baraita concludes that possession of one of ten fields sold in ten regions acquires all of them.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's qualification: the acquisition applies only when the buyer paid for all the land; otherwise he acquires only the land matching his payment.
The baraita supports Shmuel, who holds that taking possession of one of ten fields sold in ten countries acquires all of them.
Rav Aha bar Rav Ika offers a proof: ten animals on one bridle given to him, with acquire said, are all acquired.
A Sage objects that the cases differ, since the bridle is in the buyer's hand there but not with the ten fields.
Another version of Rav Aha's argument holds that possession of one field does not acquire all, since acquiring one animal does not acquire the rest.
The cases differ: the animals are separate entities, but the earth is one mass, so acquiring one plot acquires the rest.
The mishna teaches that a partial admission on movables binds the land so the defendant must swear about it too.
Ulla asks where in the Torah the extension of an oath is derived.
Numbers 5:22 is cited about the sota, whose double amen shows an oath extended to other claims.
The Gemara asks what the case of a betrothed sota looks like.
If she secluded herself while betrothed and drank while married, the mishna says betrothed women do not drink, which contradicts this.
Rather, she was warned and secluded herself while betrothed, and only the drinking happened after marriage.
Does the water test a betrothed woman at all, given the verse that the man must be clear from iniquity?
Rather, it is clear that the oath is administered by extension, covering her conduct during the betrothal.
The Gemara asks from where we know that a sota has a monetary dimension.
A baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael uses an a fortiori argument from the sota.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori: if money claimable by one witness can have its oath extended, then a sota's oath can be extended too.
The Gemara asks where we learn that extension applies to uncertain claims, not only certain ones.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: the Torah makes uncertainty like certainty for both internal and external oaths.
The Gemara asks how far the extension of an oath reaches.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, rules a plaintiff may make the defendant swear that he is not the plaintiff's Canaanite slave.
The Gemara objects that the court would ostracize someone who calls another a slave.
A baraita sets out the penalties for insults: ostracism for calling someone a slave, forty lashes for mamzer, and harassment for wicked.
Rava rules a plaintiff may extend an oath by demanding the defendant swear he was not sold to him as a Hebrew slave.
The Gemara asks whether this is novel, since it is a monetary claim.
Rava follows his own view that a Hebrew slave is acquired by his master in his person, so the claim concerns ownership.
The Gemara asks whether this is like a land claim, where the mishna already allows an extended oath.
The ruling is needed because a land sale could be private, but a slave sale would be public, so the claim might seem implausible.
Mishna: in a barter, once one party acquires the item he receives, he bears the loss of the item he gave.
The Gemara asks whether the item given in exchange refers to a coin, which cannot effect acquisition.
Rav Yehuda explains the mishna refers to items that can be appraised relative to another item, excluding coins.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's wording is precise: its example uses animals, so the mishna concerns exchange of items rather than coins.
The Gemara asks what the mishna's example means if a coin itself effects exchange.
The reading: produce as well as coins can effect exchange, as with exchanging the meat of an ox for a cow.
If produce effects exchange (Rav Sheshet) that works, but on Rav Nachman's view produce does not, what can be said?
On Rav Nachman's view the mishna concerns money alone, forming an exchange-like transaction through a forgiven debt.
Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds money acquires by Torah law; pulling was decreed lest the seller claim the goods burned.
The decree applied only to common cases, while the mishna's example is rare, so no decree applies there.
How does the mishna fit Reish Lakish, who holds pulling is explicit in the Torah?
It works if Reish Lakish holds with Rav Sheshet, who says produce effects exchange.
But if he holds with Rav Nachman, that produce does not effect exchange, how does he explain the mishna?
Perforce Reish Lakish holds with Rav Sheshet.
Mishna: the Temple treasury acquires by paying money, a commoner by possession, and a vow to Heaven acts as transfer to a commoner.
Baraita: the Temple treasurer acquires by paying coins even at the far end of the world, while a commoner must pull.
Baraita: a declaration to Heaven, such as this ox is a burnt-offering, consecrates it even at the far end of the world, while a commoner must pull.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A commoner who pulled a consecrated item at one hundred but failed to redeem it before the price reached two hundred pays two hundred.
Asks the reason for the rule in the first case.
Cites Leviticus 27:19 to show acquisition from the Temple treasury requires actual transfer of money.
The reverse case: pulled when worth two hundred, not redeemed before it fell to one hundred, pays two hundred.
Asks why the reverse case works this way.
A commoner should not have more power than the Temple treasury, so the treasury cannot suffer a loss.
Redeemed at two hundred, not pulled before the value fell to one hundred, the commoner pays two hundred.
Asks the reason for the redemption case.
Cites Leviticus 27:19 showing redemption of consecrated property is effected with money.
Redeemed at one hundred, not pulled before the value rose to two hundred, what was redeemed stays redeemed and he pays one hundred.
Challenges the rule: the treasury should have no greater power than a commoner, as with a fellow commoner.
A commoner who changes his mind before acquiring is still bound by the curse against breaking one's word.
Mishna: men are obligated in all mitzvot a son owes his father, while women are exempt.
Men and women alike are obligated in all mitzvot a father owes his son.
Men are obligated in time-bound positive mitzvot, while women are exempt.
Men and women alike are obligated in positive mitzvot that are not time-bound.
Men and women alike are obligated in all prohibitions, whether time-bound or not.
Exceptions to the prohibitions, applying only to men: the head and beard corners, and corpse impurity for priests.
Asks what the mishna means by mitzvot of a son toward his father.
Proposed reading: the mitzvot a son must do for his father, which women would be exempt from.
A baraita on honoring parents shows women are obligated too, contradicting the proposed reading.
Rav Yehuda replies that the mishna speaks of mitzvot a father imposes on a son, so women are exempt.
A baraita listing a father's duties to his son supports Rav Yehuda's reading, including teaching a trade.
Asks from where circumcision of a son is derived.
Genesis 21:4 shows Abraham circumcised Isaac, so the father is obligated.
If the father did not circumcise, the court is obligated to do so.
Genesis 17:10 commands circumcision to all males, binding the court.
If the court did not circumcise him, the son is obligated to circumcise himself.
Genesis 17:14 says an uncircumcised male is cut off, establishing the son's own obligation.
Asks from where we know the mother is not obligated to circumcise.
Genesis 21:4 says God commanded him, not her, excluding the mother.
Asks how the circumcision command extends to all generations, not just Abraham's time.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: the word command always signals both immediate and future generational obligation.
Deuteronomy 3:28 and Numbers 15:23 show command applies immediately and for all generations.
Asks from where the obligation to redeem a firstborn son is derived.
Exodus 34:20 says the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem, so the father is obligated.
If the father did not redeem, the son must redeem himself.
Numbers 18:15 uses a repeated verb to show redemption applies even when the father neglects it.
Asks from where we know a mother is not commanded to redeem her son.
The verb tifde read as tippadeh shows who must redeem himself also must redeem others.
Whoever must redeem himself must redeem others; whoever need not redeem himself need not redeem others.
Asks from where we know a woman is not obligated to redeem herself.
The repeated verb tifde shows the same principle that binds the redeemer to others binds the redeemed.
Someone others are commanded to redeem must redeem himself; someone others need not redeem need not redeem himself.
Asks from where we know others are not commanded to redeem a daughter.
Exodus 34:20 specifies sons and not daughters, so daughters are not redeemed by others.
The Sages teach that a father's own redemption takes precedence over redeeming his son.
Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: the son's redemption takes precedence because the father's duty was first on his own father.
Rabbi Yirmeya says everyone agrees with the ruling as stated.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If only five sela exist, the father's own redemption takes precedence over redeeming his son.
Asks the reason the father's own mitzva comes first.
A mitzva that concerns one's own person is preferable to one performed for others.
Defines the dispute: five sela of liened land versus five sela of unencumbered land.
Rabbi Yehuda holds a loan recorded in the Torah binds like a written document, so the liened land can pay for the father's redemption.
The Rabbis hold a Torah loan is not like a document, so the father should redeem himself with the free land.
Baraita: a man redeems his son first, and only afterward goes up to Jerusalem for the Festival.
Rabbi Yehuda: he goes up to Jerusalem first, because the Festival mitzva passes while redemption can wait.
Accepts Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning but asks what the Rabbis' reason is for redeeming the son first.
Exodus 34:20 places redeeming the firstborn before the verse about not appearing before God empty-handed.
Baraita: a man with five sons from five wives must redeem all of them.
The word all in Exodus 34:20 includes every firstborn son.
Asks whether this is not obvious, since the mitzva depends on the opening of the womb.
The derivation is needed to exclude a verbal analogy to inheritance, so every firstborn to his mother is redeemed.
Baraita: a father is obligated to teach his son Torah.
Asks from where this obligation is derived.
Deuteronomy 11:19 says you shall teach them to your sons.
If the father did not teach him, the son is obligated to study on his own.
Asks from where we know a woman is not obligated to teach her son Torah.
The verse read as ulmadtem, to study, links the duty to teach with the duty to study.
Whoever must study must teach; whoever need not study need not teach.
Asks from where we know a woman is not obligated to teach herself.
The verse read as ulmadtem shows the same linkage applies to self-teaching.
Whoever others must teach must teach himself; whoever others need not teach need not teach himself.
Asks from where we know others are not commanded to teach a daughter.
Deuteronomy 11:19 says your sons and not your daughters.
Baraita: if father and son both want to study, the father takes precedence.
Rabbi Yehuda: if the son is diligent and sharp, his study will endure, so the son takes precedence.
Introduces an anecdote about Rav Yaakov, son of Rav Aha bar Yaakov, sent to Abaye to study.
Abaye found the son's studies were not sharp.
Rav Aha said he was the better student, so the son should manage the household while he studied.
Abaye heard Rav Aha was coming, and a demon in the study hall endangered anyone who entered.
Abaye told the townspeople not to lodge Rav Aha, hoping a miracle would occur for him.
Rav Aha spent the night, faced a serpent with seven heads, and killed it with his prayers and bows.
Baraita: one should study Torah before marrying, unless that is impossible, in which case marry first.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, rules that one should marry first and then study Torah.
Rabbi Yochanan says study Torah with burdens on one's neck, that is, while supporting a family.
The amoraim do not disagree: one ruling is for Babylonia and the other for Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Hisda praises Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man.
Rav Huna asks Rav Hamnuna to come to him, and notices he does not cover his head with a cloth.
Rav Huna asks why Rav Hamnuna does not cover his head.
Rav Hamnuna replies that he is unmarried, and unmarried men did not cover their heads.
Rav Huna turns away in rebuke and tells him not to appear before him until he marries.
Rav Huna's view: a man who has not married by age twenty will be in a state of sin.
Asks whether one could really be in a state of sin all his days.
Rather, all his days he will be in a state of sinful thoughts, a habit formed by not marrying young.
Rava and the school of Rabbi Yishmael: until twenty, God waits for a man to marry.
If a man reaches twenty and has not married, God says let his bones rot.
Rav Hisda says he surpasses his peers because he married at sixteen, and would have done better at fourteen.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava advises a father to find his son a wife while he still has authority over him, between about sixteen and twenty-two.
Proverbs 22:6 instructs training a child in the way he should go.
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nehemya disagree on the exact age range the verse refers to, sixteen to twenty-two or eighteen to twenty-four.
Asks how far a man is obligated to teach his son Torah.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says to emulate Zevulun ben Dan, who was taught Bible, Mishna, Talmud, halakhot and aggadot.
A baraita says a father who taught Bible need not teach Mishna, contradicting Shmuel's ruling.
Rava explains the baraita: Bible means the Torah itself, so nothing beyond it is required.
Shmuel's statement is reconciled: emulate Zevulun in his father's teaching, but not in the breadth of subjects taught.
Asks whether one's father's father is obligated to teach him Torah.
A baraita says Deuteronomy 11:19 teaches sons and not sons' sons, challenging the grandfather's obligation.
Asks how the Gemara reconciles this with Deuteronomy 4:9, which mentions sons' sons.
Whoever teaches his son Torah is credited by the verse as though he taught his son's son and all later generations.
The baraita's tanna follows the view of another baraita, which is then cited.
A baraita derives that sons' sons are included in the obligation, and the word sons alone excludes daughters.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: teaching one's son's son is credited as if one received the Torah at Mount Sinai.
Deuteronomy 4:9 and 4:10 are juxtaposed, linking the teaching of grandsons to Horeb, which is Mount Sinai.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba sees Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his child to the synagogue to study.
Rabbi Hiyya asks why the fuss, since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was hurrying without dressing properly.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the verse linking teaching sons to Horeb is not insignificant, so the duty is urgent.
Rabbi Hiyya and Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat breakfast before reviewing Torah with their children.
Rav Safra cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya as the source of an interpretation of the verse.
Deuteronomy 6:7 veshinnantam is read as veshillashtam, meaning study, review and study again in three parts.
A person should divide his years into thirds: Bible, Mishna and Talmud.
Asks how one can divide his life into thirds when no one knows how long life will be.
The division applies to each day, not to the whole span of one's life.
The early Sages were called counters because they counted the letters of the Torah.
The vav in gahon is the midpoint of the letters of a Torah scroll.
The word darosh darash is the midpoint of the words of the Torah.
The verse beginning with and he shall be shaven is the midpoint of the verses in the Torah.
The ayin in ya'ar, from Psalms 80:14, is the midpoint of the letters of Psalms.
The verse in Psalms 78:38 is the midpoint of the verses of Psalms.
Rav Yosef asks which side the vav of gahon belongs to, since it is at the midpoint.
The Sages propose bringing a Torah scroll and counting the letters to resolve the question.
Rabba bar bar Hana's precedent: they did not leave until they brought a scroll and counted the letters.
Those earlier experts knew the plene and defective spellings, while later scholars cannot count precisely.
Rav Yosef asks which side the midpoint verse and he shall be shaven belongs to.
Abaye suggests that even without counting letters, one can bring a scroll and count the verses.
Rav Yosef replies that they are not experts in counting verses either.
Rav Aha bar Adda reports that in Eretz Yisrael Exodus 19:9 is divided into three verses, so verse divisions are uncertain.
The Sages teach the verse count of a Torah scroll, and the counts for Psalms and Chronicles relative to it.
The Sages teach that veshinnantam means Torah should be sharp and ready in one's mouth.
One should answer a question immediately and not stutter, as the verse teaches.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A chain of verses in Proverbs and Psalms compares Torah knowledge to arrows and a full quiver of children who will not be shamed.
Asks what it means that sons and students become enemies in the gate.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba explains that study partners quarrel intensely but end in love, read through Numbers 21:14.
Baraita: the verse about placing these words in your hearts is read as sam tam, a perfect elixir of life.
A parable: a father binds his son's wound with a bandage that heals only while it stays on.
Applying the parable, God created the evil inclination as the wound and Torah as its spice or antidote.
Those who study Torah are not handed over to the evil inclination.
Genesis 4:7 says if you do well, shall it not be lifted up, supporting the claim.
Those who do not study Torah are handed over to the evil inclination.
Genesis 4:7 says sin crouches at the door, showing the danger.
The evil inclination's whole concern is with you, but you can rule over it if you wish.
Baraita: the evil inclination is so hard that even its Creator calls it evil, citing Genesis 8:21.
Rav Yitzhak says the evil inclination renews itself daily, as Genesis 6:5 indicates.
Rabbi Shimon ben Levi says the inclination overpowers a person daily, and God must help him prevail.
A Sage from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: pull the evil inclination into the study hall.
Whether the inclination is stone or iron, Torah study softens or shatters it.
Jeremiah 23:29 compares God's word to fire and a hammer that breaks rock.
Isaiah 55:1 calls all who thirst to the water, showing water is stronger than stone.
Job 14:19 says water wears down stones.
Asks from where we derive that a father must marry off his son.
Jeremiah 29:6 tells parents to take wives for sons and give daughters in marriage.
Asks how a father can fulfill this for a daughter, whose marriage is not in his power.
Jeremiah means the father should give his daughter a dowry and suitable dress so men will want to marry her.
Asks from where we derive that a father must teach his son a trade.
Ecclesiastes 9:9 says enjoy life with the wife you love, cited to link life with marriage or with Torah and a trade.
Just as a father must marry his son off, so must he teach him a trade, and in the Torah reading too.
Some say a father must also teach his son to swim in a river.
Asks what the reason is for teaching a son to swim.
Swimming is necessary for his life, since it could save him.
Rabbi Yehuda: a father who does not teach his son a trade effectively teaches him banditry.
Asks what the difference is between the first tanna and Rabbi Yehuda.
The difference lies in whether teaching business suffices, or a real trade must be taught.
Mishna: men and women are both obligated in all mitzvot of a father toward his son.
Asks what the mishna means by all mitzvot of a father toward his son.
Proposed reading: all mitzvot a father must do for his son, in which women would be obligated.
A baraita says a father must circumcise and redeem his son, but the mother is not obligated, contradicting the proposal.
Rav Yehuda says the mishna means mitzvot a son must perform for his father, in which both men and women are obligated.
A baraita derives from the plural tira'u in Leviticus 19:3 that both a man and a woman are obligated.
Asks what the word man in the verse is then teaching, if both are obligated.
A woman is under her husband's authority and cannot always attend to her parents, so the word man has a purpose; divorce makes them equal.
Exodus 20:12 and Proverbs 3:9 equate honoring parents with honoring God, using the same term honor.
Leviticus 19:3 and Deuteronomy 6:13 equate fearing parents with fearing God.
Exodus 21:17 and Leviticus 24:15 equate cursing or blessing parents with cursing or blessing God, but striking is not comparable.
The equation is logical, since a person's attitude toward parents and God follows from their shared role in creation.
Baraita: a person has three partners in creation, God, father and mother, and God credits parents who are honored.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: it is known before God that a son honors his mother more than his father, because of her role.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: God placed the mother's honor-fear before the father's in Leviticus because a son naturally fears his father more, since the father teaches him Torah.
Baraita: God says He did well not to dwell among people who cause their parents suffering, lest they cause Him suffering too.
Rabbi Yitzhak: one who sins in private pushes away the feet of the Divine Presence, citing Isaiah 66:1.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi forbids walking four cubits with an upright, arrogant posture, and Rav Huna's practice shows reverence for the Divine Presence.
A widow's son asks Rabbi Eliezer which parent to serve first when both ask for water.
Rabbi Eliezer says to set aside the mother's honor and honor the father, since both are obligated to honor him.
Rabbi Yehoshua gives the same answer when the son asks him.
The son asks what the halakha is when a mother is divorced.
Rabbi Yehoshua sarcastically replies that the son is a widow's child, and when divorced both parents receive equal honor.
Ulla the Great expounds a verse at the entrance to the house of the Nasi.
Psalms 138:4 speaks of the words of Your mouth in the plural, which indicates God's commandments.
The nations thought God gave the first commandment only for His own honor, until He said honor your father and mother.
Upon hearing honor your father and mother, the nations conceded the earlier commandments were true.
Rava derives from Psalms 119:160 that the beginning of God's word is true, shown by the end.
The Sages ask Rav Ulla how far one must go to fulfill honoring father and mother.
Rav Ulla points to Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon, who did not wake his sleeping father even for a large profit.
Shmuel reports the same question put to Rabbi Eliezer on how far honoring parents must extend.
Rabbi Eliezer's version: Dama ben Netina refused to disturb his sleeping father for a fortune for the High Priest's ephod.
God rewarded Dama with a red heifer, and he asked only for the money he lost by honoring his father.
Rabbi Hanina reasons a fortiori: if a gentile is rewarded for honoring a parent, one commanded to do so is greater still.
Rav Yosef, who was blind, reasons about whether the blind are exempt from mitzvot, and changes his view after Rabbi Hanina's teaching.
Rav Dimi reports Dama ben Netina endured his mother's abuse among Roman nobles without shaming her.
Avimi, son of Rabbi Abbahu, teaches that a son who feeds his father pheasants is still removed from the World-to-Come if he grinds him at millstones.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Such honoring of parents brings a person to the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Abbahu praises his son Avimi, who ran to open the door for him and answered before he arrived.
Avimi stood over his dozing father with a cup until he woke, and was then rewarded with success in interpreting Psalm 79.
Rav Yaakov bar Avuh asks Abaye how he should act when his parents serve him so lovingly.
Abaye says to accept from the mother but not the father, since a Torah scholar would be disheartened by a son's deference.
Rabbi Tarfon describes how he lifted and helped his mother on and off her bed, and boasts of it in the study hall.
The Sages object that he has not even reached half the honor due, since his mother once threw a purse into the sea before him.
Rav Yosef stood before his mother's approach, and Rabbi Yochanan and Abaye were orphaned from birth.
Objection: Abaye said my mother told me, so he did know his mother.
That mother was actually a foster mother, not his birth mother.
Rav Asi's elderly mother asked for jewelry, a husband, and a man as handsome as him, so he left for Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Asi learned she was following him and came to ask Rabbi Yochanan about leaving the Land.
Asks whether it is permitted to leave Eretz Yisrael for abroad.
Rabbi Yochanan says leaving the Land is forbidden.
Asks whether one may leave to greet his mother.
Rabbi Yochanan says he does not know.
Rav Asi waited, returned, and Rabbi Yochanan blessed him to return in peace, saying nothing more.
Rav Asi asks Rabbi Elazar whether Rabbi Yochanan was angry at him for wanting to leave.
Rabbi Elazar reasons that a blessing for peace shows he was not angry and had given permission.
Rav Asi learned his mother's coffin was arriving, and regretted that he had left the Land.
Baraita: one honors a father in his life, such as by not claiming he sent someone on his own business.
Baraita: after death, one says so-and-so my teacher may I be an atonement for his soul, for twelve months, then May his memory be for a blessing.
Baraita: a Sage lecturing in public must not mention his father or teacher by name, but the disseminator may.
Asks whose father is meant, since a disseminator would otherwise violate the duty to honor his own father.
Rava: it means the name of the Sage's father and teacher, as Mar bar Rav Ashi quoted his father as Rav Ashi.
Baraita: fear of a father means not standing or sitting in his place, and honor means providing food, drink and clothing.
A dilemma is raised before the Sages.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda says food for a father comes from the son's money, Rav Natan bar Oshaya from the father's; the halakha follows the father's money.
Objection from a baraita: honor the father with wealth is read like honoring God with wealth, so the son bears a monetary loss.
A baraita on mutual redemption and feeding of second tithe and poor man's tithe among relatives is brought as proof.
Explanation: the proof works only if the son has already covered his father's basic needs from his own money.
If surplus is at issue, why is one who feeds his father poor man's tithe cursed?
Even so, feeding one's father with charity money is disrespectful.
A baraita: a father may throw his purse into the sea before his son, and the son must not embarrass him.
If the money is the father's, why would the son care about a loss to his own inheritance?
The case is a son who is fit to inherit, so he has reason to be angry.
Rav Huna tore silk garments before his son Rabba to test whether he would become angry.
Objection: testing him might cause the son to sin, violating the prohibition against a stumbling block before the blind.
Tearing clothes violates the prohibition against destroying, so how could Rav Huna do this?
He tore the seam, so the garment could be repaired.
Perhaps the son did not get angry because he saw no real damage.
Rav Huna tore him when the son was already angry for another reason, so he did not notice.
Rav Yehezkel teaches his son Rami that mixed burned and stoned offenders are judged by stoning, per Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Yehuda objects: the majority are stoned, so one should follow the majority rather than the severity argument.
Rav Yehezkel counters: the Rabbis' ruling of burning would then similarly rest on the majority rather than severity.
Rav Yehuda answers: the Rabbis were responding to Rabbi Shimon's reasoning, so the point was about severity.
Shmuel rebukes Rav Yehuda, his son, for speaking so bluntly to his father.
A baraita: if one's father transgresses a Torah matter, he should not say so directly but quote the verse.
Objection that direct quoting causes suffering, so the son should instead say the verse is written in the Torah.
Elazar ben Matya: a son performing a mitzva while his father asks for water sets aside honor and performs the mitzva.
Isi ben Yehuda: if others can perform the mitzva, the son should go and honor his father.
Rav Mattana rules that the halakha follows Isi ben Yehuda.
Rav Hisda: a father who forgoes his honor loses it, but a rabbi who forgoes his honor does not.
Rav Yosef: even a rabbi who forgoes honor loses it, as God did in guiding Israel by day, citing Exodus 13:21.
Rava distinguishes: God owns the world and the Torah, so He may forgo honor; a human rabbi cannot.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a teacher can forgo honor for Torah that is his own.
Rava: once one studies, the Torah becomes his own, as Psalms 1:2 indicates by shifting from the Lord's Torah to his Torah.
Objection: Rava once served drinks at his son's wedding and was angered when two Sages did not rise before him.
Rav Pappa served at his son's celebration, and when a Sage did not stand before him he became angry.
Even when a rabbi forgoes full honor, others must still show some reverence, such as preparing to stand.
Rav Ashi: even per the view that a rabbi's forgone honor is forgone, a Nasi's forgone honor is not forgone.
Objection: at Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding, Rabban Gamliel served drinks while Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup, questioning this.
Rabbi Yehoshua replies that Abraham, greater than Rabban Gamliel, served his guests, citing Genesis 18:8.
Rabbi Tzadok argues that God Himself serves all creatures, so even a Nasi may forgo honor.
Rav Ashi's view is restated: a king's honor is not forgone, since Deuteronomy 17:15 makes his fear binding on the people.
Baraita: the honor of an elder in Leviticus 19:32 refers to a wise man, as in Numbers 11:16.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: an elder is one who has acquired wisdom, read as zeh kanna, citing Proverbs 8:22.
Standing is required only where there is reverence and not from far away.
The honor of standing involves no monetary loss, so one need not spend money to show reverence.
One need not stand in a lavatory or bathhouse, since such places do not show reverence.
One may not close his eyes as if he does not see the elder; fear of God covers hidden matters.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: an elder must not trouble others to honor him; Isi ben Yehuda: any hoary head counts.
Asks what the difference is between the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, since both say an elder is wise.
The difference is a young wise man: the first tanna requires age plus wisdom, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili requires only wisdom.
Asks the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, since the Torah separates hoary head from elder.
The separate terms show that one who is young and wise is also called an elder.
The first tanna juxtaposes elder with fear, so an elder should not trouble others to honor him.
Asks the first tanna's reasoning for limiting the duty to elders who are wise.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verse in Leviticus repeats the elder and hoary head terms, supporting the claim that they are one category.
The Gemara infers that since the verse does not separate the two terms, they refer to one type of person.
Baraita: one might think honor means paying money; the verse teaches standing and reverence involve no monetary loss.
Objection: standing does cause loss, since a pearl-piercer must stop his lucrative work to rise.
Reply: the verses juxtapose standing and reverence, so each excludes actions that cause neglect of work or monetary loss.
Conclusion drawn from the verse: craftsmen may not stand for Torah scholars while they are working.
Objection: are craftsmen then really exempt from standing before scholars? A mishna seems to say otherwise.
Mishna: craftsmen stand before first-fruit bringers and greet them with welcome, showing honor for those performing a mitzva.
Rabbi Yohanan resolves it: craftsmen stood for first-fruit bringers but not for Torah scholars.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin: see how beloved a mitzva is when performed at its proper time.
Support: craftsmen stood for those bringing first fruits but not for Torah scholars.
Gemara: that case is special, since first-fruit bringers must be honored or they would stop coming and sin.
Baraita: one might think standing applies in a lavatory or bathhouse; the verse limits it to places of reverence.
Objection: Rabbi Hiyya did not stand for Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in a bathhouse, so honor applies there.
Further objection: bar Kappara did not stand for Rabbi Shimon in a bathhouse, and Shimon complained to his father.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies that the student may have been sitting and pondering Torah, so he did not notice.
The Gemara explains the proof: the excuse implies that without it, the student would owe standing even in a bathhouse.
Resolution: the exemption applies to inner bathhouse rooms where all are naked; standing applies in the outer rooms.
Support: Rabba bar bar Hana cites Rabbi Yohanan that Torah may be contemplated anywhere except bathhouse and lavatory.
Rejection: perhaps a person whose study is involuntary is different and simply forgot where he was.
Baraita: one might think a person may close his eyes so as not to see the elder and avoid standing.
The Gemara asks whether this means the verse speaks of wicked people deliberately avoiding a mitzva.
Reinterpretation: one may close his eyes before the obligation arises, when the elder is still far off.
The verse says to stand and to fear, meaning one should fear God who knows the secrets of the heart.
A Sage taught that the standing showing reverence is within four cubits of the elder.
Abaye limits this to a non-primary teacher; for one's primary teacher, standing is required once he is in sight.
Abaye stood when he saw the donkey ear of Rav Yosef approaching; rabbis across the river did not stand for him.
Abaye argues that he is their primary teacher, so they must stand for him even from a distance.
The rabbis reply that this never entered their minds, since they had not seen him at all.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: from the verse, an elder should not trouble others to stand up for him.
The verse pairs elder with fear of God, supporting the lesson that an elder should not trouble others.
Abaye states a tradition: a Sage who walks around an area so others need not stand lives a long life.
Abaye and Rabbi Zeira both walked around areas to avoid making others stand for them.
Story: Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya when a man passed without covering his head.
Ravina calls the man insolent for not covering his head in honor of a rabbi.
Rabbi Yirmeya replies that the man may be from a city where scholars are common and so honor is less expected.
Isi ben Yehuda: the verse Before the hoary head covers any elderly person, not only a Torah scholar.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that the halakha follows Isi ben Yehuda.
Rabbi Yohanan himself stood before elderly gentile Aramean sages.
Rabbi Yohanan explains that these elders have had many experiences and deserve honor for their wisdom.
Rava did not stand for them but still showed them honor in other ways.
Practices: Abaye offered his hand to elders to lean on, Rava sent an agent, and Rav Nachman sent servants to assist them.
Rav Nachman says that without Torah, many people named Nachman bar Abba would be found in the marketplace.
Chain of transmission: Rabbi Aivu reports Rabbi Yannai's teaching.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A Torah scholar may stand before his teacher only morning and evening, so the teacher's honor does not exceed the honor of Heaven.
Objection from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: an elder should not trouble others, and the verse adds fear, so the elder must fear God too.
Explanation of the objection: if standing is only morning and evening, why warn against troubling others? Answer: standing is required only twice daily, and the elder should not impose it.
Rabbi Elazar: any Torah scholar who does not stand for his teacher is called wicked, will not live long, and will forget his studies.
Support: Ecclesiastes says the wicked do not prolong their days because they do not fear God.
The fear in that verse is unclear, but Leviticus links fear to the elder's face, so it refers to standing for him.
Why not read the fear as the fear mentioned for interest or for weights instead of standing?
Rabbi Elazar derives the law from the verbal analogy of the word face in both verses, not from the word fear.
Dilemma: must a son who is also his father's teacher stand before his father?
Support: Shmuel told Rav Yehuda to stand before his father, even though Rav Yehuda was a great scholar.
Rav Yehezkel was different because he was a man of good deeds, and even Shmuel stood before him.
What did Shmuel mean if not that a son who is a teacher must stand for his father?
Shmuel meant that his father might approach from behind and he might not notice, so the son should stand without concern for Shmuel's honor.
Dilemma: must a father stand before his son if the son is his teacher?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says he does not stand for his son because of Torah greatness, but does stand out of honor for the Nasi's household.
Inferring from this: he would stand for his son if the son were his teacher, since the reason given is the teacher relationship.
Rejecting the inference: he would not stand for his son even if the son were his teacher, because he is the father.
Dilemma: if a teacher rides an animal, is that like walking, so that one must stand, or is it like sitting?
Abaye cites a mishna on ritual impurity under a tree: an impure person sitting there renders a pure standing person impure, so riding is treated like movement.
Rav Naḥman bar Kohen concludes from this mishna that riding is always treated like walking.
Dilemma: must one stand before a Torah scroll?
Rabbi Ḥilkiya, Rabbi Simon and Rabbi Elazar argue a fortiori: if one stands before those who study Torah, one should all the more stand before the Torah itself.
Story: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed while Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were studying, and they stood for him.
Rabbi Shimon bar Abba says they were not obligated, since they are ordained and he is only an associate, and the Torah does not stand before its learners.
Explanation: Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar, who held a scholar may not stand for his teacher while studying; Abaye cursed anyone who acted otherwise.
The verse says the people looked after Moses until he entered the tent, a source for the dispute about its meaning.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa dispute the verse: one reads it as unfavorable, the other as praise.
Each reading follows its own source: the unfavorable reading follows the midrash, and the favorable reading follows Ḥizkiyya.
Ḥizkiyya reports a chain of transmission from Rabbi Ḥanina, son of Rabbi Abbahu, supporting the favorable reading.
Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa: a passing Torah scholar is stood for within four cubits, and one sits once he passes four cubits away.
For the head of the court, one stands as soon as he is in sight and sits once he passes four cubits away.
For the Nasi, one stands as soon as he is in sight and does not sit until the Nasi himself sits in his place.
The verse says they looked after Moses until he entered the tent, which supports waiting for the leader to sit first.
The mishna's principle: women are exempt from all positive commandments that are time-bound.
Baraita listing time-bound positive mitzvot: sukka, lulav, shofar, and tzitzit.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna lists time-bound positive mitzvot such as phylacteries, sukka and matza, which women are obligated in, and not time-bound ones, which women are not exempt from.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: one does not derive practical halakha from general statements, even where the text includes an exception.
Support from a mishna on eiruv: all foods work except water and salt, which is a general statement with exceptions.
Objection: truffles and mushrooms also cannot serve as eiruv food, so the mishna's list is not exhaustive.
Conclusion: general statements with exceptions cannot be used to derive the halakha, even when the text states an exception.
Principle: women are exempt from all positive time-bound mitzvot.
Where is this principle derived from?
Derivation by analogy from phylacteries: women are exempt from phylacteries, so they are exempt from all time-bound positive mitzvot.
Phylacteries are exempt for women by analogy to Torah study, which they are also exempt from, as the two appear together in the Shema.
Why not juxtapose phylacteries to mezuza, which women are obligated in, and so include women?
Phylacteries are juxtaposed with Torah study in both paragraphs of Shema, but not with mezuza in the second paragraph.
Proposal: juxtapose mezuza to Torah study, so women are exempt from mezuza too.
Rejection: mezuza is tied to long life, and the verse addresses both men and women, so women are obligated in it.
Sukka is a time-bound positive mitzva, so why does the principle not apply to it, given women are exempt?
Support: the verse says to dwell in sukkot for seven days.
The verse says all the native-born shall dwell in sukkot, and the word the excludes women; without it, women would be obligated.
Abaye: a special verse was needed to exempt women, since one might otherwise derive that husband and wife must dwell together in the sukka.
Rava's view is introduced, and the text ends at the point of its statement.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse about the homeborn is needed because one might derive sukka from Passover, where women are obligated in matza, so it excludes women.
But appearance at the pilgrimage Festivals is also a time-bound positive mitzva, so does the principle not hold universally?
Support: the verse about all your males excludes women from appearance, showing they are exempt by an explicit verse.
Had the verse not excluded women, they would be obligated, so women are not exempt from every time-bound positive mitzva.
The exclusion of women from appearance is needed, since one might derive appearance from assembly, which women are obligated in.
Why not derive the obligation from rejoicing on the Festival, which women are obligated in?
Abaye: the mitzva of rejoicing does not apply to women directly; the husband is responsible for making his wife rejoice.
What can be said about a widow, who has no husband yet is still obligated to rejoice on the Festival?
The mitzva of rejoicing for a widow applies to the men who are with her, who must make sure she rejoices.
Why not derive the obligation for all time-bound mitzvot from assembly, where women are explicitly obligated?
Matza and assembly are two verses that come together to teach the same point, and such verses do not establish a general precedent.
If so, phylacteries and appearance are also two verses teaching the same exemption, so they should not establish a precedent either.
Both are needed: without the phylacteries verse, one would link them to mezuza, and without the appearance verse, one would link appearance to assembly.
If so, matza and assembly are also both needed and do not form a pair that teaches no precedent?
Without the matza verse, one would derive matza from the sukka; without the assembly verse, one would reason from children to women, so both are needed.
This works if two verses that come together teach no precedent, but what if they do teach one?
Where do we derive that women are obligated in positive mitzvot that are not time-bound?
The obligation derives from the mitzva to fear one's mother and father, which women are obligated in, extending to all non-time-bound positive mitzvot.
Why not derive the opposite exemption from Torah study, which women are exempt from, applying to all non-time-bound mitzvot?
Torah study and procreation are two verses that come together and both exempt women, so they do not establish a precedent.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka reads the verse of Genesis 1:28, be fruitful and multiply, as addressed to both men and women.
Given that view, what can be said about the other mitzvot women are exempt from, if the principle is limited?
Torah study and redemption of the firstborn are two verses that come together, so they set no precedent for other mitzvot.
Why not also treat procreation and fear of parents as two verses that come together, setting no precedent?
Both verses are needed: fear of parents and procreation would otherwise each be inferred to exempt women by its own reasoning, so each must be stated.
Under the view that two verses coming together do set a precedent, what explains the exemptions?
Rava says the Sages of Pafunya know the reason, which is Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov's teaching.
The verse about the sign on the arm and the memorial between the eyes ties the whole Torah to phylacteries.
Rav Aḥa's inference: women are exempt from all time-bound positive mitzvot, so non-time-bound ones they are obligated in.
If phylacteries are a non-time-bound mitzva, what can be said about the principle?
That view belongs to Rabbi Meir, who holds that two verses coming together set no precedent.
What about Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that two verses coming together do set a precedent and considers phylacteries non-time-bound?
The verses on matza, rejoicing and assembly are three verses coming together, and all agree three such verses set no precedent.
The mishna teaches that men and women are both obligated in all prohibitions, whether or not time-bound.
From where are these matters derived?
Rav Yehuda cites Rav, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught the same, as their source for this equation.
Numbers 5:6 on a man or woman who sins equates women with men for all punishments in the Torah.
The school of Rabbi Eliezer derives from Exodus 21:1 that women equal men for all monetary judgments in the Torah.
The school of Ḥizkiyya derives from Exodus 21:29 that women equal men for all capital punishments in the Torah.
All three verses are needed, since each would otherwise be limited by the reasoning of mercy for atonement or business dealings, so each must be stated.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ransom verse must name men and women separately, since otherwise one might exempt women from ransom in every case, or exempt them from every case.
The mishna teaches that women are obligated in all prohibitions except rounding the head, destroying the beard, and defiling oneself for the dead.
Priests' daughters are exempt from defilement for the dead by verse, but where is the exemption from rounding the head and destroying the beard derived?
Rounding the head and destroying the beard are juxtaposed, so whoever is included in the beard prohibition is included in the head prohibition, and women are excluded from both.
From where is it derived that women are not obligated in the prohibition against destroying the beard?
Either a logical reason, since women have no beard, or the verse's singular beard shows that only a man's beard is included, not a wife's.
Is a woman not included, given a baraita that treats a woman's facial hair as a beard for all purposes, so the prohibition would apply?
Abaye: the baraita does not refer to destroying the beard; women are exempt by a verbal analogy with the sons of Aaron.
If the sons of Aaron verse covers the whole chapter, why would the Torah need to state the beard prohibition for all Jews, and could it be derived a fortiori?
The verbal analogy is still necessary, since otherwise the exclusion would end with the impurity halakhot that immediately precede it.
If the analogy is needed, why does the exclusion apply only to priests, given the rest of the chapter?
A baraita: priests are forbidden to shave the beard, and the all-Israel verse teaches liability only for destruction to the root, not with scissors.
The baraita continues: tweezers and small planes are not shaving, so the prohibition covers only razor shaving that destroys the beard.
If the analogy only defines the action, the phrase corners of your beard would be superfluous, so it teaches both the action and the exemption of women.
Returning to the baraita on a woman's or eunuch's facial hair: what halakha is it teaching?
Mar Zutra says it teaches a rule of ritual impurity from leprosy: a sore in a woman's or eunuch's beard follows beard rules.
Objection: the verse explicitly says a man or woman with a plague on the head or beard, so the baraita cannot be stating that.
Mar Zutra's reply: the baraita refers to ritual purification from leprosy, so women can also be purified of beard plagues.
Purification of women from leprosy is obvious, since impurity applies to women, so why state it?
It is needed because one might read the verse disjunctively, limiting the beard phrase to men, so the baraita teaches women are included.
Isi taught a baraita: women are exempt from the prohibition against making baldness for the dead.
Isi's source: Deuteronomy 14:1 addresses sons and not daughters, and the verse concerns baldness, so only men are included.
Does the sons-only limitation refer to baldness, or to the prior prohibition against cutting?
The verse after holy people applies to cutting for both men and women, so the sons-only limitation is needed for baldness.
What did you see that includes cutting and excludes baldness? Perhaps the opposite is true.
Cutting is included because its prohibition is broader, applying both in a place of hair and outside it, while baldness applies only where hair grows.
But the sons-only limitation could apply to both baldness and cutting, with the holy people verse referring to scoring the skin.
Isi holds that cutting and scoring are the same, with the holy people verse referring to scoring the body.

ranges.en: The two prohibitions are a single prohibition, as the Gemara concludes.
Abaye: Isi's reason for exempting women from baldness is a verbal analogy with the priests' prohibition, where the daughters of Aaron are excluded.
If the sons-of-Aaron verse covers the whole chapter, why would the Torah state baldness for all Jews, and could it be derived a fortiori?
The verbal analogy is still needed, since otherwise the ritual impurity halakhot would close the discussion and the baldness rule would cover women too.
If so, why not conclude the same for daughters of Aaron, and what is the baraita's verbal analogy for korḥa showing?
Baraita: the word korḥa makes a priest liable for each separate bald spot, not just one violation for several.
Baraita: the words upon their head extend the prohibition to the entire head, like the spot between the eyes.
Baraita: the shared word baldness shows the rules for priests apply equally to all Israelites, including each spot and the whole head.
Baraita, conversely: as the Israelite rule applies only to baldness for the dead, so the priestly rule applies only to baldness for the dead.
If the purpose were only the bald-spot rule, the verse would say keraḥ, so korḥa teaches both the women exemption and the per-spot liability.
Rava: Isi's reason is a verbal analogy from between your eyes in phylacteries, from which women are exempt, so women are exempt here too.
Why did Rava not give Abaye's reason?
Rava learns nothing from the slight difference between keraḥ and korḥa, so he gives a different reason.
Why did Abaye not give Rava's reason?
Abaye could say the phylacteries place is itself derived from baldness, since between the eyes refers to the upper head where hair grows.
What do Abaye and Rava derive from the verse: you are sons of the Lord your God?
That verse is needed for a baraita teaching a separate point, so it cannot be used for the exemption.
Baraita, Rabbi Yehuda: you are called sons when you act as sons, and not called sons when you do not.
Rabbi Meir: you are always called sons, supported by Jeremiah, Deuteronomy, Isaiah and Hosea verses.
Why are these additional proofs needed if they all make the same point?
Each verse answers a possible reading: sons are still called sons when foolish, or when lacking faithfulness, so each proof closes a gap.
Come and hear: a verse says sons without faithfulness, supporting the view that they are still called sons.
Objection: perhaps they are not called sons when they worship idols.
A verse calls them a seed of evildoers and sons who corrupt, which the Gemara uses to test the idolatry objection.
Objection: perhaps corrupting sons are not called sons of the great ones once they sin.
A verse says they will be called sons of the living God, showing that they are restored when they repent.
Mishna: laying hands, waving, bringing near, handful removal, burning, pinching, receiving blood and sprinkling apply to men, not women, except the sota and nazirite meal-offerings.
Verse: the sons of Israel lay hands on offerings, and the daughters of Israel do not.
Waving is derived from a verse about the sons of Israel waving, and the daughters of Israel do not wave.
Verse: the sons of Aaron bring the meal-offering near, and not the daughters of Aaron.
Verse: the sons of Aaron take the handful, and not the daughters of Aaron.
Verse: the sons of Aaron burn the sacrificial parts, and not the daughters of Aaron.
Pinching is juxtaposed to burning, so it is limited to men just as burning is.
Verse: the sons of Aaron present the blood, which the Master then goes on to explain.

ranges.en: Opening exegesis: the verse about the priests presenting offerings refers to collecting the blood.
Asks which sprinkling the mishna means, since women are excluded from the red heifer and Holy of Holies sprinklings.
Concludes the sprinkling in question is the blood of a bird-offering.
A kal vachomer from sheep offerings: priests sprinkle sheep blood, so priests must also sprinkle bird blood, since pinching parallels slaughter.
The mishna's exception: women wave only the meal-offerings of a sota and of a nazirite.
Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yoshiya to explain why the sota's meal-offering requires waving.
Rabbi Yoshiya replies that the waving is already stated in that same passage, which mentions waving the meal-offering.
Restates the real question: from where do we know the waving is performed by the owner.
A verbal analogy of the word hand, linking the sota's meal-offering to the peace-offering, supports the derivation.
Derived conclusion: a priest waves here as there, and the owner waves here as there, so both participate.
Asks how the priest and the owner can both perform the waving.
The owner places his hands beneath the offering, and the priest places his hand under the owner's hand to wave together.
Asks from where the nazirite woman's meal-offering also requires waving, having sourced the sota's.
A verbal analogy of the word palm, linking naziriteship to the sota, derives the nazirite's waving.
Mishna: mitzvot dependent on the land apply only in Eretz Yisrael; those not dependent on it apply everywhere.

ranges.en: Mishna exception for orla and diverse kinds, plus Rabbi Eliezer's addition that the new grain prohibition is also included.
Asks what counts as land-dependent and non-dependent mitzvot, proposing that dependence means the verb coming is written for it.
Counterexample: tefillin and firstborn donkey redemption use the verb bringing yet apply both inside and outside the land.
Rav Yehuda's reading: body obligations apply everywhere, while obligations tied to the land apply only in Eretz Yisrael.
Asks where these principles are derived from.
A baraita derives the rule from the verses on the land and the dwelling, then from the command to destroy idolatry sites.
Idolatry is a body obligation applying everywhere, so the principle follows; the Gemara then restates the mishna's rule.
Poses a dilemma: does Rabbi Eliezer dissent leniently or stringently from the first tanna?
The first tanna's position: the new grain is a land obligation, so it applies only in Eretz Yisrael, despite the possible reading.
Asks the reason for the first tanna's view.
The term dwelling means a time after inheritance and settlement of the land, so the rule is limited to Eretz Yisrael.
Rabbi Eliezer's position: the new grain prohibition applies both inside and outside Eretz Yisrael.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Eliezer's view.
The term dwelling means wherever you live, so the prohibition applies everywhere.
Alternative readings of the dispute: a lenient or stringent reading of Rabbi Eliezer, and the reading that the new grain applies only in the land.
Asks what the word even means in Rabbi Eliezer's opening statement.
Abaye's proof: a baraita identifies Rabbi Yishmael as the one disagreeing with Rabbi Eliezer, limiting dwelling-based mitzvot to after settlement.
Rabbi Akiva objects that Shabbat uses the term dwellings yet applies everywhere.
Rabbi Yishmael replies with a kal vachomer: if lighter mitzvot apply everywhere, the stringent Shabbat certainly does too.
Abaye's conclusion: Rabbi Eliezer disputes with stringency, since Rabbi Yishmael's view shows where dwelling-based mitzvot apply.
Asks where Rabbi Yishmael's view applies, to which specific mitzva it refers.
Rabbi Yishmael refers to libations offered with the offerings, which apply only after the land is settled.

ranges.en: Notes that both coming and dwelling are written in the verse, so the example seems to conflict with Rabbi Yishmael's principle.
