Recalls Rabbi Akiva's objection that Shabbat uses the term dwellings yet applies everywhere.
Asks why Rabbi Yishmael did not simply answer Rabbi Akiva by pointing to the kal vachomer.
Rabbi Yishmael gives two reasons: his principle covers only cases where coming and dwelling are both written, and Shabbat is derived by a kal vachomer.
Asks what exactly Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute.
They dispute whether libations were offered in the wilderness, and Rabbi Akiva derives a different halakha from the term dwelling.
Abaye notes that a Rabbi Yishmael school tanna's ruling conflicts with another ruling from the same school.
A baraita of Rabbi Yishmael's school derives from the king appointment verse that coming means after inheritance and settlement, generalizing to all such cases.
Objects that this is no proof, since first fruits also use the terms coming, inheriting and dwelling, so the verses teach the same matter.
Replies that both verses are necessary, since neither case can be derived from the other, and offers further arguments for the distinction.
Asks why the term dwelling is needed for Shabbat, if obligations of the body apply everywhere anyway.
The term is needed to rule out that Shabbat requires court sanctification like the festivals, which depend on the New Moon.
Asks why the term dwelling is needed for the prohibition of forbidden fat and blood.
It is needed to rule out that the prohibition applies only while the Temple stands, since it is written with offerings.
Asks why the term dwelling is needed for the matza and bitter herbs obligation.
It is needed to rule out that eating matza and bitter herbs depends on a Paschal offering being present.
Asks why the term coming is needed for phylacteries and the firstborn donkey, which are body obligations.
It is needed to teach that donning phylacteries is a mitzva through which one enters Eretz Yisrael, per Rabbi Yishmael's school.
Asks how the dwelling wording in the new-crop prohibition fits the verse about eating the land's produce after Passover.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: They sacrificed the omer first and only afterward ate the new produce.
Objects: if dwelling means the new-crop ban starts only after settlement, why not let them eat the new produce immediately?
They did not need the new produce because they still had manna, so their abstention was not due to a prohibition.
The verse about eating manna until they reached a settled land and the borders of Canaan appears to contradict itself, presented as a source.
Asks how the two clauses of the manna verse can be reconciled.
Moses died on the seventh of Adar, the manna stopped, and they ate leftover manna until the sixteenth of Nisan, even after entering the land.
Another baraita resolves the forty-year count: they tasted manna in the unleavened cakes from Egypt, so the verse is not literal.
A baraita proves Moses died on the seventh of Adar from several verses, including the thirty days of mourning and the timing of crossing the Jordan.
Asks from where we derive that Moses was born on the seventh of Adar.
The word today in the verse about Moses being one hundred and twenty shows his birth date, and God completes the righteous years exactly.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai teaches that three mitzvot, the new crop, diverse kinds and orla, were commanded upon entering the land and apply everywhere.
A kal vachomer extends each of these mitzvot to apply everywhere, comparing their prohibition types, including for diverse kinds and orla.
Introduces Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon's view, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mitzvot given before entering the land apply everywhere; those given after entry apply only in the land, except debt cancellation and slave release, which apply everywhere.
Asks what the point is of stating debt cancellation applies everywhere, since it is a body obligation not tied to the land.
The ruling is needed only for what a baraita teaches.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from the two kinds of release in the verse that debt cancellation depends on the Jubilee being in effect.
Suggests that the juxtaposition means debt cancellation applies only in Eretz Yisrael, as land release does.
The verse says the release is proclaimed to God, from everywhere, so debt cancellation applies in any place.
Asks what is novel about the slave release, since it too is a body obligation.
Without the extra Jubilee phrase one might restrict liberty to the land, so the verse states it applies in all places.
Asks what the phrase throughout the land then adds.
Liberty applies outside the land exactly when it applies inside, depending on whether the Jubilee is in effect, not on place.
The mishna teaches the new crop is forbidden by Torah law everywhere, orla outside the land by halakha, and diverse kinds outside by rabbinic law.
Asks what the halakha regarding orla refers to.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, calls it local custom, while Ulla, citing Rabbi Yohanan, calls it a halakha given to Moses from Sinai.
Ulla argues his Sinai view explains the mishna's distinction between uncertain orla and uncertain diverse kinds, citing a mishna on orla and a mishna on diverse kinds.
Objects to Rav Yehuda's view: if neither orla nor diverse kinds is forbidden by Torah law, the distinction remains unexplained.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes the mishna should phrase both cases uniformly, either both as purchasing or both as gathering the produce.
Shmuel's instruction to Rav Anan, and the lenient reading of the mishna, support the uniform phrasing with gathering permitted.
Levi and others supply uncertain orla produce outside the land, and the sharp Sages of Pumbedita hold orla does not apply there at all.
Rav Yehuda sends Rabbi Yohanan a query about orla outside the land.
Rabbi Yohanan's ruling: permit uncertain produce, forbid certain produce, and curse whoever holds there is no orla outside the land.
Asks which tanna the Pumbedita sages follow in their view.
A baraita of Rabbi Eliezer the Great's tradition states orla does not apply outside the land.
Objects that Rabbi Eliezer must hold orla applies outside the land, since the mishna cites him as saying even the new crop.
Resolves the objection: the mishna should teach only the new crop, meaning only that prohibition applies outside the land.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yohanan, holds that orla is forbidden outside the land by a halakha given to Moses at Sinai.
Rabbi Zeira objects with a baraita: uncertain orla is permitted in Syria, which conflicts with a Sinai halakha.
Narration: Rabbi Zeira is briefly dismayed by the objection.
Rabbi Asi reformulates the Sinai halakha: outside the land uncertain produce is permitted, certain produce is forbidden.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yohanan, holds offenders are flogged for diverse kinds outside the land by Torah law.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei objects with a mishna that diverse kinds outside the land are only rabbinic.
Resolves the conflict: the mishna concerns diverse kinds in a vineyard, while Rabbi Yohanan concerns grafting trees.
Shmuel derives from the verse on keeping statutes and the animal and field prohibitions that diverse kinds apply everywhere.
Asks how the phrase your field fits with the prohibition applying everywhere.
The phrase excludes planting diverse seeds, which is prohibited only in the land, not outside it.
Rav Hanan and Rav Anan see men mixing seeds and vines abroad, and the Gemara accepts Rabbi Yoshiya's rule that only one sowing sequence is liable.
Abaye objects: didn't we learn the mishna says diverse kinds outside the land are only rabbinic?
Rav Yosef replies that the vineyard case is decreed, while diverse seeds, not forbidden for benefit in the land, were not decreed abroad.
Rav Yosef retracts his view, citing Rav's garden planted in rows of different species as proof that mixing is forbidden abroad.
Asks whether Rav's planting in rows was not due to concern about the mixing of diverse kinds.
Abaye rejects this as proof, arguing that Rav's act could have been meant only to teach the halakha.

ranges.en: Rav's separate beds were for beautification or to spare his attendant the trouble, so they do not show concern about diverse kinds.
Mishna: one who performs a mitzva is rewarded with goodness and length of days, while one who performs none is not.
Raises a contradiction from a mishna in Peah listing mitzvot whose reward is enjoyed in this world.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Shemaya reconcile: one mitzva tips the scale in one's favor, equal to fulfilling the whole Torah, when merits and sins balance.
Raises a baraita contradiction: a person with more merits than sins suffers here, while one with more sins is rewarded here.
Abaye: the mishna means one good day and one bad day, with the bad day cleansing sins.
Rava: the mishna and the baraita are two opinions; the baraita follows Rabbi Yaakov, who denies reward for mitzvot in this world.
A baraita of Rabbi Yaakov ties mitzva rewards to resurrection, and a case of a son who died after dispatching a mother bird illustrates it.
Asks where the goodness and length of days are for the man who died after honoring his father.
The verses promise good and length of days in the world that is entirely good and long, i.e., the World-to-Come.
Asks whether the incident Rabbi Yaakov describes ever occurred at all.
Rabbi Yaakov himself witnessed such an incident.
Asks whether the man was punished for contemplating sin rather than for the deed.
God does not join an evil thought to an action, so one is not punished for a thought alone.
Asks whether the man was contemplating idol worship, which the verse says is punished in the heart.
If mitzvot brought reward in this world, they would have protected him from contemplating idolatry, so the reward is only in the World-to-Come.
Objects with Rabbi Elazar's view that those performing a mitzva are not harmed, which seems to contradict the death.
Rabbi Elazar's view applies only on the way to performing a mitzva, which is different from the return.
Objects that Rabbi Elazar's principle covers both going and returning from a mitzva.
A rickety ladder created a known danger, and one may not rely on a miracle where danger is established, as with Samuel's anointing of David.
Rav Yosef says that had Aher read the verse homiletically as Rabbi Yaakov did, Aher would not have sinned.
Asks what caused Aher to sin.
Two accounts: he witnessed the case of the son who died, or he saw a disseminator's tongue dragged through the street.
Rav Tuvi bar Rav Kisna raises a contradiction to Rava from the mishna on performing a mitzva.
Quotes the mishna: one who performs a mitzva is rewarded, and one who does not perform it is not.
Cites a second baraita: one who sits and does not transgress is rewarded like one who performs a mitzva.
Rava: that refers to a case where a transgression was offered and the person was saved from it, not mere sitting.
Illustrative case of Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, who resisted a noblewoman's enticement and was saved, supporting Rava's reading.

ranges.en: The guards ask a man whether a sexual temptation came before him and he was saved, which is why a miracle happened for him.

Narrative: Rabbi Tzadok's near-seduction and his fasting, then Rav Kahana's near-fall from a roof, rescued by Elijah who rebukes him.
Rav Kahana asks: was it not poverty that brought him into this temptation, since his trade put him in contact with women?
Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars so he would not need the work that exposed him to temptation.
Rava raises a contradiction to Rav Nahman from the Pe'ah mishna on mitzvot whose profits are enjoyed in this world.
Quotes the Pe'ah mishna: honoring parents, acts of kindness, peacemaking and Torah study are equal and yield profits in this world.
Rava cites a verse for each item in the mishna, including a gezera shava from pursuing peace and kindness, and Torah study as life.
Rava asks why the mishna omitted sending away the mother bird, which also has a promise of good days and length of days.
Rav Nahman replies that the tanna taught some cases and omitted others.
Rava objects that the tanna listed these matters explicitly, so he could not have omitted others.
Rava offers Rav Idi's reading of the verses on the righteous and wicked: only those who are good toward people earn profits in this world, not the bird case.
Principle: a mitzva has a principal reward and profits, while a sin has a principal penalty without profits, citing Isaiah.
Asks how to reconcile this with the verse that the wicked eat the fruit of their own way, which suggests added punishment.
Only a sin with practical consequences, such as teaching others, has profits in punishment; a sin without consequences has none.
God links a good thought to an action, as the verse on those who think upon His name shows.
Asks what the phrase and who think upon His name means.
Rav Asi: one who intended a mitzva but was prevented is credited as if he performed it.
God does not link an evil thought to an action, citing the verse that God does not hear iniquity in the heart.
Asks how to reconcile this with the Jeremiah verse about the fruit of thoughts that bring evil.
God links a thought that produces fruit to the action, but not a thought without fruit.
Asks what the Ezekiel verse about taking the house of Israel in their heart, punishing thoughts alone, refers to.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov: that refers to idol worship, which is so severe that even contemplating it is punished.
Ulla: explain this through Rav Huna's view that a repeated transgression becomes permitted.
Objects: can a transgression become permitted through repetition? Rather it becomes like permitted, as one grows used to it.
Rabbi Abbahu in Rabbi Hanina's name says it is better to sin in secret than profane God's name publicly; Rabbi Ilai says to hide one's identity.
Objects with a baraita: one who does not care about his Creator's honor would have been better not to come into the world.
Asks who counts as one who does not care about his Creator's honor.
Rabba: one who gazes at a rainbow; Rav Yosef: one who transgresses in secret.
Not contradictory: the baraita refers to one who can control his inclination yet sins in secret, the other to one who cannot.
Mishna: no credit is given for profaning God's name, whether one sinned unintentionally or intentionally.
Asks what the phrase no credit is given means.
Mar Zutra: God does not extend credit but punishes immediately; Mar bar Rabbana: the profanation tips the scale toward sin when merits and sins are equal.
A new baraita opens, cut off at the daf's end: The Sages taught: always.

ranges.en: One should see himself as evenly balanced: one mitzva tips him toward merit, one sin toward liability, citing Ecclesiastes.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon: since the world and the individual are judged by majority, one act tips both himself and the world.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: a righteous person who sins at the end loses his past merit, and a wicked person who repents is no longer reminded of his wickedness.
Asks why a person who did mitzvot all his life and then sinned is condemned, since his record should be balanced.
Reish Lakish: this applies to one who regrets his earlier mitzvot, so those mitzvot no longer count.
Mishna: one engaged in Bible, Mishna and proper conduct will not easily sin, and one lacking them is not part of society.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok's parable: the righteous are like a tree pure at its root, cleansed of afflictions for the World-to-Come, while the wicked are rewarded here to be cast down.
Narrative: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether action or study is greater, and all agree study is greater because it leads to action.
Baraita of Rabbi Yosei: Torah study preceded the ḥalla, terumot, Sabbatical and Jubilee mitzvot by the number of years before each took effect.
Asks why the baraita says 103 years for the Jubilee, since the arithmetic seems to give 104.
The Jubilee releases from the start of its year, so 103 years is correct for the Jubilee count.
Just as study precedes action, judgment for Torah study precedes judgment for mitzva action, citing Rav Hamnuna's verse.
Reward for study likewise precedes reward for action, supported by the verse about observing the statutes and the Torah.
Anyone who lacks Bible, Mishna and proper conduct is disqualified from testimony, per Rabbi Yohanan and a baraita; Rav Idi bar Avin rules accordingly.
Bar Kappara teaches that an angry person is a further case, cut off at the daf's end.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Closing teaching on scorners, followed by the end-of-chapter marker that opens the next chapter on betrothing a woman.
Mishna: a man can betroth a woman himself or through an agent, and a father can betroth his daughter when she is a young woman, by himself or an agent.
Asks why the mishna needs to state betrothal by oneself, since betrothal through an agent was already stated.
Rav Yosef: it is more fitting for the man himself to perform the mitzva, like Rav Safra singeing an animal and Rava salting fish for Shabbat.
Some hold betrothal also carries a prohibition unless the man sees the woman, citing Rav and loving one's neighbor as oneself, and the clarification of Rav Yosef's statement.
Asks why the mishna states that a woman can be betrothed by herself, once it says she can use an agent.
Rav Yosef: it is more fitting for the woman herself to perform the mitzva than through an agent, like Rav Safra and Rava.
Reish Lakish: women prefer marriage to widowhood, so an agent-arranged betrothal raises no concern about repugnance.
The mishna's ruling that a daughter may be betrothed only when a young woman is inferred to exclude a minor, supporting Rav.
Ruling of Rav, or Rabbi Elazar: a father may not betroth his minor daughter until she grows up and says whom she wants.
Asks from where we derive that an agent can effect betrothal.
A baraita derives agency from the divorce verse's words for sending, showing that an agent, and an agent of an agent, can act.
Asks how agency is derived for betrothal, since divorce differs as it can be done against the woman's will.
The verse juxtaposes leaving a marriage with entering one, so agency for betrothal follows from the verse on the divorce's exit.
Objects with a Terumot mishna: an agent separating teruma must follow the owner's mindset, which seems to conflict with the betrothal derivation.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: if an agent miscalculates the teruma amount, the separation is still valid teruma.
Asks from where we derive that one can appoint an agent to separate teruma.
Proposes deriving it from divorce, but objects that divorce is non-sacred while teruma has its own halakhot.
The verse says you also, with also including an agent, so teruma may be separated by an agent.
Asks why not write agency in the teruma verse and derive divorce and betrothal from it.
That derivation can be refuted, since teruma can be set apart by thought alone, so its leniency may not extend to agency.
A mishna on a group whose lost Paschal offering was replaced shows an agent may slaughter the offering on behalf of others.
Asks from where we derive that one may appoint an agent to slaughter an offering.
Proposes deriving it from divorce and teruma, but objects that offerings may have their own halakhot as sacred matters.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha derives from the verse that the whole congregation slaughters, so an agent's status equals the principal's.
Asks why not write agency in the offerings verse and derive the other cases from it.
Refutable, since most offering service is performed through agents, so it is not a typical case of agency.
Asks which of the three cases can be derived from the other two, since none can derive from one alone.
Lays out each of the three possible derivations and notes each can be refuted, except for one option.
Rather, teruma is derived from offerings and divorce, since offerings are more sacred yet accept agency.
Asks why the word also is needed, given that the derivation is already established.
Rabbi Yannai: as you are covenant members, your agents must be as well, so a gentile cannot separate teruma.
Asks why a verse is needed when the principle can be derived from Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba: a slave cannot act as agent in matters that do not apply to him, so gentiles cannot separate teruma.
The verse is still needed, since a gentile might seem qualified by his own teruma, and the word also excludes gentiles.
Objects that Rabbi Shimon exempts a gentile's teruma from the added penalty, so the gentile-agent halakha seems unnecessary.
Asks why the words you also are needed if the gentile-agent halakha is unnecessary.
Without also one might limit agency to a person's own produce, excluding sharecroppers, partners and stewards, so also includes agents.
Asks the source of agency for offerings according to Rabbi Yonatan, whose reading of the verse differs.
Baraita of Rabbi Yonatan: from where do we know all of Israel fulfils its obligations, cut off at the daf's end.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yonatan's reading of the Paschal verse: all Israel fulfils the obligation through one offering slaughtered by one representative.
Asks from where Rabbi Yonatan derives that one may act as agent for offerings.
Objects that the slaughterer there has a partnership in the offering, so the verse does not prove agency without a share.
Another verse, that each household takes a lamb, is brought to derive that one person takes and slaughters for the whole family.
Objects again that the agent in that verse also has a partnership in the offering.
Replies: if so, why two verses for one halakha? The verse must apply even where the agent has no share.
The verse serves Rabbi Yitzhak's derivation that only an adult, not a minor, can acquire on behalf of others.
Asks why the every-man phrase is still needed, if it is for the one-person slaughter of an individual's offering.
Rabbi Yonatan follows the view that one may not slaughter a Paschal offering on behalf of an individual.
Asks from where Rav derives that an agent's status equals his principal's, citing the prince of each tribe.
Proposed derivation: one prince of each tribe in the land division shows agency, from the verse about taking one prince.
Objects that this is agency and minors cannot act as agents, so the verse cannot prove agency for the land division.
Rather, Rava bar Rav Huna's principle applies: one may gain for another in his absence, which explains the princes acting for minors.
Objects that the allotment is not purely a benefit, since a land portion may suit one person and harm another.
Rav Giddel's principle: if orphans divide their father's estate, the court appoints a steward who may act for their benefit and sometimes to their temporary loss.
Asks why the steward would act to the orphans' disadvantage at all.
The steward acts to their disadvantage only in order to secure a later benefit, as the prince verse indicates.
Shmuel: orphans' steward chooses fine portions, and the adult orphans cannot protest; Rav Nahman adds that the court's authority requires finality.
Asks whether Rav Nahman really holds that the court's authority must be final, given that it undermines the court's advantage.
Objects with a mishna on judges' valuation errors, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that sales stand is the lenient position, contrary to Rav Nahman.
Rav Huna bar Hinnana, citing Rav Nahman: the halakha follows the Rabbis' view.
Not a difficulty: the mishna's ruling does not conflict with Rav Nahman's position, since the Rabbis' view is the halakha.

ranges.en: Asks: if Rav Nahman's ruling concerns cases without a sixth-part error, what protest can the orphans make after growing up?
They may protest about the location of the portion they received.
Rav Nahman: brothers dividing an inheritance are like buyers and sellers, so an error under a sixth stands and above a sixth is void.
Rava: the under-a-sixth rule holds only when the short-changed brother did not appoint an agent, since an agent acts only to his benefit.
Rava: an error above a sixth is valid if the division was made by court appraisal, citing the mishna on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rava: fraud rules differ for land and movables, and an error in measure counts as fraud even below a sixth, per Rabba.
Objects with a mishna: one who sends fire by a competent agent is liable, which seems to conflict with the rule that an agent is like his principal.
Asks why the competent agent should not be treated as the principal himself.
There is no agency for transgression, since a student's words cannot override those of the master, so the agent alone is responsible.
Objects with a baraita on misuse of consecrated property, where the owner is liable when the agent carried out the agency, which again conflicts with no agency for transgression.
Misuse of consecrated property is different, derived from the word sin in teruma; a single verse for agency cannot be generalized because two verses teach the same matter.
Asks what verse teaches the parallel case of misappropriating a deposit.
Baraita: the verse for every matter of trespass about a bailee is disputed by Beit Shammai, who count thought as action, and Beit Hillel, who require actual misappropriation.
Beit Shammai object to Beit Hillel: the verse says every matter of trespass, so liability does not require actual misappropriation.
Beit Hillel reply: the verse about not putting one's hand on the neighbor's goods requires actual misappropriation.
Beit Shammai object: if liability requires actual misappropriation, why is every matter of trespass needed at all?
Beit Hillel: the phrase covers one who orders a slave or agent to misappropriate, so the bailee is liable for his agent's act.
Challenges this route: it explains Beit Hillel, but Beit Shammai read the verse as thought equal to action and do not derive liability for agents.

ranges.en: Not derived from misuse of consecrated property, since it and slaughter or sale are two verses that teach the same matter, so no precedent follows.
The verse on slaughtering or selling is read by analogy: sale is done through another, so slaughter can be too; two schools add the words or and for to include agents.
Asks why not derive agency for transgression from misuse and slaughter-or-sale, on the view that two verses do teach a precedent.
A verse marks slaughter outside the Temple: the man who spilled the blood is liable, not his agent, so no agency for transgression there.
Asks from where this halakha, derived from offerings slaughtered outside, extends to the whole Torah.
Asks why not derive the principle from misuse and slaughter-or-sale instead of from the outside-slaughter case.
The verse repeats that man in the cut-off penalty, so the emphasis is applied to the whole Torah: liability is only for one's own act.
Asks what the two that man phrases teach, if the other side derives nothing from the parallel verses.
One phrase excludes two who slaughter together, and the other requires full awareness, excluding those compelled, unwitting or mistaken.
The other opinion derives the halakhot from the two parts of the word hahu, article and pronoun, so no separate halakhot come from one part.
Objects with a baraita: one who tells an agent to kill is exempt, but Shammai the Elder holds the sender liable, citing David and Uriah.
Asks Shammai the Elder's reasoning for holding that agency for transgression exists.
Shammai holds that two verses teach a precedent, and he does not interpret the variation from hu to hahu.
Alternatively Shammai does derive it, and liable means liable by heaven, though no human court punishes him.
Asks whether the first tanna then holds the sender is exempt even by heaven.
The first tanna also holds liability by heaven; the dispute is between great and lesser degrees of judgment.
Alternatively all agree there is no agency for transgression, but killing is singled out by the explicit verse on the sword of Ammon.
The first tanna reads the verse as: this killing is like the sword of Ammon, so the sender is not punished, since Uriah was a rebel.
Asks the reason Uriah was a rebel deserving death.
Uriah called Joab his lord before the king, indicating he answered to Joab rather than to the king, which is rebellion.
Rava: if Shammai derived agency for transgression, he would have to accept that an agent who commits adultery or eats forbidden fat is liable, which the Torah never shows.
Dispute among the Sages: Rav holds an agent can become a witness, while the school of Rabbi Sheila holds not.
Asks the reason of the school of Rabbi Sheila for denying agents testimony.
Objects: if they say the sender did not appoint him as a witness, the same logic would void betrothal in the presence of two people without an explicit appointment.
Rav: the agent's testimony is strengthened since he knows the act; the school of Rabbi Sheila: the agent is like the principal, so cannot testify.
Objects with a baraita: to three people, one is the agent and two witnesses, per Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel say all three are agents.
The disagreement is only for three people; for two, all agree agents cannot be witnesses.
Rav follows the tanna of Rabbi Natan, who records Beit Shammai as saying an agent and one witness suffice.
Asks whether Rav would then rule like Beit Shammai.
Reverse the attribution: it is Beit Hillel who say the agent and one witness suffice.
Rav Aha son of Rava reports the dispute in reverse, with Rav holding agents cannot be witnesses and the school of Rabbi Sheila holding they can.
Ruling: an agent can become a witness; Rava, citing Rav Nahman, says the two people who betroth are both agents and witnesses, and likewise for divorce.

ranges.en: The same rule applies to monetary cases: agents appointed to pay a debt can testify that it was paid.
Each domain must be stated: betrothal alone might suggest bias toward forbidding, divorce alone might suggest no bias, and money alone could be divided between agents.
Asks what Rav Nahman holds: if a debt must be repaid before witnesses, the agents have a motive to lie about having repaid it.
Rav Nahman holds that a debt need not be repaid before witnesses, so the agents have no motive to lie and are credible.
Since the rabbinic oath of inducement was instituted after Rav Nahman, the agents now have a motive to lie and must swear instead.
Mishna in Gittin: a betrothed young woman and her father may each receive her get; Rabbi Yehuda holds only the father may, since two hands cannot acquire together.
Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan dispute whether the betrothal case follows the divorce dispute, with Rabbi Yohanan limiting the dispute to divorce.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina introduces his question on the reasoning behind Rabbi Yohanan's distinction.
Asks the reason of Rabbi Yohanan's distinction between divorce and betrothal.
In divorce she returns into her father's authority, so either may receive it; in betrothal she removes herself from his authority, so only the father may.
Objects: levirate betrothal removes the yevama from her father's authority, yet a baraita is cited that seems to conflict.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita on levirate betrothal of a widowed minor and a young woman: a minor needs her father's consent, while a young woman may consent herself.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina explains Rabbi Yohanan's reasoning: betrothal needs the acceptor's consent, while divorce can be given without it.
Objects: levirate betrothal is with her consent, yet the baraita lists both her and her father as acceptors.
Those cases refer to levirate betrothal without her consent, following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi against the Rabbis, per a baraita.
Asks the reason of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi for his view on levirate betrothal.
He derives levirate betrothal from intercourse with a yevama, which acquires against her will; the Rabbis derive it from ordinary betrothal, requiring consent.
Asks what the two sides actually disagree about.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from yevama matters, the Rabbis from betrothal matters, and Rabbi Yohanan's reading is the reasonable one.
Proposes that the mishna's final clause refutes Reish Lakish, who holds a young woman accepts her own betrothal according to the Rabbis.
Reish Lakish can reply that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds two hands do not acquire together.
Asks why the baraita says unlike betrothal if it follows Rabbi Yehuda, and should have said unlike divorce.
Yes, it should have said divorce, but the baraita is teaching levirate betrothal, which resembles betrothal, so it also says unlike betrothal.
Asks how levirate betrothal, which Rabbi Yehuda allows without consent, differs from divorce, which a young woman cannot receive.
Levirate betrothal is different, since the yevama is bonded to the yavam and waiting for him, so her acceptance of the money suffices.
Mishna: a man can betroth his daughter when she is a young woman, by himself or by an agent, but she cannot be betrothed by herself or by an agent.
Proposes the mishna refutes Reish Lakish, who holds a young woman accepts her own betrothal according to the Rabbis.
Reish Lakish can reply that this mishna also follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks how the mishna can be established as Rabbi Yehuda's view, since its last clause seems to follow another view.
Mishna's later clause: a man who says to a woman be betrothed with this date and be betrothed with that date is betrothed only if one date is worth a peruta.
Asks who the tanna is, if the two dates are valued separately only with separate statements of become betrothed.
Rabba: it is Rabbi Shimon, who requires a separate oath to each person, and Rabbi Yehuda is in fact following Rabbi Shimon in the specifics.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda actually holds Rabbi Shimon's view on separate oaths.
Objects with a baraita: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon dispute liability for multiple false oaths, showing Rabbi Yehuda disagrees with Rabbi Shimon.
Rather, the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, and on agency it follows Rabbi Yehuda, that only the father can appoint an agent for betrothal.
Narrative: Rabbi Asi missed the study hall and found Rabbi Zeira.
Asks what was said that day in the study hall.
Report: Rabbi Avin said the whole session sided with Rabbi Yohanan, while Reish Lakish protested citing the verse on departing and becoming another's wife; no one heeded him.
Asks whether Rabbi Avin can be relied on to report accurately.
Rabbi Zeira: yes, the interval between catching a fish and frying it was short, so he is reliable.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: he quotes this statement only in the name of Rabbi Avin, without a patronymic.
Asks what difference it makes which Rabbi Avin is named.
It matters for detecting contradictions between that Rabbi Avin's rulings and another Rabbi Avin's rulings.
Rava asks Rav Nahman a question, cut off at the daf's end.

ranges.en: Asks whether a young woman can appoint an agent to receive her get, comparing her to her father's hand or courtyard.

Rava asks whether she is as strong as her father's hand, enough to appoint an agent.
Rav Nachman answers that she cannot appoint an agent.
Rava objects from a mishna about a minor who asks an agent to receive her get, implying a young woman can.
Asks in what case the mishna speaks, given that a young woman's get is valid.
Explains the case as one where she has no father, so she is under her own authority.
Argues that the latter clause implies the first clause concerns a young woman who has a father.
Replies that the mishna is incomplete and must be read with a missing clause, upholding the view.
Restates the mishna's rule for a minor and a young woman, limited to a case where she has no father.
Reports Shmuel's view that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both a get and refusal.
Karna challenges Shmuel as contradictory: why a get if the betrothal is valid, and refusal if it is not.
Messengers propose bringing the case to Mar Ukva and then to Rav to settle the disputed opinions.
Rav rules she needs both a get and refusal, and swears Shmuel would never hold otherwise.

Rav Aha son of Rav Ika gives the reason: uncertainty about the father's consent and the sister betrothal rule.
Rav Nachman limits the concern to cases where the match was arranged before her betrothal.
Ulla says she needs not even refusal, even when the match was arranged.
Resolves the conflicting versions of Ulla's statement, saying one version teaches only the non-arranged case.
Another version attributes to Ulla that no refusal is needed in any case of betrothal without consent.
Rav Kahana objects from a Yevamot mishna listing cases where rival wives are permitted, including refusal.
Asks who betrothed her in the case of a refusal.
Rejects the reading that her father betrothed her, since then she would need a proper get, not refusal.
Concludes the mishna must mean she betrothed herself as a minor, so refusal is required.
Rav Kahana resolves the objection: she became an orphan during her father's lifetime, so her self-betrothal is rabbinic only.
Rav Hamnuna objects from a baraita that a father may sell his minor daughter as a maidservant even to relatives.

ranges.en: States the baraita's agreed rule that a widow, divorcee or halutza may be sold to priests of various ranks.
Asks what case this widow who may be sold by her father refers to.
Suggests the father betrothed her, then objects that a father cannot sell a daughter after betrothing her.
Explains instead that she betrothed herself as a minor, so she is still called a widow.
Rav Amram explains the baraita as a betrothal of designation, following Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda on sale money.
Rav Huna reports Rav: a levirate betrothal requires refusal, but her bond to the yavam does not.
Explains the requirements: after levirate betrothal she needs a bill of divorce, halitza and refusal.
Gives reasons for each requirement, based on whether the father may have consented to each betrothal.
Without a levirate betrothal, she requires only halitza and no refusal.
Objects: if she needs refusal lest betrothal to her sister fail, why not require it here as well?
Everyone knows the sister of a halutza is forbidden only by rabbinic law, so the concern is unnecessary.
Brings Reish Lakish's reading of a Yevamot mishna distinguishing the sisters of a divorcee and a halutza.
Relates a Babylonian story of two men drinking, with a betrothal by cup, and Ravina's point that the father's consent remains doubtful.

ranges.en: The Rabbis object to Ravina, asking whether we must worry that the son himself may have consented.
Replies that no son would dare appoint his father as agent, or he may have wished to please him.
Rabba bar Shimi objects that Ravina explicitly disagrees with Rav and Shmuel, contradicting their view.
Ravina rules that even by the view that we worry about the father's consent, a betrothal in the market stands.
Limits these rulings to a betrothal done in an honorable manner, not a disgraceful one.
Rav Aha of Difti asks which disgrace is meant: of the vegetables, of the market, or of the bowl at home.
Replies that both are disgraceful ways of betrothing, so the rule still applies.
Relates a case of a betrothal by letter to a woman, after a meal with the relatives involved.
Abaye cites Zephaniah 3:13 about the remnant of Israel not speaking falsehood, to support a presumption.
Rava states the principle that a person does not exert himself at a feast and then lose out on it.
Asks what difference there is between the two cases of the betrothal.

Presents a case where a woman was betrothed with her father's consent, he left overseas, and she married.
Rav rules she may eat terumah until her father returns and nullifies the betrothal.
Rav Asi rules she may not eat terumah, since her father may return and nullify the betrothal.
Describes an incident where she ate terumah retroactively, and Rav was concerned with Rav Asi's view.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says Rav agrees that if she dies the husband does not inherit, keeping money with its owner.
Presents a case of betrothal with consent, marriage without consent, with her father still alive.
Rav Huna rules she may not eat terumah in this case.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba rules she may eat terumah.
Rav Huna again rules she may not eat terumah.
Explains that Rav's leniency applies only when no father is present, whereas here the silent father became angry.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba rules she may eat terumah.
Explains Rav Asi's strictness applies where the father may return, but here his silence settled the matter.
Another case: betrothed without consent, married without consent, with the father still alive.
Rav Huna rules she may eat terumah.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba rules she may not eat terumah.
Ulla identifies this as the view of Rav Huna.
Cites Proverbs 10:26, a sluggard is like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, to support the ruling.
Argues a fortiori: if she may not eat terumah after a Torah-law betrothal, she certainly may not eat here.

ranges.en: Rava says the student's view seems correct.
Asks what Rav Huna's reason is.
Explains that since she became like an orphan while her father was alive, the case follows the earlier ruling.
Introduces the case of a minor betrothed without her father's consent.
Rav holds that she and her father can both block the betrothal, while Rav Asi holds only the father can.
Rav Huna raises an objection against Rav Asi's view from a baraita, and it is restated to Rav Asi.
Cites Exodus 22:16 and derives from its wording that the woman herself may refuse, not only her father.
Rav warns against the reverse inference, since one might distinguish the case by intent to marry.
Explains that the verse is needed for a seducer who acted without intent to marry.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the seducer must pay a fine like one who seduced a woman.
Rav Yosef objects: if so, that is what we already learned in a mishna.
Cites Exodus 22:15 that he must pay the bride-price and she becomes his wife, supporting the mishna.
Asks why betrothal is needed at all if the seducer acted with intent to marry.
Abaye replies that she requires betrothal with her father's consent.
Mishna: a man betroths a woman with a series of items, and she is betrothed only if one item is worth a pruta.
Asks who the tanna is behind the repeated phrasing of the mishna.
Rabba attributes the view to R. Shimon, who requires an oath for each item.
Asks which clause of the mishna this refers to.
Asks why the mishna mentions eating, when even a handed-over gift would also apply.
Objects that this is a loan, which would not count as a valid betrothal.
Rabbi Yochanan illustrates with a table, meat and a knife, which she cannot eat.
Rav and Shmuel say the mishna refers to the first clause, and that eating requires a pruta's value.
R. Ami says the mishna refers to its end, requiring a pruta's value in the last item.

ranges.en: Concludes from the previous discussion that money in general is returned.
Presents the case of one who betroths his sister, with Rav holding the money is returned and Shmuel holding it is a gift.
Explains Rav's view: knowing betrothal to a sister is ineffective, he intends a deposit, and she would not accept it.
Explains Shmuel's view that the money is a gift, reasoning by analogy to the final clause of the case.
Ravina objects: one who separates challah from flour has not separated challah, and the priest's share is taken from him.
Asks why it should count as theft from the priest, rather than assuming the person knows it is a gift.
Explains the case differs, since the priest could end up with less than five quarters of flour and suffer loss.
Objects to a view where one mixes the dough and, thinking it fixed, eats it untithed, contrary to the rule.
Asks the reasoning behind the cases of one who knows the rule and one who does not.
Explains the reason is the priest's trouble, so it should be made terumah instead.
States that it becomes terumah and she may not eat until challah is separated from elsewhere.
Cites a mishna on a perforated vessel: it is terumah, and one may not eat until terumah and tithe are separated elsewhere.
Resolves the cases by distinguishing two vessels from one, or alternatively by the priest's compliance.
Proposes that the householder thinks his dough is fixed and eats it untithed.
Objects again: a person knows one does not separate challah from flour, so he would not eat it untithed.
Asks the reason for the case of one who knows and one who does not know.
Explains the reason is the priest's trouble: he accepts it upon himself, and it becomes terumah.
Cites a mishna: separating from a non-perforated over a perforated vessel is terumah, and he separates again.
Resolves the two cases: with two vessels the rule applies, with one it does not.
Objects from a mishna on separating cucumber found bitter and melon found spoiled, which must separate again.
Distinguishes that there, by Torah law, the terumah is valid, so the case differs.
R. Elai derives from Numbers 18:32 that terumah taken from bad produce over good is valid terumah.
Rava opens a new point in the discussion.

ranges.en: Clarifies the mishna: it teaches only when he says by this, and this, and this; if he says by these, even eating makes her betrothed.
Cites a baraita that agrees with Rava's view.
Cites a baraita on betrothal by several fruits: she is betrothed only if one item is worth a pruta.
Asks what the case of walnut, palm and nut looks like.
Proposes that he said or, so she is betrothed if the items together are worth a pruta.
Objects: but he said or, and if the reading were and, it would match the case of this, this and this.
Rather, he said by these, as the latter clause shows, so the case is a betrothal by these items.
Explains how the case works: he said by these, as the latter clause teaches.
Baraita's latter clause: by taking and eating one, she is betrothed if one item is worth a pruta.
Objects that the first clause does not distinguish between eating and a gift.
Concludes that when he says by these and she eats it herself, the case is clear for one who reads it as the latter clause.
Explains that view: until one item, or the last item, is worth a pruta.
Rav and Shmuel hold that the first clause applies, and eating is included.
Explains the general listing is distinct from specific items, since no difference is made between olive and olive.
Rav rules that one who betroths with a loan is not betrothed, since a loan is given for spending.
Asks whether this is a dispute between tannaim, where some say she is betrothed.
Asks whether the dispute is whether a loan is given for spending.
Objects: if a loan is given for spending, how would one acquire in sale, if the two cases are equal?
Rav Nachman says the Sages place this case in other matters, not betrothal.
Explains the case: he said by a maneh and a dinar is short; one holds the latter clause applies, the other does not.
Cites R. Elazar's ruling: she is betrothed when he gives a dinar and must complete, and asks if this is a tannaitic dispute.
Explains R. Elazar's teaching: a maneh less a dinar follows the latter clause, but less ninety-nine does not.
Objects with a baraita: betrothal with a deposit requires a pruta to remain, while with a loan, even if none remains, she is betrothed.

ranges.en: Concludes that here the parties do not disagree: she is like a deposit.

Rava resolves that the ruling holds when she did not accept responsibility; if she did, she is betrothed even without a pruta left.
Baraita: with a loan she is not betrothed, even if a pruta remains.
R. Shimon ben Elazar cites R. Meir that the case is a loan, supporting the baraita's ruling.
Asks what the parties dispute about, since she is like a deposit.
Rabbah reports the Sages' dispute over who bears the risk of accidental loss on a loan.

Argues a fortiori from borrowing: if a borrower who returns the item bears accidental loss, a loan certainly does.
Explains the real difference between a loan and borrowing: the loan is in the owner's hands for return.
Asks whether Rav Huna's case of a borrowed pickaxe, acquired by use, is a dispute between tannaim.

Asks whether this is a dispute between tannaim.

Asks what the case of a debt note looks like.
Objects that if it is others' note it is a loan held by others, so it must be her note and the dispute concerns betrothal with a loan.
Answers that it is always others' note, and here they dispute about a loan written in a note versus an oral loan.
Asks what they dispute about in a loan with a note, given the dispute of R. and the Sages.
Cites a baraita: R. says documents are acquired by delivery, while the Sages require both writing and delivery.

Explains the disagreement: one master holds Rav Pappa's rule, the other does not, or all accept it.

ranges.en: Rules that a seller of a debt note who forgives it has forgiven it, and even an heir may forgive.

Explains one master holds Resh Lakish's view and the other does not, or all accept it.
