Rabbi Elazar: the mishna assumes the woman knows second-tithe money is not desacralized, so she will eat it in Jerusalem
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: a person buying a non-kosher animal, slaves or land also knows, yet the mishna rules differently
Rather, the mishna concerns a woman meticulous about tithes who knows the money must go to Jerusalem
Restates the mishna: if one bought such items, he must eat other food corresponding to their value
Why not say the money returns to its place, as Rabbi Yehuda ruled for intentional desacralization
Shmuel's ruling is introduced as the answer on the same question

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The case: the seller fled, and the rule is that we penalize the seller when he has not fled, and the buyer otherwise
It is not the mouse that steals but the hole, so the seller who provided the hiding place is the one penalized
But if not for the mouse, what did the hole do, since both are integral to the prohibited act
Stands to reason: wherever the forbidden money is, here with the seller, that is where the penalty applies
Mishna: betrothal with orla, diverse kinds, a stoned ox, a heifer, leper's birds, and similar items fails, but sold proceeds work
From where do we know that benefit from orla is prohibited
Baraita: the verse Arelim is a prohibition on eating, and orlato adds all benefits, such as painting or lamp oil
From where do we know that diverse kinds in a vineyard are prohibited for benefit
Hizkiyya: the verse pen tikdash is read as pen tukad esh, so the diverse seed must be burned
Rav Ashi: pen tikdash makes it comparable to consecrated property, so benefit is forbidden
Objects: if so, like consecrated property it would transfer its sanctity to the redemption money, contrary to the mishna
Rather, the correct derivation is that of Hizkiyya
From where do we derive that benefit from a stoned ox is prohibited
Baraita: the verse on a stoned ox teaches the flesh is forbidden to eat even if slaughtered after sentencing
Baraita continues: the owner shall be clear is derived as in Shimon ben Zoma's view that he has no benefit from it
From where do we know the verse teaches the case where it was slaughtered after sentencing, rather than permitting it
Continues: Rabbi Abbahu cites Rabbi Elazar that such verses prohibit both eating and benefit unless specified otherwise
The Gemara answers: the prohibition of eating is derived from stoning, so the verse must be for benefit, and its flesh is forbidden even when slaughtered
Mar Zutra objects: this applies only when a sharp stone was used, since the Torah does not mention a knife
Reply: a baraita permits slaughter with any cutting item, so there is no difference between a knife and a stone
Now that both prohibitions are derived from one verse, what is the other phrase owner shall be clear teaching
It comes to teach the prohibition on benefit from its hide
Objects: one might think the flesh is forbidden but the hide is permitted, since the verse says flesh
For the tanna who derives the half atonement money from owner shall be clear, from where do they learn the benefit from the hide

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shimon HaAmasoni did not expound the particle et, withdrawing from that method once he reached the verse about fearing God
His students ask what will become of all the et expositions he had made until now
He replies that he was rewarded for the exposition and equally for withdrawing from it
Rabbi Akiva's exposition: the particle et in the verse about fearing God includes Torah scholars
From where do we know that a broken-neck heifer is forbidden for benefit
The school of Rabbi Yannai: the atonement wording written for the heifer makes it forbidden like sacrificial animals
From where do we know that the leper's birds are forbidden for benefit
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: enabling and atoning rites inside and outside the Temple are treated alike in their forbidden status
Amoraim dispute when the leper's birds become forbidden: at slaughter for Rabbi Yohanan, at taking for Reish Lakish
From when is the broken-neck heifer itself forbidden
Rabbi Yannai: the heifer becomes forbidden at its descent to the valley, unlike the birds taken and immediately slaughtered
Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from a baraita on the leper's bird, which would be unneeded if forbidden while alive
The verse is needed to exclude the sacrificial case, where slaughter renders the animal fit, so the bird stays forbidden
Rabbi Yohanan objects again from the tereifa bird, which would be forbidden before slaughter if the prohibition applied while alive
Reish Lakish: the slaughtered bird was a tereifa in its inner organs, so the consecration never took effect
Another objection from a baraita: a bird slaughtered without hyssop or cedar, where Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Shimon differ
Rabbi Yohanan infers the dispute: whether an incomplete slaughter counts as slaughter, but all agree it is forbidden only after slaughter
Reish Lakish concedes that baraita does not fit his view, but the dispute is among tanna'im per the school of Rabbi Yishmael
The baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael equates the leper's birds with the broken-neck heifer, and teaches the verse on clean birds
Objects: reverse it, Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai says no animal is forbidden in that way, and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak objects

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Forbidden idol-offerings and idol-worshipped animals differ: forbidden only for the Most High, so common benefit is allowed
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: animals that copulated are living yet forbidden, so the explanation must be emended to the general rule
The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the word field that the released bird is permitted, as a field is permitted
Is the word field coming to teach this, or for another halakha
The word field teaches where the bird must be released: to the field, not the sea, desert, or outside the city
The other tanna: if only that were taught, the verse would say field; so the word field yields two rules
Rava: the Torah did not command a release that could cause a stumbling block by unwitting eating
From where do we derive that a nazirite's hair is forbidden for benefit
The verse says the nazirite shall be holy, so his hair growth is holy, like consecrated property
If the hair is holy, why does it not transfer sanctity to the redemption money, as consecrated property does
The verse uses kadosh, not kodesh, which is the term for consecrated property, so the rules differ
Suggests the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, since a firstborn donkey is forbidden for benefit, not Rabbi Shimon
Rav Naḥman: the mishna means a donkey whose neck was broken, which everyone agrees is forbidden
Everyone agrees on meat cooked in milk, so from where do we derive its prohibition on benefit
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: three verses teach the prohibitions on eating, benefit, and cooking meat in milk
The mishna is not like this school: a baraita says Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda permits benefit from meat cooked in milk
Proof from the verse calling Israel holy and from the verse of holy people, applying the same rule to both
From where do we derive the prohibition on benefit from non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard
Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Meir: the Torah says slaughter for Me in My place, so the rule runs both ways
If so, just as slaughtering consecrated animals elsewhere incurs karet, so should slaughtering non-sacred animals in the courtyard
The verse about bringing the offering to the Tent of Meeting limits karet to offerings, not non-sacred animals in the courtyard
The comparison can be refuted: karet makes the consecrated case severe, but the non-sacred case is not punished by karet
Abaye: the source is the three superfluous it-verses on peace-offerings, plus the baraita on slaughtering far from the place
Baraita derives that the verses include blemished animals and birds, while the hair and meat rules stay limited to the unblemished

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: the three it-verses teach that blemished, undomesticated, and bird non-sacred offerings are included in the prohibition
Baraita continues: one may not eat such meat, but may cast a tereifa to dogs, and the word it excludes courtyard animals
Mar Yehuda finds Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at Rabba's study hall and cites a baraita on Rabbi Shimon's betrothal rule
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon says a woman is betrothed with a firstborn donkey, meat in milk, or courtyard animals; the Rabbis disagree
Mar Yehuda infers that for Rabbi Shimon the courtyard prohibition is not from the Torah, which is why betrothal works
Mar Yehuda cites a contrary baraita: Rabbi Shimon says courtyard animals must be burned, implying they are forbidden
Rabba: the baraita concerns an animal found to be a tereifa after slaughter, where Rabbi Shimon's view differs
Baraita supports Rabba: Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from courtyard tereifa animals, and betrothal with them is valid
From where do we derive that money received for a forbidden item is permitted
The verse about the idolatrous city being banned like it teaches that money from it is like it, so other prohibitions are permitted
Can we derive a general principle from idolatry to other prohibitions
No: idolatry and Sabbatical produce are two verses that come as one, so the principle is not extended
The source for idolatry is what was said, and the source for Sabbatical produce follows
What is the source for the Sabbatical produce halakha
The verse calls the Jubilee holy, so Sabbatical produce transfers its sanctity to the redemption money like consecrated property
Objects: then, like consecrated property, the Sabbatical produce should be desacralized when redeemed
The verse says it shall be in its nature, so the Sabbatical produce is not desacralized
Explains: buying meat with Sabbatical produce binds the meat, and the chain of purchases transfers sanctity to the last item only
On the view that verses teach common aspects, why is money from a forbidden item not likewise forbidden
Restriction words are written in both cases: banned in the idol verse and a Jubilee in the Sabbatical verse, so no other item follows
Mishna: betrothal with terumot, tithes, priestly gifts, or purification water and ashes is valid, even by an Israelite
Ulla rules that the benefit of a forbidden item is not money
Rabbi Abba objects to Ulla from the same mishna, which validates betrothal with those items, even by an Israelite
Reply: here an Israelite who received teruma from his mother's priestly father, who holds unseparated gifts are like separated ones
Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin asks Rav Huna whether the benefit of a forbidden item is money or not
Rav Huna: you learned the mishna; we explained even an Israelite is the one who received teruma from his mother's priestly father

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna tells R. Hiyya bar Avin he is out, which the other takes as a rebuke
Rav Huna explains that he meant the opposite: the other is correct
Rav Asi of Huzal agrees with you, so the Gemara suggests a tannaitic dispute
Baraita: a thief of untithed produce pays full value per R. Yehuda HaNasi, but R. Yosei b. R. Yehuda disagrees
Is the dispute not about whether the benefit of discretion has monetary value
One Sage holds the benefit of discretion has monetary value, the other denies it
No, all agree the benefit of discretion is not money, so the proposed resolution fails
Here the case is untithed produce from a priestly grandfather and unseparated gifts, where the dispute is whether they count as separated
One Sage holds unseparated gifts count as separated, the other denies it
Alternatively, everyone agrees gifts count as separated and the benefit of discretion has no value
Here the dispute concerns Shmuel's view that one grain exempts the whole pile
Alternatively, everyone rejects Shmuel's view
Explains why R. Yehuda HaNasi penalizes the thief: the Sages penalized the thief
Alternatively, everyone accepts Shmuel's view
Explains R. Yosei b. R. Yehuda's reason: the Sages penalized the owner for not waiting to tithe
Mishnah: one who betroths with terumah, maaser, gifts, sotah water or ashes of the red cow is betrothed even if he is an Israelite
Contradiction: a baraita says one who takes payment for judging or testifying is disqualified from sprinkling and sanctifying
Abaye replies the cases differ: one concerns payment for bringing and filling, the other for sprinkling and sanctifying
Textual evidence supports Abaye: the Mishnah mentions sotah water and ashes, while the baraita says sprinkling and sanctifying
Chapter-ending formula and the start of the next chapter
Mishnah: if one tells another to betroth a woman and he betroths her himself, she is betrothed to the first
Mishnah: if a man tells a woman she is betrothed to him after thirty days, and another betroths her within thirty days, she is betrothed to the second
Mishnah: an Israelite woman married to a priest may eat terumah from now, and after thirty days, the status changes
Mishnah: if another betroths her within thirty days she is not betrothed, so the case is different
Mishnah: an Israelite woman to a priest, or a priest's daughter to an Israelite, may not eat terumah
Mishnah repeats: one who tells another to go and betroth
Baraita: what he did stands, but he acted deceitfully
Our Mishnah also says the one who went acted deceitfully, supporting the baraita
Why does this case say one who tells another, when the other case is phrased differently

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the difference between the agent wording in the earlier mishnah and this one
Each wording teaches a novelty, so both formulations are needed
If the tanna said only agent, one might think only the agent is a deceiver since he relied on the agent
Otherwise one might think the other party is not a deceiver, so the wording teaches something new
If the tanna said to a friend, one might think the friend is at fault since he did not go to the trouble of betrothing elsewhere
But the agent troubled himself, so one might say the place is merely indicated; the wording teaches the novelty
Rabin the pious went to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself
A baraita says the deceiver's act stands but he acted fraudulently, so the act should not be given to him
He should have informed them, but meanwhile another man betrothed her
Rabbah bar bar Hana paid Rav to buy a field for him, but Rav bought it for himself
The same baraita again: what he did stands but he acted fraudulently
Explains the difference: Rav had powerful supporters who honored him, while Rabbah bar bar Hana did not receive honor
He should have informed him, but meanwhile another man bought the land from Rav
Rav Gidal had sold the land, and R. Abba bought it
Rav Gidal approached R. Zeira, who approached Rav Yitzchak the smith
Story: Rav Yitzchak told him to wait until after the festival, but a poor man bought the field in the meantime and was called wicked
Why did the sage act this way
He replied that he had not known
Proposal that now too the field should be returned to the first owner
He replied that he would not sell it because it was the first land, and that the field could be given as a gift if he wished
Rav Gidal accepted it and did not go down to it
Scripture: one who hates gifts will live, supporting Rav Gidal's refusal to take a gift
R. Abba did not take it because Rav Gidal had turned it, meaning he had reclaimed it
Neither Rav Gidal nor R. Abba went down to the field
The field is therefore called the field of the Rabbis
Mishnah: if a man tells a woman to be betrothed to him
If another betrothed her within thirty days, what is the law
Rav and Shmuel both say she is betrothed, even though the money was already eaten
What is the reason; the money is not like a loan's money
The money resembles a deposit, which is used with the owner's permission
A deposit is eaten with the owner's permission, and these were eaten with her permission, but a loan is not similar
A loan is for expenses, but these were given as betrothal money
If another betrothed her and she then retracted, what is the law
R. Yohanan says she returns, since a later utterance can cancel an earlier one
Resh Lakish says she does not return, since no utterance cancels a prior one
R. Yohanan objects to Resh Lakish from a mishnah: if one cancelled before terumah was separated, the terumah is not terumah
But here it is one utterance and another, and a later utterance cancels an earlier one
Here the giving of money to a woman is an act, and an utterance does not cancel an act
Objection from a baraita: a man who sends a get to his wife and the agent delivers it, but he says the get was given to her, is cancelled
But giving a get through an agent is like giving money to a woman, and the mishnah states it is cancelled
There too, as long as the get has not reached her hand, it is word and word, so a later utterance cancels
Resh Lakish objects to R. Yohanan: all vessels become impure through thought, and they regain purity only through an act of change

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Principle: an act of the woman removes a betrothal instantly, while a thought alone does not
Granted, act-to-act does not cancel, but thought-to-thought should be considered; this is restated
Thought in matters of impurity is treated as an act, which answers the point
Rav Pappa raises a contradiction from a verse
Leviticus 11:38 is read two ways, yitein and yiyten, to resolve the reading
Just as yitein means it pleases him, so yiyten also means it pleases him, resolving the contradiction
Rav Zevid taught this case: a woman who gave her agent permission to betroth her, and she betrothed herself
If the permission was hers, her betrothal takes effect; if it was the agent's, the earlier one takes precedence
She betrothed herself and then retracted, what is the law
R. Yohanan says she returns, since a later utterance cancels an earlier one; Resh Lakish says she does not return
R. Yohanan objects to Resh Lakish from a mishnah on terumah cancelled before separation
Rava explains: the case is where the owner preceded and separated his terumah, which was an act
Resh Lakish objects from a baraita: vessels become impure through thought but regain purity only through an act of change
The principle restated: an act removes a betrothal from an act, but thought does not remove it
Granted, act-to-act does not cancel and an utterance does not cancel an act, but thought should be considered
Thought in matters of impurity is like an act, as with Rav Pappa's case
Rav Pappa raises a contradiction, as it is written
The verse is read as yitein and yiyten to resolve the contradiction
Just as yitein means it pleases him, yiyten likewise means it pleases him
R. Yohanan objects to Resh Lakish from a baraita: a man who sends a get to his wife, which is cancelled
This is a refutation of Resh Lakish, and the halakha follows R. Yohanan even in the first case
Even though giving money to a woman is like an act, an utterance still cancels an utterance, which is difficult
The halakha follows Rav Nachman, as the Gemara affirms
Whether a man may return and divorce with the same get
Rav Nachman says he may return and divorce with it
Rav Sheshet says he may not return and divorce with it
The halakha follows Rav Nachman
Granted he cancelled it as agent's authority, he did not cancel it as a get
Rav says she is betrothed to the second; Shmuel says also betrothed to the second
Shmuel: until thirty days, the second betrothal stands; after thirty days, the second lapses and the first is completed
Rav Hisda asks: how does the second betrothal lapse
Rav Yosef answers: you teach the first part; Rav Yehuda teaches the end, and it is not difficult
The mishnah: from now, and after thirty days
Rav and Shmuel dispute: Rav says betrothed and not betrothed, Shmuel says only until thirty days, then the second lapses
Rav doubts whether it is a condition or a retraction; Shmuel holds it is a condition, a dispute between tannaim
Baraita: from today, and after death, is a get but not a get, the words of the Sages
R. Yehuda HaNasi says it is a get
Let Rav say halakha like the Sages and Shmuel say halakha like Rabbi
It was necessary to state both, since if Rav said like the Sages I would think he speaks of a distant case
I would think it applies only to a distant case, but here it applies to a close one, so Rav agrees with Shmuel that it is a condition
If Shmuel had said halakha like Rabbi I would think it applies only where there is no get after death, but here betrothal after thirty days exists, so Rav agrees; both are necessary
Abaye says, according to Rav's reasoning
Case: a man says to a woman you are betrothed to me from now and after thirty days; another comes and says the same with twenty days

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Case: a man tells a woman she is betrothed to him now, and a second man does so ten days later; the first needs a get, the middle one does not
Dilemma: either the wording is a condition, so the first betrothal is valid, or a retraction, so the last is valid; either way the result is obvious
One might think the wording suggests both condition and retraction, so should a get be needed from each
The Gemara answers that the case teaches a get is needed from each
Ulla and R. Assi report R. Yohanan: even a hundred betrothals take effect
Rav Mesharshiya explains R. Yohanan's reasoning: each betrothal is like a candle that extinguishes the one before
Rav Chanina objects from a baraita: from today and after death a get is not a get, and if he died she performs chalitzah, not levirate marriage
Granted, this supports Rav, and for Shmuel it is the view of the Sages; but for R. Yohanan, who holds a remainder is nothing, levirate marriage applies
Rava: a get removes the woman, death removes her, and what a get leaves, death completes
Abaye objects: is a get comparable to death, since death brings her into the levir's domain
Abaye replies the reason is a rabbinic decree lest one extend from now to death, and so it is only a rabbinic concern
Mishnah: a man who tells a woman she is betrothed to him on condition that he gives her two hundred zuz
Mishnah continues: if he gives within thirty days she is betrothed, otherwise she is not
Mishnah: betrothal on condition of showing her two hundred zuz; if he shows them on the table, she is not betrothed
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute the wording: he will give, or when he gives
Rav Huna says the condition holds and the betrothal takes effect; Rav Yehuda says only when he gives
Now the betrothal is not in effect
What is the practical difference between them
The difference: if she extended her hand and accepted betrothal from another, the betrothal is valid according to Rav Yehuda, but not Rav Huna
A mishnah in tractate Gittin is a similar case, supporting this reasoning
Mishnah: a man says to a woman, this is your get on condition you give me two hundred zuz, and she is divorced
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute whether she will give, or when she gives; Rav Huna holds the condition is kept
Rav Yehuda: when she gives it, it is then a get; now it is not yet a get

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the practical difference between the two positions
If the get is torn or lost, Rav Huna holds it is a valid get, while Rav Yehuda holds it is not
Both cases are needed: betrothal concerns the near party, divorce the far, so Rav Yehuda would agree
If the dispute concerned the same case, Rav Huna would say the husband does not want to demand it, but here the wife does, so Rav Yehuda agrees
Objection from a baraita: a get on condition of two hundred zuz remains valid even if torn or lost, and the levirate rules follow
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view: she may give it to her brother, her father, or a close relative; they do not disagree this far
Rather, they dispute whether the condition benefits only the husband or also his heirs; either way it is a condition, refuting Rav Yehuda
Rav Yehuda replies that this is the view of Rabbi, who held as Rav Huna says
Rav Huna reports Rabbi: anyone who says on condition is like one who says from now, and the Sages disagree
Rav Huna again reports Rabbi: anyone who says on condition is like one who says from now
Rabbi Zeira reports that in Babylonia they said Rav Huna's statement, with the Sages disagreeing
Rabbi Assi reports in the name of R. Yohanan that all agree conditional betrothal is like betrothal from now
They disagree only about from today and after death
A baraita supports this: from today and after death is a get and not a get, the words of the Sages; Rabbi says it is a get
For Rav Yehuda, who holds a conditional statement too, they dispute the same question, and Rabbi holds it is a get
The Sages hold that the permission to act outweighs a condition from here on; this is obvious
One might think it is not a condition but mere encouragement; the Gemara teaches otherwise
Case: on condition that I have two hundred zuz
Should we suspect he has it, as a baraita teaches that we are concerned lest he has it
No difficulty: one case concerns certain betrothal, the other doubtful betrothal
Baraita: on condition that I show her two hundred zuz; the tanna intended only to show from his own; if on the table she is not betrothed
This is obvious, but the case is needed because the tanna used the expression of a deal
Mishnah: on condition that I have a house of a kor of dust, she is betrothed; and if he has it in a certain place
Mishnah: on condition that I show her a house of a kor of dust; if he shows it in the valley she is not betrothed
Should we suspect he has it, as a baraita teaches concern lest he has it
No contradiction: one is certain betrothal, the other doubtful
Why teach about land and why teach about money
It is needed: money is taught because people hide money, but land is publicly known, so the mishnah teaches both
Mishnah: on condition that I have it in a certain place, and if he has it there
Is this obvious, and what is the point: what do you gain from it
It teaches us that otherwise one might say he would have to bring it, so the case is taught
Baraita: the tanna did not intend it except to show from his own; if shown in the valley, not betrothed
It is needed: the case of a dish-like object, as the mishnah teaches regarding consecrated property

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: one who consecrates his field in the Jubilee year, with pits or cliffs ten handbreadths deep or high, is measured with them or not
We asked: if they are not consecrated along with the land, are they consecrated on their own, and if so why not
A baraita contradicts this: the verse says the field, so we ask where we get the sowing measure of barley for fifty shekels
The verse says the field from any place, which includes smaller measures, supporting the inclusion
Mar Ukva explains the case of pits filled with water, because they are not fit for sowing; the mishnah's wording supports this
Mishnah on sale: one who tells another, I sell you a house of a kor of dust, with pits ten handbreadths deep or high, is measured with them
Mar Ukva says the same even when the pits are not filled with water
Rav Pappa explains: a person does not want to put his money in one field and have it appear as two or three places
Here, do we liken it to consecration or to sale
It is reasonable to liken it to consecration, since he says I will work, sow and bring the produce
Mishnah: R. Meir says any condition that is not like the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuven is not a condition
The verse in Numbers says if the Gadites and Reuvenites cross over, and then, if they do not cross over as armed men
R. Chanina ben Gamliel says the matter must be stated, since otherwise it would imply they would not inherit even in Canaan
R. Chanina ben Gamliel rightly said this to R. Meir
R. Meir replies: if you think it is not a condition, the verse is a repetition written to say and if they do not cross over

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why is this needed; learn from it that it is a repeated condition
R. Chanina ben Gamliel: if the Torah had not written in the land of Canaan, one might think the inheritance applies only in Gilead
One might think the verse 'they shall possess among you' refers to Gilead, and not to the land of Canaan at all
R. Meir reads 'among you' as applying wherever there is an implication for you
Baraita: R. Chanina ben Gamliel's parable of a man dividing his property among his sons, with conditions on the field and the two hundred zuz
The parable does not apply to the mishnah, since there the verse teaches they will not inherit even in Canaan
Explains the difference: in the parable the doubling applies to the other property, not to the land of Gilead
No difficulty: one is before R. Meir's statement and the other after it
Genesis 4:7 supports R. Meir: if you do well, you shall be lifted up, and if not, sin crouches at the door
But for R. Chanina ben Gamliel, why is the verse needed
One might think it is a reward for good and nothing for bad; the verse teaches neither reward nor punishment
Genesis 24:41 supports R. Meir: then you will be clear of my oath
But for R. Chanina ben Gamliel, why is it needed
One might think it applies where it pleases the one party, not the other, so the husband brings her against her will; the verse teaches otherwise
Leviticus 26:3 and 26:15 support R. Meir: if you walk in my statutes, and if you despise my statutes
For R. Chanina, one might think if you walk it is a blessing, and if you despise it is not a blessing, so the verse teaches neither blessing nor curse
Isaiah 1:19 supports R. Meir: if you are willing and obedient, and if you refuse and rebel
For R. Chanina, one might think if you are willing it is good, and if you refuse it is not good, so the verse teaches neither good nor bad
What is the final point of this discussion

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava explains the verse about eating dry food: dry bread with salt and onions is hard on the body
Numbers 5:19 supports R. Chanina ben Gamliel: if no man has lain with you, and if you have not gone astray, the innocent wife
But for R. Meir it should read strangled
R. Tanchum replies that the verse says the innocent, so it is written
The word innocent supports R. Meir
For R. Chanina ben Gamliel, one might think if no man lay with her she is innocent, and if he did she is neither innocent nor strangled, so the verse teaches it is just a prohibition

A married woman can also be distinguished: the other relations have no permit while the wife lives, unlike a married woman.
Rather, Rabbi Yona or Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua says: a verse links all forbidden relations to the wife's sister.
Leviticus 18:29 says those who commit these abominations are cut off, and the verse equates all forbidden relations to the wife's sister.
Just as betrothal does not take effect with a wife's sister, it does not take effect with any forbidden relation.
Asks what follows if so, as the rule would then apply to all forbidden relations.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye asserts all agree that intercourse with a menstruant or a sota does not make the child a mamzer.
Chizkiyahu cites Leviticus 15:24 that the impurity applies even at the very moment of her menstruation.
Challenges the comparison: why liken this to the wife's sister rather than to a menstruant, and what was seen in it?
Rav Aha bar Ya'akov derives by a fortiori from a yevama that other lav-liable relations also do not allow betrothal.
Rav Pappa says that those liable for lav violations are explicitly written in the verse.
Reads Deuteronomy 21:15 on two wives, one loved and one hated, to show the verse's intended meaning of loved and hated.
Asks how Rabbi Akiva, who denies betrothal for lav-liable women, explains the verse's 'when you shall be'.
Explains it as a widow to the High Priest, following Rabbi Simai.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Simai: Rabbi Akiva would make every offspring a mamzer except a widow to the High Priest, per Leviticus 21:6.
Rabbi Yishbav says: come, let us denounce Akiva ben Yosef, who said any without lawful intercourse in Israel has a mamzer child.
Grants that this explains Rabbi Yishbav's view if it excludes Rabbi Simai's position.
If the view is Akiva's own reasoning, asks how the case of positive-commandment liability is explained.
It is explained as a married woman to the High Priest, since the positive commandment is not equal in all cases.
The Rabbis explain the verse as concerning lav-liable women, while we explain it as concerning positive-commandment liability.
Asks which positive-commandment-liable women are meant, and whether the verse can be read as applying to a priest.
Rabbi Akiva, unable to read the verse naturally, sets it aside and gives his own explanation.
Quotes the mishna's general phrase: any woman who cannot be betrothed to him, and so on.
Asks from where we learn that a Canaanite maidservant cannot be betrothed.
Rav Huna cites Genesis 22:5, Stay here with the donkey, to show that betrothal does not take effect with her.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where we know that a child of such a union follows the mother's status.
Cites Exodus 21:4, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, to show the child follows the mother.
Asks the same question again, for a different source.
Cites Deuteronomy 7:3 forbidding intermarriage, so betrothal does not take effect and the child is like the mother.
Asks from where this is derived, according to Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yohanan cites Shimon ben Yohai's reading of Deuteronomy 7:4: your son is called yours only from an Israelite woman.
Ravina infers that a child of a gentile's daughter's son is not yours but is yours only through an Israelite mother.
Challenges Ravina: does he hold that a gentile slave who has relations with an Israelite woman yields a mamzer child?
Granted he is not a mamzer, he is still disqualified; the seven nations are listed, so the rest must be derived.
Asks from where we learn that the other nations are included in the same rule.
The phrase for he will turn away your son is included to cover all who turn him away from following God.
Granted for Rabbi Shimon, who derives the reason from the verse's wording, the matter is clear.
But for the Rabbis, what is the reason?
Rabbis derive from Deuteronomy 21:13 that the marriage follows the captive, so betrothal did not take effect at first.
We find that betrothal does not take effect in such cases, and the child is like the mother.
Asks from where we derive that the child is like the mother in the captive-woman case.
Cites Deuteronomy 21:15, that children are born to a man when the verse is read this way, and when not, not.
If so, asks whether a maidservant too is included.
Yes, so too, a maidservant's child follows her status.
Asks why the verse on the woman and her children belonging to her master is needed, if the rule is already known.
Introduces a baraita as the source for the answer.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A man tells his maidservant she is free and her child is a slave, so the child follows her status.
Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's ruling stands, and the Sages agree his words remain valid.
Cites Exodus 21:4, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, as the source for the child following the mother.
Asks what the Talmud concludes from this.
Raba objects that this contradicts Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's own position.
Mishna: Rabbi Tarfon says mamzerim may purify themselves, meaning their status can be improved.
Asks how this works.
Example: a mamzer marries a maidservant, the child is a slave whose master frees him, so the child is free.
Rabbi Eliezer says such a child is a slave and a mamzer, with no improvement.
Raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Tarfon speak ab initio, or only after the fact?
A baraita reports Rabbi Tarfon was told he purified the males but not the females, supporting the after-the-fact reading.
If he meant ab initio, a mamzeret would also marry a slave, but a slave has no compassion for her.
Cites the story of Rabbi Shmelai's mamzer son and the remark that if he had been first, he would have purified them.
If after the fact, asks what the advice was that the mamzer received.
The advice was to steal and be sold as a Hebrew slave, so the child is freed in the Jubilee.
Objects that a Hebrew slave applies only when Jubilee applies, so the case must be ab initio.
Rather, learn from this that Rabbi Tarfon speaks ab initio.
Rav Yehuda says Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Tarfon.
Rabbi Eliezer says such a person is a Hebrew slave and a mamzer.
Rabbi Elazar asks what is the reasoning behind Rabbi Eliezer's view.
Rabbi Eliezer derives from Deuteronomy 23:3 that the child follows the disqualified parent.
The Rabbis object: could one think the child of an Israelite who married a mamzeret is a mamzer?
Cites Numbers 4:2, by families and by fathers' houses, against the Rabbis' reading.
Explains the verse as excluding such a case, and that the Rabbis read the verse on the woman and children similarly.
The Rabbis hold that a child in the womb of a Canaanite maidservant is like a child in the womb of an animal.
Marks the end of the chapter and begins the next chapter's opening mishna.
Mishna: ten lineage categories came up from Babylon; priests, Levites and Israelites may intermarry with each other.
Converts, freedmen, mamzerim, Netinim, shetuki and asufi may all intermarry with each other.
Defines shetuki as one who knows his mother but not his father, and asufi as one gathered from the marketplace.
Asufi is one who knows neither his father nor his mother.
Abba Shaul used to call a shetuki a bedoki.
Restates the mishna's list: ten lineage categories came up from Babylon.
Asks why the mishna specifies came up from Babylon rather than went to the Land of Israel.
It is incidental, mentioned along the way, to teach the halakha that follows.
Cites Deuteronomy 17:8 to show the Temple is higher than the Land of Israel, which is higher than all other lands.
Granted the Temple is higher than the rest of the Land of Israel, as the verse states.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Deuteronomy 17:8 that the Temple is higher than the Land of Israel, which is higher than all other lands.
Asks from where this is derived.
Cites Jeremiah 23:7-8: the Lord who brought Israel out of Egypt and from all lands; the later exodus outweighs the first.
Asks why the mishna specifies came up from Babylon rather than came up to the Land of Israel.
This supports Rabbi Elazar's view.
Rabbi Elazar holds Ezra did not ascend from Babylon until it was made like fine flour, meaning until it was purified.
Abaye says they went up on their own, as the mishna teaches.
Rava says they were brought up, as the mishna teaches.
The Sages dispute how to read Rabbi Elazar's ruling in the mishna.
Restates Rabbi Elazar's ruling that Ezra did not ascend until the land was made like fine flour.
Abaye lacks Rabbi Elazar's view, while Rava has it.
Alternatively, everyone holds Rabbi Elazar's view, so the dispute is not about his ruling.
The dispute is whether they went up of their own accord or were forced; one side says forced.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: all lands are dough for the Land of Israel, and the Land of Israel is dough for Babylon.
On the view that they were brought up, they would know the lineage only for that generation, not later ones.
Cites Ezra 8:15 about gathering the people and Levites at the river, showing Levites were absent, consistent with a brought-up view.
On the view they were brought up, they were warned about disqualified people but not about fit ones.
Asks from where we know that priests, Levites and Israelites were included in this process.
Cites Ezra 2:70 that priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, Netinim and all Israel dwelt in their towns.
Asks from where we know that the disqualified, converts and freedmen are included.
A baraita: Rabbi Yosei says a strong presumption applies, citing Ezra 2:61-63 on those seeking their lineage and Tirshata's ruling.
Tirshata tells them they remain in their status: as they ate sacred food in exile, so here too they eat sacred food of the boundaries.
Introduces the alternative view that they were raised from terumah to lineage status.
Those who ate terumah came up; there the case differs, since their presumptive status was disputed.
Asks what then is the point of a greater presumptive status.
They first ate rabbinic terumah, and later ate Torah-level terumah.
Alternatively, even now they eat rabbinic-level terumah but do not eat Torah-level terumah.
Do we conclude lineage from terumah by Torah law or by rabbinic law? If so, what is the greater presumptive status for?
Asks again what the point of the greater presumptive status is, from the start.
Since Torah-level terumah cannot be a basis from the start, a rabbinic-level basis is used, though Torah-level terumah is a concern later.
Cites Ezra 2:63 that they may not eat the holy of holies until a priest with Urim and Thummim stands, to show the verse's scope.
Explains the verse: the holy of holies is not eaten by a zar, and nothing called holy or holy items is eaten by one who is not a priest.
Cites Leviticus 22:12 that a priest's daughter married to a zar may not eat the terumah of holy offerings.
The master said this concerns what is lifted from the holy offerings.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where we learn that converts and freedmen may not eat terumah.
Rav Hisda cites Ezra 6:21 that everyone separating from the impurity of the land's gentiles, including mamzerim, joined them.
Asks from where we learn that a mamzer is included in this exclusion.
Cites Nehemiah 2:10 and 6:18 about Tobiah and the Judean husbands of Tobiah's relatives, to show mamzerim and their kin were included.
Holds that a gentile or slave who has relations with an Israelite woman yields a mamzer child.
This works for the view that the child is a mamzer.
But for one who holds the child is fit, what can be said?
Asks how we know they had sons at all, and whether those in the other place had sons, since it could be that they had none.
Cites Nehemiah 7:61 about those who went up from Tel-Melah and Tel-Harsha, and who could not show their fathers' house.
Explains the verse's terms: Tel-Melah and Tel-Harsha as those whose deeds resemble Sodom, and whose father is unknown, as an asufi who was gathered from the market.
Rabbi Abbahu says in the name of the Lord: I said Israel would be esteemed before me like a cabbage.
Rabbi Abbahu's variant: Israel named themselves like a leopard, yet are esteemed before me like a cabbage.
Rabba bar bar Hana rules that one who marries an unfit woman is considered to have plowed the whole world and his seed is salt.
Cites Nehemiah 7:61 about those who went up from Tel-Melah and Tel-Harsha to support the salt-seed rule.
Rabba bar Rav Adda says in Rav's name: one who marries for money has children who are not fit.
Cites Hosea 5:7: they have dealt treacherously with the Lord, for they have borne strange children.
Shows from Hosea 5:7 that the money is not lost, and that a new month will consume their portions and not their lineage.
Asks what this derivation implies.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak: a new month enters and a month leaves, and their money is lost.
Rabba bar Rav Adda cites Rav Hamnuna: one who marries an unfit woman is bound by Elijah and cut by the Holy One.
A teaching: Elijah writes and the Holy One seals; woe to one who disqualifies his seed, and he does not speak in praise.
Shmuel says that one who disqualifies someone for a blemish is disqualified himself.
Story: a man from Menahardea visited the butchers in Pumbedita and asked for meat; they told him to wait until he paid Rav Yehuda bar Yehezkel's apprentice.
The man protests: who is Yehuda bar Shvishkal, who took the meat before me?
They told Rav Yehuda, who excommunicated the man; they said he was accustomed to calling people slaves, so Rav Yehuda proclaimed him a slave.
That man summoned him to court before Rav Naḥman, and Rav Yehuda went before Rav Huna.
Rav Yehuda asks Rav Huna whether he should go or not.
Rav Huna says he need not go on account of the man's great status, but out of respect for the house of the Nasi, so he should go.
Rav Huna came and found him building a parapet.
Asks whether the master does not hold the rule Rav Huna bar Idi cited from Shmuel.
Quotes Shmuel: once a man is appointed communal leader, he may not do work in front of three people.
He replies that he is only making a small sort of parapet.
Asks whether a parapet is a Torah-level requirement or a barrier the Sages established.
He tells him to sit on a cushion instead, evading the question.
Asks whether a bench is a rabbinic enactment or a shelf people call one.
He tells him to eat an etrog instead.
Shmuel rules that whoever names the fruit as the Sages named it, the etrog, speaks correctly, and not as common speech does.
Asks whether the fruit is called an etrog as the Sages name it, or an etrogah as people say.
He tells him to drink instead, evading the question about the name.
Asks whether the plant is called by the Sages' name or by the common name.
He tells him to drink something else instead, evading the question.
Shmuel says that one may not make use of a minor woman, as stated explicitly.
Shmuel says that one may not make use of a woman at all, whether adult or minor.
Asks the messenger to convey a greeting, whether adult or minor, from the master.
Conveys Shmuel's view that a voice is a form of nakedness for a woman, and may be conveyed through a messenger.
Repeats the ruling that Shmuel says this.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A woman may not be greeted in the name of her husband, as a rule.
Shmuel's ruling: one may not inquire after a woman's welfare at all.
Shmuel's wife sent a greeting; he permitted him to rebuke her so she would not become like an ordinary person.
Asks what the matter is with the master here.
Recounts the summons: the messenger was sent to fetch him, and the document was brought out and shown.
The man says the master came here to speak with him, so that the scholars would not accuse each other of flattery.
Asks why the master excommunicated the man, who had troubled the Sages' emissary, and what the reason was for that.
Explains the reason: the man was accustomed to calling people slaves, so he was proclaimed a slave.
Teaching: one who disqualifies is disqualified, and does not speak in praise, always.
Shmuel says one who disqualifies someone for a blemish is disqualified.
Asks whether Shmuel's view should lead one to proclaim the man, and whether he actually said so.
Interjects that a man from Nehardea came in.
The man says Rav Yehuda called him a slave, and that Shmuel said whoever comes from the Hasmonean house is a slave.
Asks whether the master does not hold the ruling Rav Huna cited from Rav.
Rav Huna cites Rav: a Torah scholar whose ruling precedes his deed is heard; otherwise he is not heard.
Counters that Rav Matna stood with him, a counterexample to the rule.
Notes that Rav Matna did not visit Nehardea for thirteen years.
One day someone came and asked whether the master remembered what Shmuel said.
Quotes Shmuel's image: one foot on the bank and one in the boat.
Shmuel's ruling is told: the one who came from the Hasmonean house is a slave, and a woman who fell from a roof and died was the case.
The man was proclaimed a slave on account of this.
The householders threatened to expose them if they stayed silent, recalling Shmuel's teaching.
Shmuel says Nehardea has two families: one called the house of Yonah and one the house of Orbetai, marked by the purity signs.
They threw the stone from their hands, and the man stood, becoming impure in the king's river.
Rav Yehuda proclaimed in Pumbedita that Adda and Yonatan, Yehuda bar Pappa, a mamzeret, and others, were all disqualified.
Rav Yehuda says the Gibeonites, Gevaites, Tsardonites, and others are disqualified.
Rav Yosef says that the house of the dyers of Pumbedita are all disqualified.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: four hundred slaves, or four thousand, were Pashhur son of Immer's, and they all merged into the priesthood.
Any priest with impudence is only one of those.
Abaye says they are all sitting in the market of Nehardea.
This disagrees with Rabbi Elazar's view.
Rabbi Elazar says: if you see a priest with brazen face, do not question him.
Cites Hosea 4:4, your people are like those who contend with the priest, to support Rabbi Elazar.
Rabbi Abin bar Rav Adda cites Rav: when God rests His presence, He testifies about all tribes, but not about one who married an unfit woman.
Cites Psalms 122:4, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony for Israel.
Asks when this is a testimony for Israel: only when the tribes are tribes of the Lord.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina: God rests His presence only on the distinguished families of Israel.
Cites Jeremiah 31:1 that God will be God to all the families of Israel, reading the verse as including all those families.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: there is a further advantage of Israel over converts.
Ezekiel 37:27 is written of Israel: I will be their God and they will be My people.
Jeremiah 30:21 is written of converts: who is this who pledged his heart to approach Me, and you shall be My people.
Rabbi Helbo says converts are hard for Israel like a scab, citing Isaiah 14:1.
The same word for joined appears in Isaiah and in Leviticus 14:56 about leprous scab.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says that when the Holy One, blessed be He, does something.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Malachi 3:3 that the tribe of Levi is purified first, and the sons of Levi are refined like gold and silver.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: silver purifies mamzerim, as Malachi says the Lord sits refining and purifying silver.
Asks what is meant by bringing offerings in righteousness.
Rabbi Yitzhak: God showed righteousness to Israel by letting a family that was absorbed be absorbed, and so it is.
Shmuel rules that all lands are dough for the Land of Israel, and the Land of Israel is dough for Babylon.
In the days of Rabbi, they sought to make Babylon dough for the Land of Israel.
Rabbi rebukes them: you are placing thorns in my eyes; let your will be joined with yours.
Rabbi Hanina bar Hama joined them and told them a tradition.
The tradition from Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei, citing his father, repeats that all lands are dough for the Land of Israel.
In the days of Rabbi Pinhas, they sought to make Babylon dough for the Land of Israel, and he spoke to them.
Pinhas tells his servants that when he speaks two matters in the study house they should pull him from the cradle; he then says there is no slaughter of birds in the Torah.
They sat and considered the matter.
He said again that all lands are dough for the Land of Israel and the Land of Israel for Babylon; they pulled him from the cradle, then reconsidered until they reached danger, and separated.
Rabbi Yohanan: the sanctuary is in our hands, but great men of the generation were absorbed by it, so what can I do?
Rabbi Yohanan holds like Rabbi Yitzhak, who said a family that was absorbed is absorbed.

Abaye cites a mishna that the family of the house of the hut was beyond the Jordan and was distanced by Ben Zion, and another was brought near, like Elijah who came to make impure and pure, distance and bring near.
A family that was absorbed is absorbed; a tanna teaches there was yet another family.
The Sages did not want to reveal it, but they transmit it to their children and students once a week.
Others say it is transmitted several times a week.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak: it is reasonable to follow the view that it is transmitted once a week.
A baraita: I will be a nazirite if I do not reveal the families; he shall be a nazirite and not reveal the families.
Rabba bar bar Hana: Rabbi Yohanan says the four-letter name is transmitted to students once a week, or several times.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak concludes it is reasonable to follow the view of once a week.
Cites Exodus 3:15, this is my name forever, the name written as a forever name.
Raba intended to expound the matter in a lecture.
An old man objected to Raba: the text reads forever.
Rabbi Avina raised a contradiction between two verses in Exodus 3:15, this is My name and this is My remembrance.
God said: when written I am called, I am written with yod and heh, and called with aleph and dalet.
A baraita: the name of twelve letters was transmitted to everyone; when the impudent multiplied, it was transmitted to the modest priests, who swallowed it in their brothers' chanting.
Rabbi Tarfon recounts that he once went up to the platform after his brother and mother, and heard the high priest swallow it in his brothers' chanting.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: the name of forty-two letters is transmitted only to one who is modest, humble, and of middle age, and so on, rewarded in both worlds.
Shmuel cites an elder: Babylon is held to be fit until one knows what disqualified it, while other lands are held disqualified until one knows what made them fit.
The Land of Israel is held as disqualified and presumed disqualified, and presumed fit and considered fit.
This itself is difficult: you said presumed disqualified is disqualified, but a generic is fit; another teaching says presumed fit is fit and generic is disqualified.
Rav Huna bar Tehalifa cites Rav: the difficulty does not stand.

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Distinguishes marrying a woman off to a man from taking a wife out of his hand, as two separate matters.
Rav Yosef: where a man's conduct is known in Babylon, we arrange a marriage for him; nowadays, with deceivers, we are concerned.
Ze'iri used to avoid Rabbi Yohanan, who would tell him to marry his daughter; once they were on the road, they came to a stream and he carried Rabbi Yohanan on his shoulders.
Ze'iri asks: your daughters are fit, but the daughters of Netinim are not? What do you think?
Challenges the claim from the mishna: did all the lineage groups come up from Babylon, so that the priests, Levites and Israelites are all equal in this?
Ze'iri simply forgot Rabbi Elazar's ruling that Ezra did not ascend until the land was made like fine flour.
Ulla came to the study house of Rav Yehuda and saw Rav Yitzhak, Rav Yehuda's son, who had grown up but not married.
Ulla asks Rav Yehuda why he does not arrange a wife for his son.
Rav Yehuda replies that he does not know where to find one for him.
Ulla retorts: do we know where we came from ourselves?
Cites Lamentations 5:11 about women in Zion humbled, virgins in the cities of Judah, as the possible source.
If you say a gentile or slave who has relations with an Israelite woman yields a fit child, the verse does not seem to apply.
Perhaps the source is Amos 6:4 about those who lie on beds of ivory and recline on couches.
Rabbi Yossi bar Hanina: these are people who urinate in front of their beds naked, and blaspheme in it.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Amos 6:7 that they will go into exile at the head of the exiles, because they urinate before their beds naked.
Rabbi Abbahu's alternative: these are people who eat and drink with one another, join their beds, swap their wives, and foul their couches with seed that is not their own.
Asks what he should do.
Tells him to follow silence, as the sons of the West do when they test for lineage.
When two people quarrel, they test which one speaks first and stays silent.
They say this one is more distinguished.
Rav says the silence of Babylon is a form of lineage.
Asks whether this is so.
But Rav came to a house and examined them; so it must be about lineage, not silence, and he tells them to be tested.
Rav's instruction: test them, whether they stay silent or not.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: if you see two people quarrelling and one has a blemish, do not let him join with the other.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: if you see two families quarrelling, and one has a blemish, do not let it join with the other.
Rav Papa cites Rav: Babylon is healthy and Mishon sick; Persia dying. The majority of the healthy live, and most of the dying die.
Asks how far Babylon extends.
Rav says up to the river Azak, Shmuel says up to the river Yuani.
Asks how far, in Diglat above, the boundary extends.
Rav says up to Bagda and Avvana; Shmuel says up to the tributary, and whether it is included.
Objects: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba cites Shmuel that the tributary is like exile for lineage; rather, up to the tributary and including it.
Asks how far the lower Diglat boundary extends.
Rav Shmuel: the lower apfamayya; there are two, one upper and one lower, one fit and one disqualified, with a parasang between them, and they are not to mix.
The mnemonic: what is disqualified is what the Mishnah described above at Perat.
Asks how far Rav's boundary extends.
Rav says up to the Ekra of Tulbakni, Shmuel says up to the bridge of the house of Perat.
Rabbi Yohanan says up to the crossing at Gizama.
Abaye, or as some say Rav Yosef, reports that one curses in Rav's name but not in Shmuel's name, and the reverse is objected to.
Another answer: one may curse in Rav's name, but not in Shmuel's, even though the reasoning is weighed the other way.
The bridge of the house of Perat was standing for its lower part.

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Notes that nowadays the Persians are the ones who say this about the Perat, as an aside.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef how far this side of the Perat extends.
Rav Yosef replies: Pumbedita's lineage is reckoned from Biram, and they marry from Biram.
Rav Pappa: the dispute about lineage is like the dispute about divorce documents; Rav Yosef says lineage only, and all agree on divorce to the second bridge.
Rami bar Abba: the sea is divided; the Babylonian indigo is the Shuniya and Guvia, and the indigo of the divided sea.
Ravina: the Tsitsura is also taught this way; Hanan ben Pinhas says the sea is divided, and Babylonian indigo is Shuniya, Guvia and Tsitsura.
Rav Pappa: nowadays Cutheans have mixed among them, and the woman who asked was not given a marriage.
Asks what the sea-divided term means.
Rav Pappa: this is the Perat of Borsi.
An anecdote: a man said to them, I am from the wash, and Rabbi Yitzhak the smith stood up and said, the wash is between the rivers; what then is the status?
Abaye cites Rabbi Hama bar Uqba citing Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: between the rivers is like exile for lineage.
Rabbi Yohanan says it stands from where it is dug and above.
But Rabbi Yohanan said up to the crossing at Gizama, which conflicts with that.
Abaye: it is a strip that exits, resolving the conflict.
Rav Ika bar Avin cites Rav Hananel citing Rav: the Helzon of Neihvand is like exile for lineage.
Abaye objects: do not accept him, for it is a levirate case; they went to ask Rav Hananel, who ruled as Rav did.
Rav Hananel's reply: thus said Rav, the Helzon of Neihvand is like exile for lineage.
This disagrees with Rabbi Abba bar Kahana, who cites what is written in Kings.
Cites 2 Kings 18:11 on Halah, Habor and the river Gozan, identifying each with a place in the region.
Others say Neihvand is the identification and its neighbors.
Asks what its neighbors are.
Shmuel: the large town, Mushki, Huskhi, and Rumaki.
Rabbi Yohanan: all of them are disqualified.
Asks whether Mushki is the same as Mushkhani.
Objects: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abin cites Shmuel that Mushkhani is like exile for lineage.
Rather, Mushki alone and Mushkhani alone are separate.
Cites Daniel 7:5 on a three-ribbed beast with teeth in its mouth.
Rabbi Yohanan identifies the creature in Daniel 7:5, which swallows some and spits out others.
Rav Yosef teaches that the second beast in the vision, like a bear, represents the Persians.
Persians eat and drink like a bear, are clumsy like a bear, grow hair like a bear, and have no rest like a bear.
Rabbi Ami, seeing a Persian riding, says it is a moving bear; Rabbi asks Levi to show him Persians.
Levi replies that they resemble the soldiers of the house of David, and shows him the companions, who resemble destroying angels.
He shows him Ishmaelites, who resemble goats of the outhouse, and the Sages of Babylon, who resemble ministering angels.
When Rabbi was pleased, he said there are Humanians in Babylon.
All of Babylon is Ammonite.
There are locksmiths in Babylon, and all of Babylon is mamzer.
There are sedge-gatherers in Babylon, and there are two brothers who exchange their wives.
There is a Pirta of Sutia in Babylon; they went out from the place which surrounded the fruit in the baskets on Shabbat, hunted on Shabbat, and Rabbi's brother Yashia set them aside.
There is a reed-field in Babylon; Adda bar Ahava is in it.

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opens with the saying that today a sage sits in Abraham's bosom and today another sage was born in Babylon, as the master said.
Each sage's death coincides with the birth of the next: Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi, Rav Yehuda, Rava, Rav Ashi.
This teaches that no righteous man dies before a righteous man like him is created.
Cites Ecclesiastes 1:5, the sun rises before it sets, to show the sun of Eli had not set before the sun of Samuel rose.
Cites 1 Samuel 3:3, the lamp of God had not yet gone out, with Samuel sleeping, to illustrate the same idea.
Cites Lamentations 1:17 that the Lord commanded Jacob that his neighbors be his adversaries.
Rav Yehuda says it is like the people of Humania by the river, citing Ezekiel 11:13.
Cites Ezekiel 11:13 on Pelatiah ben Benaiah dying, and Ezekiel falling on his face crying out, Ah Lord God.
Rav and Shmuel disagree: one says the death is for good, and the other says it is for bad.
Those who say it is for good point to the story of Ishtandar, the son-in-law of Nebuchadnezzar, who sent for a captive, and the request to send him Israelites.
Pelatiah ben Benaiah tells the king: we who are counted will go away, while those here are doing their work, let them go there.
A prophet said: whoever does good in Israel dies in the middle of his days; those who say it is bad hold this view.
Cites Ezekiel 11:1 on the prophet being brought to the gate of the house of the Lord facing east.
Ezekiel sees among the twenty-five men at the gate Jaazaniah ben Azzur and Pelatiah ben Benaiah, the leaders of the people.
Cites Ezekiel 8:16 about twenty-five men at the entrance of the Temple, with their backs to the Temple and faces eastward.
States that one does not know that their backs faced west.
Asks why the verse needs to say their backs were to the Temple of the Lord.
The verse teaches that they were turning their backs to the Temple and facing upward in order to provoke the Lord.
The prophet said: whoever does this evil in Israel will die on his bed, and it is fulfilled.
Shmuel's view that it is bad: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abin says Shmuel said that Mushkhani is like exile for lineage.
Mushkhani is like exile for lineage.
The people of Mishon were not concerned about it, neither as a matter of slavery nor as a matter of mamzerut.
Only the priests who were there were not careful about divorcees; in any case, I tell you Shmuel said it is for good.
Shmuel said it is for good.
Shmuel follows his view that one who leaves his slave free, he goes free and needs no writ of manumission.
Cites Exodus 12:44 on a slave bought with money, to show a slave whom the master can make use of is called a slave, but not one over whom the master has no right.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: this is the view of Rabbi Meir; the Sages say all lands are presumed fit.
Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mahoza.
Rav Ashi asks: what do you think, given that Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel?
Shmuel's view is that of Rabbi Meir; the Sages say all lands are presumed fit.
But in the houses of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid they did not teach it that way, and yet they did not accept it, because they had heard it from Rav Zevid of Nehardea.
A baraita: mamzerim and Netinim will be pure in the future; Rabbi Yosei holds this, but Rabbi Meir says they will not be pure.
Rabbi Yosei objects: has it not already been said in Ezekiel 36:25, I will sprinkle clean water on you and you shall be clean.
Rabbi Meir replies: the verse says from all your impurities and all your idols, not from mamzerut.
Rabbi Yosei rebuts: the verse says I will cleanse you, so it should say that even mamzerut is included.
For Rabbi Meir this is what is written, a mamzer shall dwell in Ashdod, in Zechariah 9:6.
But for Rabbi Yosei, what is the meaning of a mamzer dwelling in Ashdod?
Rav Yosef translates it as Israel dwelling among those who bathe in the land, where they were mixed with gentiles.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef: were it not for Rav Yehuda's citation of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, Elijah would come and remove from us the collars and the shackles.
A baraita: a convert may marry a mamzeret, according to Rabbi Yosei; Rabbi Yehuda says a convert may not marry a mamzeret.
One convert and one freed slave and one defiled person are permitted to marry a priestess.
Asks what is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's view.
Five congregations are written in the verse, so Rabbi Yosei reads them as distinct.

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists the congregations: one for priests, one for Levites, one for Israelites, and one for the mamzer and shetuki.
The shetuki among Israelites is not called a congregation of converts.
Rabbi Yehuda says priests and Levites come from one congregation, and he brings it to the congregation of converts.
Alternatively, there are two congregations: the mamzer and shetuki on one side, and shetuki among Israelites on the other.
Cites Deuteronomy 23:3: a mamzer shall not enter the Lord's assembly; a certain mamzer may not enter, but a doubtful one may.
Alternatively, these too are two congregations, and Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning comes from here.
Cites Numbers 15:15, one statute for you and the convert, which Rabbi Yosei reads as one law for the convert, freedman and defiled, who may marry a priestess.
This supports Rav, who holds that the fit were not warned to marry the disqualified.
Rabbi Zeira taught in Mahoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the people stoned him with their etrogs.
Raba objects: is there anyone who teaches such a thing in a place where converts are common?
Raba taught in Mahoza that a convert may marry a priestess; they accused him of being a fool, and he taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret.
They told him he had ruined the earlier teaching, and he replied he is doing good for them, by whatever means they wish.
The halakha: whichever way one takes, the convert may marry a mamzeret, from here or from there.
A convert may marry a priestess, and a convert may marry a mamzeret, following Rabbi Yosei.
Raba says that a shetuki, one who knows his mother but not his father, is fit by Torah law.
Asks what the reason is.
Most fit people are with her and a minority disqualified; if they went to her, whatever separates from the majority is separated.
What do you say: perhaps she goes to them; she would be fixed, and a fixed case is equal to a half-and-half case.
Cites Deuteronomy 23:3 again: a mamzer shall not enter, a certain mamzer is excluded, a doubtful one enters the assembly.
Asks what the reason is that they called a shetuki disqualified.
As a decree, lest he marry his sister from his father.
But then a shetuki should not marry a shetukit, lest he marry his sister from the father, since many such cases exist.
The case is not common, so it does not matter; they treated it as a matter of lineage.
Raba says: by Torah law, an asufi is fit.
Asks what the reason is.
A married woman is presumed to be with her husband; the minority of betrothed women and of those whose husbands went overseas, or who were starving, is half and half.
Cites Deuteronomy 23:3 once more: a certain mamzer may not enter, while a doubtful one enters the assembly.
Asks what the reason is that they called an asufi disqualified.
Lest he marry his sister from his father.
But then an asufi woman should not marry lest he marry his sister from either parent, as many such cases exist.
The case is uncommon, so it does not matter; they treated it as a matter of lineage.
Raba bar Rav Huna says: they found him circumcised.

73b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists items with no concern of asufi, such as a beam-like seat, and a note; the Gemara teaches the examples.
Lists further items: a plaster of oil, a kohl container, and a written note or charm, with no concern of asufi.
A palm-tree amulet carries no concern of asufi.
If an animal reaches him, there is concern of asufi; if not, there is no concern.
A thorn-bush near the town carries concern of asufi; otherwise it does not.
A synagogue near the town where many people gather carries no concern of asufi; otherwise it does.
Ammimar's list: some items carry concern of asufi and some do not, such as things in the public domain.
Raba says: in a time of famine there is no concern of asufi.
Asks what Raba's statement refers to: if it concerns the public domain, then famine would kill him, so what is the point?
Why specify famine; it applies even without famine. Rather, Raba's statement was said in the context of another case.
Rav Yehuda cites Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Zavdi citing Rav: as long as an abandoned child is in the market, his parents are believed about him.
Once he is gathered from the market, his father and mother are not believed about him.
Asks what the reason is.
Raba: since the designation asufi has attached to him, his parents are not believed.
Raba: even in a time of famine, once gathered from the market, his father and mother are believed about him.
Rav Hisda: three are believed immediately: an asufi, an animal, and one who releases her companions, as explained earlier.
A baraita: an animal is believed to say this one left first and this one left second, under conditions; if she left and returned, she is not believed.
Rabbi Eliezer says: if she was presumed to stand, she is believed; if not, she is not believed.
Asks what the difference between them is, namely the case where she turned her face and released her companions.
The mishna: three women slept on a bed, blood was found under one, all are impure; if one examined herself and found her blood, she is impure and the rest are pure.
Rav Hisda says this applies where she checked herself, in the proper measure of her regular flow.
The Sages taught: an animal is believed to say this is a priest and this a Levite, this a Netin and this a mamzer, but if a protest was raised against her, she is not believed.
Asks: shall we say one protest is enough?
But Rabbi Yohanan said no protest is fewer than two; it needs two protests.
Alternatively, say the case is one protest, and Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that no protest is fewer than two stands.
These matters apply where there is a presumption of fitness; where there is no presumption of fitness, one witness is also believed.
A seller is believed to say to this one I sold, and to that one I did not sell.
This applies when the sale is in his hand; if it is not in his hand, he is not believed.

74a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from whom the money is taken, and answers that the case is needed where he takes from both.
Says one of the two is from his own will and one against his will; a judge is believed to say to one I awarded and to the other I obligated, only when the litigants stand before him.
Asks the parallel question: from whom is the merit taken, and whether the case needs the merit torn and the judgment reconsidered by a court.
Rav Naḥman: three are believed about the firstborn: the animal, the father, and the mother; the mother immediately and the father always.
Cites Deuteronomy 21:17: he shall acknowledge the firstborn, so that others will recognize him.

Rabbi Yehuda: a man is believed to say this one is my firstborn, and just as he is believed to say this is my firstborn, he is believed to say this is the son of a divorcee and this one the son of a halutza.
The Sages say he is not believed.
Abba Shaul used to call a shetuki a bedoki.
Asks what bedoki means.
Suggests: they examine the mother, who says to the fit one that she was intimate with a fit man; is she believed, and according to whom? Rabban Gamliel, as we learned once.
Cites the mishna: a woman was pregnant and they asked her what the fetus is; she said it is from so-and-so and he is a priest; Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer say she is believed.
Rabbi Yehoshua says we do not live by her mouth.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
One ruling makes her fit, and another makes her daughter fit.
Granted for one who says her daughter is disqualified according to the view that makes her fit; but for one who says the daughter is fit, what then?
Asks why Abba Shaul is mentioned, and explains it teaches that Abba Shaul is superior to Rabban Gamliel, lest one think the case is only where most are fit.
Rava says the halakha follows Abba Shaul.

Mishna: all those forbidden to enter the congregation are permitted to intermarry with each other; Rabbi Yehuda forbids; Rabbi Eliezer says certain with certain is permitted, doubtful with certain is permitted, and doubtful with doubtful is
These are the doubtful cases: shetuki, asufi, and Cuthean.
Asks what the mishna means by all forbidden to enter the congregation, whether it means mamzerim, Netinim, shetuki and asufi.
But the first clause already taught that mamzerim, Netinim, shetuki and asufi are permitted to intermarry, so this cannot be the meaning.
Asks: and Rabbi Yehuda forbids; in which case?

Shall we say certain with doubtful, but Rabbi Eliezer's list shows that Rabbi Yehuda does not hold this; or Rabbi Yehuda forbids a convert marrying a mamzeret, but the mishna teaches all those forbidden.
Rav Yehuda says.

74b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the mishna's ruling that those barred from the priestly congregation may marry one another, with the scope spelled out
Objection: reading the mishna about a convert over three would make it contradict itself
Reply: the leniency applies only to a convert who was over three years and a day old
Objection: then a convert under three would be forbidden to marry those barred from the congregation
Conclusion: per Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, a convert under three is admitted and may intermarry
General rule drawn: anyone barred from entering the congregation may marry others so barred
Counterexamples to the rule: widows, divorcees, and others, plus a convert who may marry a mamzeret
Rav Natan bar Hoshaya's reading: the barred person is a convert who married a female convert
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view applied: such converts may intermarry with the congregation-barred families
Objection: a ḥalal who married a Jewish woman is barred from priesthood, yet is among those who may intermarry
Reply: the mishna follows Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda, who lets a ḥalal's daughter marry a priest
Second objection: a ḥalal married to a ḥalala, and a convert marrying a Jewish woman, break the rule
Rav Naḥman's alternative: the dispute concerns mamzerim from sibling incest versus from a married woman
Positions: the first tanna counts sibling-born mamzerim too, while Rabbi Yehuda does not
Asks what new point this teaching adds, if the matter was already settled earlier
Cites the Yevamot mishna defining mamzer, including Rabbi Akiva's broad view, as the answer
Shimon HaTimni's view: mamzer status follows unions punishable by karet, and that is the halakha
Rabbi Yehoshua's view: mamzer status follows unions punishable by court-imposed death
Rava's alternative: the dispute concerns male Ammonite and Moabite converts
Restates the rule under Rava's reading: such converts may intermarry with one another
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda would forbid these marriages, if he should permit an Ammonite to marry a mamzeret
Explains that Rabbi Yehuda's ban applies only to converts fit for the congregation, not Ammonites or Moabites
Brings a baraita on the disqualified: a nine-year-old's intercourse disqualifies the woman from the priesthood
Rabbi Yosei: a man whose offspring are unfit disqualifies a woman he lies with; otherwise he does not
Introduces Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion on the same question, stated in its opening clause only

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna's rule: whoever may marry a man's daughter may marry his widow, and the reverse also holds
Asks what practical difference exists between the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei, who seem to agree
Rabbi Yoḥanan: they differ over a Jewish woman who had relations with a second-generation Egyptian
Both sages derived their views from the High Priest and widow case, each by a different route
The first tanna's derivation: like a High Priest, anyone whose intercourse is sinful disqualifies the woman
Rabbi Yosei's derivation: like a High Priest, anyone whose offspring is unfit disqualifies the woman
Verse Deuteronomy 23:9 excludes second-generation Egyptians, whose offspring are fit
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel restates the widow rule, mirroring the same wording
Asks what difference lies between Rabbi Yosei and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
Ulla: they differ over male Ammonite and Moabite converts, and both derive from the same priest case
Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: anyone with unfit offspring, including such converts, disqualifies the woman
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: anyone whose offspring of both sexes are unfit disqualifies her
The comparison excludes male converts from Ammon or Moab, since their daughters are fit
Cites the Master's teaching that Ammonite and Moabite men, but not women, are barred from the congregation
Rav Ḥisda: all agree that a widow of uncertain lineage is unfit for the priesthood
Asks who in these tannaitic views is the lenient one
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view is that the clause excludes a widow of uncertain lineage
Asks what exactly the exclusion is meant to remove
It excludes a widow of uncertain lineage, who is unfit for the priesthood
Cites the mishna in which Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira ruled that such a widow is fit
The testimony of those two sages is recorded: a widow of uncertain lineage is fit for priesthood
