Asks the reason for this lenient ruling
A double uncertainty is treated leniently, and cases certain on both sides are permitted
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer
Shmuel objects that Hillel taught all ten lineages may intermarry, so the halakha cannot follow Rabbi Eliezer; a contradiction between sages is then raised
Dispute on a betrothed woman who became pregnant: Rav calls the child a mamzer, Shmuel a shetuki
Resolution by reversing the positions, so Rav calls the child a shetuki and Shmuel a mamzer
Asks why two instances of the same dispute need to be stated
Both cases must be stated, since each would otherwise be read differently; alternatively, the opinions need not be reversed
Asks what Rav means by the term mamzer
Rav's mamzer means only that the child may not marry a Jewish woman
Shmuel's shetuki means the child may not marry a Jewish woman
Objects that this would make Shmuel's view the same as Rav's
Asks what shetuki means, if it does not restate Rav's view: silencing from priestly status
Objects that silencing from priesthood is obvious, since a shetuki is already barred from Israel
Asks whether shetuki means silencing from the presumed father's property
Objects that this is obvious, since we do not know who the father is
Explains: the case is one where the son seized property; alternatively, shetuki means beduki and the mother is examined
Asks whether this halakha follows Rabban Gamliel, since Shmuel already said it once
Cites the Ketubot mishna on a pregnant woman whose child is declared a priest's, and the views of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer
Rabbi Yehoshua says she is not believed; Shmuel's ruling says the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel
Explains why the case needed stating: the other case has a fit majority, while this one has an unfit majority
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar says a Samaritan may not marry a Samaritan woman
Asks what the reason for that ruling is
Rav Yosef: the Samaritan is treated as a convert, and after ten generations is fit to marry a mamzeret
Baraita: a convert is barred from marrying a mamzeret until ten generations have passed
Some say the ten-generation period runs until idolatry has fully left the family
Abaye objects that the cases differ: a convert of long standing is not comparable to a fresh mamzeret
Rav Dimi's reply: Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Yishmael, which reconciles the view with the objection

75b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Yishmael, who calls Samaritans lion converts, while Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Akiva on mamzer status
Asks whether Rabbi Yishmael really follows Rabbi Akiva on this point
Objection: Rabbi Yoḥanan quotes Rabbi Yishmael deriving that a gentile or slave disqualifies a priest's daughter
The verse in Leviticus 22:13 is cited: only a woman with Jewish widowhood or divorce status returns to her father's food
If Rabbi Yishmael followed Rabbi Akiva, the verse would be unnecessary, since the child would already be a mamzer
Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Yishmael on Samaritans and Rabbi Akiva on the gentile-mamzer rule
Objection: Rabbi Elazar also says only offspring from a karet-liable union is a mamzer, so he cannot follow Rabbi Akiva
Rabin reports the tradition in several versions, naming Rabbi Yoḥanan and others, that three disputes exist on this matter
Rabbi Yishmael's view: Samaritans are lion converts, and the priests who assimilated among them were unfit
Cites II Kings 17:32 about priests of the high places as support for Rabbi Yishmael's view
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the priests came from the flawed among the people, which is why they were disqualified
Rabbi Akiva's view: Samaritans are true converts, and the priests who assimilated among them were fit
Cites the same II Kings verse, reading the priests as drawn from the chosen
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: the Samaritan priests came from the chosen ones of the people
Asks for what reason the Sages prohibited Samaritans from the congregation, if their conversion is fine
They were prohibited because they performed levirate marriage with betrothed women

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains how the Samaritans' reading of the levirate verse exempts married women, leading to their disqualification
Rabbi Akiva's line of reasoning: offspring of a prohibition with liability is a mamzer, so Samaritan descendants are mamzerim
Asks who the unnamed 'some say' refers to
Rav Idi bar Avin: it is the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer
Baraita: a Samaritan's matza is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer forbids it since they are not expert in mitzvot
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: Samaritans are scrupulous in any mitzva they accepted, so the concern does not apply
Asks in which details of marriage Samaritans are not expert
They lack expertise in betrothal and divorce, so their bills of divorce or remarriages may be invalid
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh: Samaritans include mamzerim from sibling and brother's-wife unions
Asks why details are given, since one example would suffice to teach that karet-liable offspring are mamzerim
The details are not a teaching; they simply record how the incident actually happened
Rava: Canaanite male and female slaves were assimilated among the Samaritans
Asks what prohibition is involved, and why both slave and maidservant are mentioned if one example suffices
Again, the incident took place in this way, so both cases are recorded
Mishna: a priest marrying a priest's daughter must investigate four mothers, and exemptions apply for certain lineages
Rabbi Yosei: one who signed as a witness on the Tzippori census register is also exempt from investigation
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus: one recorded in the royal military register is also exempt from investigation
Asks why women are investigated but men are not, when the lineage examination is needed for both
Women are investigated because they quarrel with one another about illicit unions, so their scandal becomes known
If a matter is actually public, the woman's reputation will reveal it, so she should also be investigated herself
Cites Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: women not warned against unfit men may marry them, which supports this view
Rav Adda bar Ahava's baraita lists four mothers as twelve, but another baraita lists sixteen, so the versions conflict

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's ruling is read as about a Levite or Israelite woman, matching the mishna's extra investigation
Objection: then the baraita would dispute the mishna, so the two cannot be reconciled this way
Reply: the mishna's phrase one more means one additional pair of mothers, so no conflict arises
Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: the mishna gives Rabbi Meir's view, while the Sages hold all families are presumptively fit
Objection: Rav Ḥama bar Gurya says Rav held an objection must be registered before investigation, so the attribution is doubtful
Alternative version: the dispute is Rabbi Meir versus the Sages on presumptive fitness, as Rav Yehuda reports Rav
Rav Ḥama bar Gurya: when an objection is raised about a family's lineage, one must investigate it
Mishna: one need not investigate a priest from the altar upward, from the platform upward, or from the Sanhedrin upward
Asks what the reason is for not investigating from the altar upward
Those who sat in those positions already vetted priestly and Levitical lineage, so no further check is needed
Asks what the reason is for the investigation rule of the baraita
Baraita of Rav Yosef: as a court is cleansed by righteousness, so priests are cleansed of every blemish
Mari asks which verse supports the sense of blemish in this context
Cites Song of Songs 4:7: you are entirely beautiful, and there is no blemish in you, as support
Objects that blemish should be read literally rather than as a moral flaw, and the verse does not show it
Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov cites Numbers 11:16 on the elders who stand with you, to support the point
Objection: perhaps the cited case concerns the Shekhinah, so it does not prove the claim about officers
Rav Naḥman cites Exodus 18:22 on sharing the burden with you, supporting the standard for officers
Mishna clause: anyone whose ancestors were known as officers of the public is presumed fit
Asks whether this means we do not appoint people from among the unfit
Objection from a baraita: all are fit to judge monetary cases, but not capital cases, which raises a conflict
Asks what the word all is meant to include
Rav Yehuda: it includes a mamzer, and Abaye adds this holds in Jerusalem
Baraita in Jerusalem: in betrothal cases of the house of Levi, and communal almoners, marriage is arranged for them
Asks what the reason is for allowing these men to marry
Because they quarrel with the public and are pledged to charity, and a known reputation is needed
Rav Adda bar Ahava's innkeeper, a convert, quarreled with Rav Bibi; each called the other a town troublemaker
The two came before Rav Yosef, who said that the mishna had taught the matter
Cites Deuteronomy 17:15: you shall set a king from among your brothers, as the basis for the ruling
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects: even if the mother is from Israel, the ruling would still apply
Reply: the mother being from Israel is what the verse means by from among your brothers
Conclusion: each sage should attend to his own domain, and Abaye says the leniency applies only to a skilled scholar
Practice in various communities: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah bar Avuh handled these matters, and in some towns the unfit were excluded
Rabbi Yosi: anyone who was a witness in the register is also held to be fit
Asks what the reason is for these standards
They were precise in records, so those who signed the register were relied on, as with Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the matter concerns the troops of the house of David
Rav Yosef asks which verse is the source
Cites I Chronicles 7:40: they were enrolled according to their genealogies for war
Asks what the reason is for this
So that their own merit and their ancestors' merit would support them
Objection: Tzeilek the Ammonite, a David warrior, shows Ammonite fitness, unless he merely came from Ammon
Objection: Uriah the Hittite was also in David's ranks, so the same reading must be given to him
Objection: Ittai the Gittite came with David, and the answer must be that he was from Gath, not a resident
Rav Naḥman's statement that Ittai came and was nullified raises a further difficulty about the same case
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: David had four hundred sons, all of handsome build, who served as the strong men of his house

77a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the daughter of a male ḥalal is unfit for priesthood forever, but the daughter of an Israelite who married a ḥalala is fit
Rabbi Yehuda: the daughter of a male convert is treated like the daughter of a male ḥalal, and so is unfit
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: unions with a Jewish partner or a convert are fit, but a convert with a female convert is unfit
Converts and emancipated slaves are unfit for priesthood, even for ten generations
That status lasts until the offspring's mother is born of a Jewish woman
Rabbi Yosei: even the daughter of a convert who married a female convert is fit for priesthood
Asks what the word forever means here
Lest one think it works like Egyptians and Edomites, who are admitted after three generations, the rule is made permanent
Asks from where this is derived for an Israelite who married a ḥalala
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites Rabbi Shimon: the wording of Leviticus 21:15 and 21:4 is compared to show the verse applies only to males
Objection: then a High Priest's daughter should be permitted, since the verse says his son's offspring
The verse makes his offspring equivalent to him, so his daughter is unfit just as his son's daughter is
Objection: then a granddaughter would also be prohibited, which would be a gezera shava
Asks what the mishna gains from the case of a ḥalal who married an Israelite
Such a ḥalal's daughter is unfit, as the mishna's second clause states
The mishna stated the first clause, so it also gave the second clause for parallel structure
This is the mishna's case: a ḥalal who married an Israelite woman
Baraita of Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda: as Israelite men cleanse ḥalalot, so Israelite women cleanse ḥalalim
Asks the reason of Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda
He reads the verse as applying to one people only, so it applies within a single nation but not across two
Baraita: the verse speaks of offspring, and the question is whether the woman herself is also disqualified
Asks from where it follows that the woman herself is disqualified
Kal vachomer: if offspring of a sinful union are disqualified, the woman who sinned should be disqualified too
Alternatively, she is disqualified in every case, so the reasoning from her own sin stands
The verse says the one who was fit and became unfit is not disqualified by offspring, so the a fortiori reasoning is rejected
Asks what the rejected objection would be, if one wishes to argue from the offspring's conception
The offspring are conceived in sin, so the comparison fails; the verse applies to the one who was fit and became unfit
Baraita: a harlot is one born of unfit persons, which determines who the disqualified woman is
Asks what unfit persons means here
If it meant unfit to him, a remarried divorcee would be unfit yet her children fit, which the verse of abomination contradicts
Rav Yehuda: the baraita means a woman born of a priestly unfit man, such as a widow or divorcee not herself born of such
Rabbah: the harlot mentioned is one who never had a period of fitness, born of an unfit priest
Asks what is meant by mentioned here
Rav Yitzḥak bar Avin: the harlot is one whose status stems from the Torah itself, needing no rabbinic explanation
Baraita on the widow, divorcee, harlot and ḥalala listed in Leviticus 21:14, showing when one is liable for each
Liable for each only when the wrongs occur in order, and otherwise only for one
The Master's teaching: liable only once for multiple widowhoods
Asks how this widow case is to be understood, and why one liability applies when he was with three widows

77b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that these are separate bodies and labels, so lashes should be given for each act.
Proposes that he had three intercourse acts with one widow instead.
Asks what the circumstances are if no forewarning was given between acts.
Without forewarning, obviously only one set of lashes applies.
Proposes forewarning before each act of intercourse with the widow.
If forewarned each time, why is he liable for only one set?
Cites the Mishnah about a nazirite forewarned repeatedly, liable for each drink.
Case of one act with a widow who was previously widowed twice; bodies, not labels, matter.
Cites the verse listing widow, divorcee, ḥalala and zona as the baraita source.
Asks which principle the tanna holds about one prohibition taking effect on another.
Rava states that this tanna holds an added prohibition takes effect only when it expands.
Illustrates Rava's principle with widow, divorcee and ḥalala for a High Priest.
Asks what expanded prohibition a zona adds beyond a ḥalala.
Rav Ḥana bar Rav Ketina: zenut disqualifies her in Israel, which expands the prohibition.
A baraita taught before Rav Sheshet excludes a High Priest who had intercourse with his sister.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion the baraita was taught.
Rav Sheshet says it follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds one prohibition does not take effect on another.
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon on eating a carcass on Yom Kippur.
If the baraita follows the Rabbis, they say one prohibition does take effect on another.
The Rabbis' view applies only when a more severe prohibition is added to a lighter one.
Offers an alternative attribution of Rav Sheshet's reply to the Rabbis' view.
If it is Rabbi Shimon, the rule that a light prohibition does not take effect on a severe one is trivial.
The baraita is needed to exclude priesthood-related prohibitions from the general rule.
Rav Pappa asks whether an Israelite's incest with his sister makes her a ḥalala, and argues both sides.
Abaye: ḥalala arises only from a prohibition specific to the priesthood.
Rava asks from where this principle that ḥalala arises only from priestly prohibitions derives.
A baraita derives the divorcee's prohibition for a High Priest by a fortiori from a common priest.
Asks why the verse would need to state the divorcee prohibition for a High Priest at all.
The verse teaches that a High Priest's divorcee is distinct from zona and ḥalala, as for a common priest.
Objects that this is obvious, since a High Priest's status is not lower than a common priest's.
Rather, the verse teaches that a widow is distinct from divorcee, ḥalala and zona for a High Priest.
Asks why the ḥalala prohibition is stated for a High Priest, since it is already known.
It teaches that ḥalala results only from a prohibition specific to the priesthood.
Asks why the zona prohibition is stated for a High Priest, since it is already known.
A verbal analogy from the word zona links the High Priest and common priest, so offspring are profaned.
Rav Ashi concludes that a priest who has intercourse with his sister is thereby a ḥalala.

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A priest who has relations with a zona makes her a zona but not a ḥalala, and a later priest does make her one.
Rav Yehuda: a High Priest with a widow is flogged twice, for the widow prohibition and the profaning prohibition.
Asks why he is not also flogged for profaning his offspring, since that act produces a ḥalal child.
That profaning verse applies only when the intercourse was not completed, so no pregnancy results.
Rava objects from a mishna: liable for two labels means only one lashing per prohibition, contrary to Rav Yehuda.
No: two labels means two lashings for the widow act, one for each prohibition, and two for the divorcee act.
If so, the mishna's later clause gives only one lashing for a divorcee who was a ḥalutza, which seems to conflict.
The mishna means one act is liable, yet two lashings apply because she is a divorcee, and the ḥalutza is rabbinic.
Asks whether a ḥalutza is forbidden to a priest only by rabbinic law.
A baraita derives from the verse on divorcee that the word and includes the ḥalutza as forbidden by Torah law.
Rejects the proof: the prohibition is rabbinic, and the verse is only a support, not the source.
Abaye: a priest who betroths a forbidden woman is flogged, and additionally flogged if he has intercourse with her.
Rava: flogged only for intercourse, since the verse ties the prohibition against taking to not profaning.
Abaye concedes that betrothing a remarried divorcee without intercourse is not flogged, citing the verse take her again.
Rava concedes that intercourse without betrothal is flogged for the High Priest, while the remarried divorcee case is not.
Rabbi Yehuda, in the mishna and a baraita: the daughter of a male convert is unfit for the priesthood, like a ḥalal's daughter.
A fortiori argument: if a ḥalal's daughter is unfit though born of a fit drop, a convert's daughter should be too.
Objects that a ḥalal is formed through a transgression, which the convert's parents were not, so the inference fails.
The High Priest who has intercourse with a widow shows that formation through transgression is not germane to the daughter's fitness.
Objects that the High Priest's own intercourse is the transgression, which the convert lacks, so the inference fails again.
The ḥalal shows that the transgression in intercourse is not germane, since his daughter is unfit regardless.
Reverts to the starting point and argues from the shared feature of being unlike most of the congregation, so the convert is included.
Rejects it: the shared feature includes a transgression in formation or intercourse, so it cannot ground the convert's case.
Revised proof: a first-generation Egyptian convert couple has children unfit for the priesthood despite no transgression.
Objects that a first-generation Egyptian is unfit to enter the congregation at all, a feature that does not show anything.
A ḥalal shows the congregation-entry feature is not germane, since his daughter is unfit though his offspring may enter.
Reverts again: the shared feature of being unlike most of the congregation, through lineage, is extended to the convert.
Objects that the shared feature is that they disqualify a priest's daughter through intercourse, which a convert does not do.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a convert also disqualifies through intercourse, so the inference rests on the shared common factor.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: the daughter of a convert and of a Jewish woman is fit to marry into the priesthood.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: a female converting before three years and a day is fit to marry into the priesthood.
Cites Numbers 31:18 and notes Pinehas was present, so the Torah permitted those girls even to priests.
The Rabbis read the same verse as referring to slaves and maidservants, not marriage.
All these tannaim expound one verse in Ezekiel 44:22 about marrying virgins of the seed of Israel.
Rabbi Yehuda requires all of the seed to be Jewish, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires only part of it.
Rabbi Yosei reads seed as conceived in Israel, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai reads hymen formed as a Jew.
Rav Naḥman turns to Rava with a challenge; the text of his challenge continues beyond the printed span.

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether it is reasonable to read this Ezekiel verse with the first clause on a High Priest and the latter on a common priest.
Rava affirms that this is the correct reading of the verse.
Rav Naḥman asks whether a verse can be written this way, addressing two subjects without demarcation.
Rava says yes, such verses exist.
Cites I Samuel 3:3 as a parallel, read so that Samuel lay outside the Temple, not inside.
Asks whether the verse then means a priest may marry only a priest's widow, not an Israelite's.
No: the verse means that the other priests, apart from the High Priest, may take widows.
A baraita supports this reading: of a priest they may take means of the rest of the priests.
Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse as allowing marriage only to widows of men whose daughters may marry priests, consistent with his view.
Rabbi Yosei holds a convert's daughter from two converts is fit; the halakha follows him, though priests since the Temple's fall followed Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rav Huna's ruling: a priest who asks should be told not to marry two converts' daughter, but if he did, she is not removed.
Mishna: a man's claim that his son is a mamzer is not credible, even if both parents agree; Rabbi Yehuda deems them credible.
Asks what the added phrase even both teaches beyond the earlier clause about the father's claim.
The phrasing says it is unnecessary: a father's claim is not credible, nor the mother's, and a fetus has no presumption of lineage.
Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse he shall acknowledge that a father is credible to identify his firstborn, and by extension other sons.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asks: for Rabbi Yehuda the verse is needed, but what is it for the Rabbis?
It is needed when the firstborn's identity is unknown and the father must identify him.
Asks which halakha this serves, since double inheritance would already be granted; a father could have given it as a gift.
The verse concerns property the father acquired after the testimony, which he could not have given earlier.
Asks, following Rabbi Meir, why the verse is needed if one can transfer property not yet in existence.
It concerns property that came to the father while he was moribund, when he could no longer transfer it.
Mishna: a father who betroths his daughter contrary to his agent's arrangement is decided by which betrothal came first.

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: when both men may have betrothed her, each may give a bill of divorce, or one divorces and the other marries her.
Explains why both the father and the woman cases must be stated, since each alone could suggest a different outcome.
Amoraic dispute: if the father betrothed her on the road and she betrothed herself in town, Rav and Shmuel disagree.
Asks when the father's betrothal occurred, and argues that Rav and Shmuel's positions would each conflict with the other.
Resolves it: the father betrothed her on the day the six months ended, so Rav and Shmuel's positions both stand.
Asks why Shmuel does not treat this like a ritual bath found deficient, which retroactively makes the items impure.
A ritual bath differs: the item's impure presumption is supported by the bath's current deficiency.
Counters: maintain the bath's pure presumption and say it was not deficient at immersion, so the items are pure.
A deficient bath now counteracts its earlier presumption of full volume.
Asks why the same reasoning does not apply: here too the grown woman now counteracts her earlier young status.
Here she only now reached majority, so the question is what changed when.
Asks why the bath case cannot likewise say the deficiency arose only now, shortly before testing.
The bath has two weakening factors, current deficiency and impure presumption; here only one, so both betrothals count.
Asks what distinguishes this case from a barrel of wine that turned to vinegar, per Shmuel.
A Tosefta on a barrel inspected for teruma: wine is taken as definitely wine for three days, then uncertain afterward.
Raises the apparent contradiction between the barrel ruling and the ritual bath ruling, both having a current deficiency.
Rav Ḥanina of Syria: the barrel ruling follows Rabbi Shimon, who treats the bath case as uncertain, removing the contradiction.
A baraita: Rabbi Shimon says impure items are impure only by uncertainty, with public and private domain rulings.
For the Rabbis, the barrel case should make the earlier wine untithed retroactively, contrary to Shmuel's ruling.
The barrel case differs: maintain the untithed presumption and say the teruma was not fixed.
Asks why not maintain the wine's presumption and say it had not yet turned to vinegar.
That is impossible, since it has already turned to vinegar before us.
Asks whether the betrothal case is the same, since she is now a grown woman, and what the difference is.
With the woman it is possible she only now reached majority, so the earlier status is not clearly overturned.
Challenges: in the barrel case too it may have turned to vinegar only now, not earlier.
The barrel case has two weakening factors, current vinegar and wine's untithed presumption; the betrothal case has only one.
Proposes that the dispute is parallel to a disagreement between earlier tanna'im.

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks who may remove property from whose possession when a claim is made that a gift was given while moribund.
Rabbi Yaakov: the claimant need not prove illness; Rabbi Natan: the burden lies on whichever side claims the opposite of current status.
Suggests Rav follows Rabbi Natan and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yaakov, to explain their dispute.
Rejects it: Rav could hold even by Rabbi Yaakov, since property stays in place, whereas maturity of a body is clearly due.
Shmuel could hold even by Rabbi Natan, since only a claim against a presumption of health needs proof, not her status.
Proposes that the Rav and Shmuel dispute parallels a dispute between two tannaim on the betrothal of a grown woman.
The two baraitot state opposite rulings on whether the father's betrothal takes effect.
Asks whether the baraitot then reflect the Rav and Shmuel dispute, one each.
Both baraitot can follow Shmuel: one case where she denies the father's right, the other where she does not.
If the baraitot do not conflict, the amoraim should not conflict either, so why did they dispute?
Rav Yosef ruled in line with Rav, ignoring the father's betrothal, and Shmuel took offense, showing a real disagreement.
If they did not disagree, why would Shmuel have taken offense at Rav Yosef's ruling?
Rav Yosef's case may have involved a woman who denied the father's right, so Shmuel would not object.
Halakha rulings: Mar Zutra reports Ameimar follows Shmuel, Rav Ashi says Rav, and the final halakha follows Rav.
Mishna: a man returning from overseas with wife and children, or without her, must prove lineage in differing ways.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: the rule that children need no proof applies when they cling to the woman as their mother.
A baraita distinguishes one overseas wife from two wives, and adults from minors, in the proof required.
Reish Lakish's statement is cut off at the end of the printed span and continues on the next line.

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A teaching limits a child's attachment to maternity to teruma, while R. Yochanan extends it to lineage as well.
The Gemara ties R. Yochanan's view to his general principle of presumptive status, reported via R. Hiyya bar Abba.
Rav Yehuda's case of a flogging on presumptive status: a menstruating woman's husband is flogged without direct testimony.
Rabba bar Rav Huna's case of a household of children who grew up together, illustrating stoning and burning on presumptive status.
An anecdote of a woman and a child she raised, stoned on presumptive status because he clung to her, not because of proven kinship.
The view of Reish Lakish that one burns teruma on the basis of presumptive status.
The contrary view of R. Yochanan that one does not burn teruma on presumptive status.
The Gemara cites a mishna in Teharot about a child holding dough, showing each side follows its own reasoning.
What is the reasoning behind R. Meir's position in the mishna about the child and the dough?
R. Meir holds that most children handle nearby items, so the dough's purity presumption stands; the Rabbis follow the majority.
Reish Lakish, citing R. Oshaya, says this case is the presumption on which teruma is burned.
R. Yochanan rejects that claim, saying this is not the presumption on which teruma is burned.
If so, what presumption does R. Yochanan accept as grounds for burning teruma?
A baraita about started dough with creeping animals and frogs: the majority kind of creature determines whether the dough is impure.
A baraita in line with R. Yochanan: two matters cannot be investigated, yet the Sages treated them as questionable.
Explains the first case in the baraita: the child who was found holding dough, whose dough is deemed impure.
What is the other additional case mentioned in the baraita?
The other case is started dough in a house with chickens and impure liquids, whose impurity is determined by the majority.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Pecked dough is held in suspension: it may be neither eaten nor burned, since the chickens may have drunk impure liquid.
Reish Lakish's teacher, R. Yehoshua ben Levi, limits the rule to white liquid, where pecks would show no color.
An objection: even in red liquid the dough might have absorbed the liquid, leaving no visible mark.
R. Yochanan answers that R. Yehoshua ben Levi heard the teaching without its interpretation: it applies only to clear liquid.
The mishna: a man may not be secluded with two women, but a woman may be with two men; Rabbi Shimon permits it with his wife present.
What is the reason a man may not be secluded with two women, while a woman may be secluded with two men?
The school of Eliyahu explains that women are light-minded and more easily seduced, so the rule applies to men only.
From where are these seclusion prohibitions derived?
R. Yochanan, citing R. Yishmael, says the Torah alludes to the seclusion prohibition.
The verse about the enticing brother, son of your mother, is read to teach that a son may not be secluded with forbidden relatives.
What is the plain meaning of that verse, which is written in the context of enticement to idolatry?
Abaye: the verse uses the style of it is unnecessary to state, so the son of a mother is included as well.
The Gemara suggests the mishna disagrees with Abba Shaul, who permits one man with two women.
A baraita on burying a child in the first thirty days, where Abba Shaul permits one man with two women.
Reply: Abba Shaul's permission applies only during acute mourning, when the inclination to sin is broken.
The Rabbis hold that seclusion is forbidden even then, following R. Yitzhak's view.
R. Yitzhak cites Lamentations 3:39 to show that one's inclination overpowers a person even in acute mourning.
Abba Shaul reads the verse as referring to one who complains about God's ways, not about his sins.
The Rabbis cite an incident of a woman who, while mourning, was seduced at her husband's grave.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says the one-woman-two-men rule applies only to fit men, not to licentious ones.
An incident where ten men carried a woman out on a bier and violated her, and Rav Yosef's reasoning that ten men can act together.
The Gemara proposes a mishna in Sota supporting Rav Yosef: two Torah scholars accompany a suspected wife, while ordinary men are not trusted.
Torah scholars differ from ordinary people, since they know the prohibitions and would not transgress.

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the escorts are there to warn the suspected husband against intercourse, which would void the water test.
Rav: two men may be alone with a woman in a town, but on the road three are required, in case one steps away.
The Gemara proposes the Sota mishna as support: two scholars accompany him, so that three men travel together.
No proof: in the Sota case the two extra men serve as witnesses, which is why there are three.
Anecdote: Rav warns Rav Yehuda to hurry past a woman walking ahead, so that they are not secluded with her.
Rav Yehuda objects: did you not say seclusion is allowed with men of fit morals?
Rav replies that he did not mean men of fit morals like the two of them.
Rather, who counts as such men?
Men such as R. Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues, who have proven they can resist temptation; others are not trusted.
Rav: a court flogs for seclusion, but seclusion does not make a woman forbidden to her husband or to a priest.
Rav Ashi limits flogging for seclusion to an unmarried woman, so that rumors about a married woman's children are avoided.
Mar Zutra flogs one secluded with a married woman and publicly proclaims the reason.
Rav Naḥman asks Rav Ashi to flog and proclaim the reason as well.
Rav Ashi hesitates: some people would hear of the flogging but not of its reason.
Rav: a court flogs one who is the subject of a bad rumor, even without proof of the transgression.
The verse about a bad report is cited, and Mar Zutra's practice of flogging on that basis is described.
Rabba: if the husband is in town, seclusion with the wife raises no concern.
Rav Yosef: if there is an open entrance to the public domain, seclusion raises no concern.
Anecdote: Rav Beivai sleeps upstairs at Rav Yosef's house, and the ladder is removed so he cannot come down.
The Gemara objects: but Rabba said that with the husband in town there is no concern about seclusion.
Rav Beivai is different, since Rav Yosef's wife was his friend and familiar with him.
Rav Kahana: men outside and women inside are fine, but men inside and women outside raise concern.
A baraita teaches the opposite of Rav Kahana's ruling.
Abaye: since Rav Kahana ruled this way and a baraita says the opposite, we act stringently in both cases.
Abaye arranges rows of pitchers between men and women, and Rava arranges reeds, to prevent crossing unnoticed.
Avin: the most vulnerable time of the year is the Festival, when men and women gather joyfully and may sin.
Anecdote: captive women brought to Rav Amram's house; overcome by desire, he lifts a heavy ladder alone and starts climbing.
The Sages reproach Rav Amram, saying he has embarrassed them since everyone sees his intention.
Rav Amram replies that it is better to be shamed in this world than in the World-to-Come, and rebukes his evil inclination.
Anecdote: Satan appears to Rabbi Meir as a woman across a river, and the evil inclination leaves him once he is halfway across.
Anecdote: Satan appears to Rabbi Akiva as a woman atop a palm tree, and the evil inclination leaves him halfway up.
Anecdote: Peleimu is tempted on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a pauper, who asks to be let in and seated at the table.

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuation of the Peleimu story: Satan tricks him with a cup, pretends to die, and Peleimu flees and hides in the bathroom.
Satan asks why Peleimu provoked him by saying an arrow in the eye of Satan.
Peleimu asks what he should say; Satan tells him to say that the Merciful One should rebuke Satan.
R. Hiyya bar Ashi's practice: whenever he fell on his face in prayer, he asked the Merciful One to save him from the evil inclination.
His wife asks why he prays that way, since he has long stopped relating to her sexually.
Anecdote: she dresses as a prostitute, he propositions her, and they have intercourse in exchange for a pomegranate.
When he comes home and sits in the oven, his wife asks what this is.
He tells her what happened, and she reveals that it was she, giving him signs to prove it.
He says he intended to transgress, and he fasted for that intention all his days until he died.
A baraita on Numbers 30:13: a woman who drinks wine unknowingly after her husband annulled her nazirite vow requires forgiveness, so intention alone is punished.
R. Akiva weeps at that verse: if one who meant to eat pork and got a lamb is forgiven, all the more so one who got pork.
R. Akiva's a fortiori argument from Leviticus 5:17 about permitted and forbidden fat, applied to intention and unknowing sin.
Isi ben Yehuda reads the same verse: all who suffer should grieve, since one is punished even for unknowing sin.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav Asi, says a man may be secluded with his sister, mother, or daughter.
Shmuel objects: seclusion is forbidden with all forbidden relations, even with an animal.
The mishna permits a man to be secluded with his mother and daughter, which seems to refute Shmuel.
Shmuel could reply that his view should be read in light of the mishna's own reasoning.
A baraita: seclusion with a sister or mother-in-law is permitted only with witnesses present, which supports Shmuel.
Rather, the matter is a dispute among tannaim.
A baraita: R. Meir and R. Tarfon warn about their daughters and daughters-in-law; a student mocked them, then stumbled even with an animal.
Abaye removes animals from his field, Rav Sheshet moves them behind a fence, and Rav Kahana sits with an animal before him.
Rav Hanan asks Rav Kahana whether he does not hold that one may not be secluded even with an animal.
Rav Kahana replies that it did not enter his mind that an animal was there.
Rava: one may be secluded with two sisters-in-law, two rival wives, a woman and her mother-in-law, or a woman and a girl old enough to know intercourse.
The mishna's ruling: when children have grown up, each sleeps in their own garment, though they may share a bed.
How old must a child be to count as grown for this rule?
Rav Asi: a girl is grown at nine years and a day, and a boy at twelve years and a day.
Others say: a girl at twelve years and a day, and a boy at thirteen years and a day.
Both views are reconciled by Ezekiel 16:7, where breasts are formed and hair grows, marking the onset of puberty.
Rafram bar Pappa, citing Rav Hisda: a man may sleep near his minor daughter only if she is not ashamed to stand naked before him.
What is the reason for that rule?
The inclination has a hold on her, since otherwise she would not be ashamed.
Anecdote: Rav Aha bar Abba visits his son-in-law Rav Hisda and holds his granddaughter on his lap.
Rav Hisda asks whether the Master thinks the girl might already be betrothed.
Rav Aha replies that Rav Hisda himself would then have transgressed Rav's ruling.
Rav's ruling, cited via Rav Yehuda: one may not betroth a minor daughter until she grows up and says whom she wants.
Rav Hisda counters that Rav Aha has transgressed Shmuel's ruling that one may not make use of a woman.
Rav Aha replies that he follows another statement of Shmuel, which he continues to cite past this daf.

82a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the prior permitted actions are acceptable when done for the sake of Heaven, out of familial affection.
Mishna: a bachelor may not teach children, nor may a woman; R. Elazar extends it to any man without a wife; R. Yehuda and the Rabbis differ on herding and sleeping together.
What is the reason a bachelor may not teach children? Perhaps it is due to the children, who might be sexually abused.
A baraita objects that Jews were not suspected of homosexual relations or bestiality, so the children explanation fails.
Rather, the reason is the mothers of the children, who visit the school; a woman is barred for the fathers of the children.
The mishna's R. Elazar: even one without a wife may not teach children.
A dilemma: does R. Elazar refer to a man with no wife at all, or to a man whose wife does not live with him?
A baraita: even a married man whose wife does not live with him may not teach children; the baraita also repeats R. Yehuda and the animal rule.
Mishna: one whose work is mainly with women may not be secluded with women, nor teach his son such a trade.
R. Meir: one should always teach a son a clean and easy trade and pray for success, since wealth and poverty depend on merit.
R. Shimon ben Elazar: animals and birds earn a living without anguish, so humans should too, as they were fallen by sin.
Abba Guryan, citing Abba Gurya: one may not teach a son trades that resemble those of robbers, such as donkey driving or shepherding.
R. Yehuda, in Abba Gurya's name, grades the trades: most donkey drivers are wicked, most sailors pious, and butchers and doctors suspect.
R. Nehorai: he teaches his son only Torah, since its reward lasts in the World-to-Come and it protects a man in youth and sustains him in old age.
The mishna's proof verses: Isaiah 40:31, Psalms 92:15, and Genesis 24:1 and 26:5, showing Abraham kept the whole Torah before it was given.
A baraita lists trades that are to be avoided with women, such as smiths, carders, barbers, launderers and tanners.
Such men may not be appointed king or High Priest.
What is the reason for that disqualification?
Not because the trades are disqualifying, but because they are demeaning, so the men would not be respected in authority.
A baraita lists ten traits said of a bloodletter, including arrogance, stinginess, envy, and suspicion of theft and bloodshed.
Bar Kappara: a person should always teach his son a clean and easy trade.
What is such a profession?
Rav Yehuda begins to answer what profession is meant.

ranges.en: Embroidery needlework is given as an example of a clean and easy trade.
A Tosefta: every trade is needed; one who sees his parents in a fine trade is fortunate, and one whose children are male is fortunate.
R. Meir: one should always teach a son a clean and easy trade and pray for compassion, since wealth comes from God, citing Haggai 2:8.
R. Shimon ben Elazar's Tosefta: animals earn their living without anguish, so humans should too; sin has cost us our livelihood, citing Jeremiah 5:25.
Mishna: R. Nehorai sets aside all trades and teaches his son only Torah.
R. Nehorai's Tosefta: other trades serve a person only in youth, while Torah sustains him in youth and gives hope in old age.
With regard to youth, what does the verse say about the Torah scholar?
Isaiah 40:31: those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles.
With regard to old age, what does the verse say?
Psalms 92:15: they shall still bring forth fruit in old age, full of sap and freshness.
Closing formula: the end of the chapter Ten Genealogies and of the tractate Kiddushin.
